Explain the difference between random selection and simply choosing whoever is easiest to reach, and explain — with an example such as a random sample of 10 pupils that happens to contain mostly Year 7s — why random sampling makes a representative sample likely but does not guarantee it
topics.p: If a school wanted to know what all its pupils think of the lunch menu but only asked children in the lunch queue on pizza day, could {{name}} explain why that might give a misleading answer — and suggest a fairer way to choose who to ask, like picking names at random from the whole school list?

topics.ds: Find the median, lower quartile and upper quartile of a data set using one explicit convention — order the data, find the median, split the data into a lower and an upper half (leaving out the median itself when there is an odd number of values), and take the median of each half as the lower and upper quartile — while recognising that other textbooks, calculators and software may use slightly different conventions; calculate the interquartile range (IQR = upper quartile − lower quartile) and interpret it as the spread of the middle half of the data; and compare what the range and the IQR reveal, including their different sensitivity to extreme values
e: Using the stated convention, find the median (9), lower quartile (6, the median of 3, 5, 6, 7, 8) and upper quartile (14, the median of 11, 12, 14, 15, 21) of the 11 values 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 21, giving IQR = 8; and for the 10 values 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, find median 7.5, lower quartile 4 and upper quartile 10, giving IQR = 6

Interpret an IQR in context (e.g. 'the middle half of the puzzle times lie between 6 and 14 minutes, a spread of 8 minutes') and explain that about half of the values lie between the quartiles, with about a quarter below the lower quartile and about a quarter above the upper quartile

Show that changing the largest value from 21 to 40 increases the range from 18 to 37 but leaves the IQR at 8, and use this to decide — and justify — whether the range or the IQR gives the better summary of spread for a data set with an extreme value or a long tail
topics.p: If {{name}} lines up the times their friends took to finish a puzzle, could they find the middle time and the 'quarter-way' times either side of it — and explain why the gap between those quarter-way times is a better guide to how spread out most of the group is than the gap between the very fastest and slowest?

topics.ds: Plan and conduct a full statistical investigation by posing and refining questions or identifying a problem, planning and carrying out data collection, analysing and interpreting the data, and communicating findings in context
e: Refine a vague question like 'Do kids like sport?' into 'How many hours of organised sport do Year 6 students play each week?'
Plan and carry out the data collection, recording who was asked, how and when
Analyse the data with a suitable display and summary values and present a conclusion with one suggested improvement to the investigation
topics.p: Could {{name}} turn a vague question like 'Do kids like sport?' into a precise one, collect the data, and present a conclusion with a suggestion for doing it better next time?

topics.ds: Distinguish a statistical question — one that anticipates variability in the data collected to answer it, so its answer must account for that variability (even when it is reported as a single summary value such as a mean or median) — from a question answered by a single fixed fact; for a statistical question, identify the population (who or what is being asked about), the attribute being investigated, and the variation expected in the answers
e: Sort questions such as 'How tall am I?', 'How tall are the pupils in my class?', 'How many days are in March?' and 'How many hours of sleep do 12-year-olds usually get?' into statistical and non-statistical, explaining each choice by whether the answers are expected to vary

For a given statistical question, name the population and the attribute being measured, describe the variation they expect (e.g. 'sleep times will differ from person to person, perhaps from 7 to 11 hours'), and explain that a good answer must account for that variability in the data — even a single-number summary such as 'a typical 12-year-old sleeps about 9 hours' stands for many differing values, unlike the one fixed answer to 'How many days are in March?'

Explain why a question about a group can still be non-statistical (e.g. 'How many pupils are in my class?' has one fixed answer), and rewrite a non-statistical question as a statistical one (e.g. 'How long is my journey to school?' becomes 'How long are journeys to school for pupils in my year?')
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} whether 'How many pets does our family have?' and 'How many pets do children in your class have?' are the same kind of question, can they explain that the second one has lots of different answers — so you'd need to collect data from many people — while the first has just one answer?

topics.ds: Before summarising a numerical data set, state its context precisely: report the number of observations (n) by counting the values in a list or the dots on a dot plot, or by adding the frequencies in a table or histogram (not by counting rows or bars); describe the attribute investigated (what was measured or counted, and for whom or what), how it was measured (the instrument or method and the precision or rounding used, e.g. measured with a tape to the nearest cm versus self-reported) and its units; and use these details to give every summary value with its units and to judge what the data can show, for example recognising when values bunch at round numbers because of how they were recorded
e: Report that a frequency table with frequencies 3, 7, 6 and 4 records 20 observations, not 4 (the number of rows) or 7 (the largest frequency)
Write a context statement such as 'hand spans of 28 pupils, measured with a ruler from thumb tip to little-finger tip, to the nearest 0.5 cm'
Explain that a pile-up of self-reported bedtimes at exactly 9:00 and 9:30 may come from people rounding their answers rather than from real bedtimes
topics.p: If {{name}} measured classmates' hand spans for a project, could they say exactly how many people were measured, what was measured, how it was measured (e.g. with a ruler to the nearest half centimetre) and in what units — before giving any averages?

topics.ds: Write a complete summary of a numerical data set in relation to its context, bringing together: the number of observations; the attribute, how it was measured and its units; a measure of centre with a matching measure of variability, each with units, chosen between median with IQR and mean with MAD; the overall pattern and any striking deviations, interpreted in context; and a justification of that choice by the shape of the distribution and the context (e.g. median and IQR for skewed data or data with extreme values, mean and MAD for roughly symmetric data without extreme values)
e: Write a summary of 25 pupils' reaction times that states n, the attribute, how it was measured and the units, a centre and a matching measure of spread with units, and any unusual value
Choose the median and IQR rather than the mean and MAD for a set of journey times with a long tail of slow journeys, and justify the choice by that tail
Rewrite the summary 'the average is 14' as 'the 30 pupils' median journey time is 14 minutes, with the middle half of times between 9 and 22 minutes'
topics.p: If {{name}} timed how long 25 friends took to solve a puzzle, could they write a short report saying how many were timed, how the times were measured, a typical time and how spread out the times were (with units) — and mention any time that stood out?

topics.ds: Use measures of centre and variability calculated from random samples of two populations to make informal comparative inferences about those populations (e.g. whether words in a Grade 7 science book are generally longer than words in a Grade 4 science book): check that each sample was randomly drawn from the population it is meant to describe and is reasonably representative; weigh the difference between the sample centres against the variability within the samples and against how much centres vary from one random sample to another; and state qualified conclusions ('generally', 'on average', 'probably') rather than claiming every member of one population exceeds every member of the other — recognising that a small difference between two samples may be due to chance alone
e: Compare random samples of 20 word lengths from two books (means 6.2 and 4.4 letters, both MADs about 0.9) and conclude that the first book probably uses longer words on average
Explain why surveying volunteers at one school's sports club cannot support a conclusion that all pupils at that school are fitter than pupils at another school
Judge that a 1-point difference between two sample medians is not convincing when repeated random samples from one population give medians that vary by about 3 points
topics.p: If {{name}} randomly picked 20 words from a Year 7 science book and 20 from a Year 4 science book, could they use the averages and spreads to decide whether the older book generally uses longer words — and explain why they'd say 'probably' rather than 'definitely'?

topics.ds: Use data from a random sample to estimate a characteristic of the population, such as a proportion, total count, or mean; present the result as an estimate rather than an exact population measurement; state the assumptions the inference relies on (the sample was randomly drawn from the population being described and is reasonably representative) and explain how the conclusion is limited or invalid when those assumptions fail
e: Use a sample proportion to estimate a population count — e.g. 18 of a random sample of 60 pupils walk to school, so estimate about 270 of the school's 900 pupils walk — and state the answer as an approximate estimate rather than an exact count

Use the mean of a random sample (e.g. the mean weekly reading time of 25 randomly chosen pupils) to estimate the population mean, and explain why the true population mean is likely to be close to, but probably not exactly equal to, the sample mean

State the assumptions behind an estimate and explain why it becomes unreliable or invalid when they fail — e.g. using a sample of only Year 7 pupils to estimate for the whole school, or using a volunteer online poll — and identify what can and cannot be concluded from the data
topics.p: If {{name}} learns that 12 out of 40 randomly chosen pupils at their school play an instrument, could they estimate how many of the school's 600 pupils play one — and explain why that number is a sensible estimate rather than an exact count?

topics.n: How far apart two groups are
topics.ds: Compare two numerical distributions with similar variability shown on a shared scale (e.g. dot plots) in two distinct ways: (1) judge their actual visual overlap directly from the displays — how much of each group's data lies among the other group's values; and (2) separately, find the difference between their centres and express it as a multiple of a clearly named measure of variability of either group, using matching measures (difference in means ÷ MAD, or difference in medians ÷ IQR), interpreting a larger multiple as centres that are further apart relative to the typical spread. Recognise that the same difference in centres means more when the variability is small, and that for similarly shaped, roughly symmetric, single-peaked distributions a larger multiple usually goes with less overlap — but that the ratio alone does not determine overlap: skew, clusters, gaps or outliers can make the visible overlap greater or smaller than the ratio suggests, so overlap is always checked on the display; and this simple ratio is only appropriate when the two variabilities are similar
e: Describe two dot plots of team heights drawn on the same scale as overlapping a lot, a little, or hardly at all, pointing to the range of heights the two teams share
Express a 10 cm difference in mean heights as about 2 MADs when each team's MAD is about 5 cm, naming MAD as the measure used
Use two dot plots whose means are 2 MADs apart, one with a long tail towards the other group, to explain why they overlap more than the 2-MAD gap alone would suggest
topics.p: If the basketball team's average height is 10 cm more than the football team's, and players on each team are typically about 5 cm from their own team's average, could {{name}} explain that the gap is about twice the usual spread — and then look at a chart of both teams' heights to check how much they actually overlap, rather than guessing it from that number?

topics.ds: Generate or compare several random samples of the same size from the same population (by drawing physically — returning and remixing the items before each new sample — from a list, or by simulation), observe that their estimates differ by chance, and use the spread of those estimates to judge how uncertain a single estimate or prediction is — distinguishing chance variation between random samples from the consistent error caused by a biased sampling method, and distinguishing variation between sample estimates from the variation among individual observations within a sample
e: Take or are given several random samples of the same size from one population (e.g. draw 20 counters from a bag without looking, record them, return all 20 and mix thoroughly, then draw the next 20 — five times; or five random samples of 20 names from a list), calculate each sample's proportion or mean, and show that the estimates differ

Explain that equal-sized random samples give different estimates because of chance in which individuals are selected, so a different result does not mean a sample was wrong — and contrast this with a biased method whose estimates are consistently too high or too low

Use the spread of several sample estimates (e.g. 'the estimates ranged from 25% to 40%') to say how far off a single estimate might be, and explain why one sample cannot make a prediction certain and why larger samples tend to give estimates that vary less

Distinguish the variation among individual observations within one sample (e.g. pupils' sleep times in one sample range from 6 to 11 hours) from the variation between sample estimates (e.g. the means of five samples of 20 pupils range from 8.6 to 9.3 hours), and explain why sample means usually vary much less than the individual values they are calculated from
topics.p: If {{name}}'s class takes turns drawing 20 sweets from the same big jar without looking — counting the red ones, then putting all 20 back and giving the jar a good shake before the next person draws — could {{name}} explain why each person gets a slightly different number of reds, and use the spread of everyone's results to say how sure they can be about the fraction of red sweets in the whole jar?

topics.ds: Plot bivariate data on a scatter graph with correctly labelled axes and appropriate scales; describe the correlation (positive, negative, none) and draw an estimated line of best fit where appropriate
e: Plot 10 data points on a scatter graph with correct axis labels and a consistent scale
Draw a line of best fit by eye, ensuring roughly equal numbers of points above and below
Use the line of best fit to estimate a y-value for a given x-value within the data range
topics.p: If {{name}} has data comparing hours of sleep and test scores for 10 students, can they plot the points on a scatter graph, draw a line of best fit, and use it to predict a score for someone who slept 7 hours?

topics.ds: Describe simple mathematical relationships between two variables using scatter graphs, identify positive, negative, or no correlation, and use a line of best fit to make predictions
e: Plot bivariate data on a scatter graph and describe the type of correlation observed
Draw a line of best fit by eye and use it to estimate a value within the data range
Explain what positive, negative, and no correlation mean in the context of real data (e.g., temperature vs. ice-cream sales)
topics.p: If {{name}} plotted a scatter graph — say, comparing hours of revision and test scores — could they draw a line of best fit, describe the pattern, and use it to make a prediction?

topics.ds: Recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
e: Fold a shape into four equal parts and identify each as 'a quarter'
Find a quarter of 12 objects by sharing into 4 equal groups
Identify whether a shape has been divided into quarters (four equal parts)
topics.p: If you fold a square piece of paper into four equal parts, can {{name}} tell you that each part is a quarter — and point to just one quarter?

topics.ds: Recognise, find, and name a half as one of two equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
e: Fold a shape into two equal parts and identify each as 'a half'
Find half of 8 objects by sharing into 2 equal groups
Identify whether a shape has been divided into halves or not (equal vs unequal parts)
topics.p: If {{name}} is helping share a sandwich equally between two people, can they cut it so both pieces are the same size — and tell you each piece is called a half?

topics.n: Decomposing a shape into more equal shares
topics.ds: Understand that decomposing a shape into more equal shares creates smaller shares
e: Explain that a quarter of a pizza is smaller than a half of the same pizza
Demonstrate that fourths are smaller pieces than halves
Compare the size of halves and quarters of the same shape
topics.p: If a pizza is shared between 2 people and then the same pizza is shared between 8 people, can {{name}} explain why each slice is smaller when more people share it?

topics.ds: Read, write, and use fraction notation correctly — fraction, numerator, denominator, unit fraction, non-unit fraction, proper fraction, improper fraction, mixed number, equivalent fraction, simplest form — and understand what each term describes, including the roles of the numerator and denominator in expressing parts of a whole
e: Point to and name the numerator and denominator in any given fraction and explain what each tells you
Correctly classify fractions as unit, proper, improper, or mixed number with an example of each
Explain in own words why 2/4 and 1/2 are equivalent fractions
topics.p: If {{name}} saw the fraction 3/4 written down, could they point to the numerator and the denominator — and explain what each number actually means?

topics.ds: Recognise, find, name, and write fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, and 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity
e: Find 1/3 of 12 objects by sharing into 3 equal groups
Shade 3/4 of a rectangle that has been divided into 4 equal parts
Identify 1/4 of a length on a number line or ruler
topics.p: If you put 12 grapes on the table, can {{name}} count out a quarter of them — and then show you what three-quarters of the grapes looks like?

topics.ds: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares and describe them using the words halves, fourths, and quarters
e: Divide a circle into two equal halves
Divide a rectangle into four equal quarters
Describe the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'
topics.p: If you give {{name}} a round pizza or a rectangular chocolate bar, can they divide it into four equal pieces and tell you each piece is called a quarter or a fourth?

topics.ds: Write simple fractions (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
e: Write 1/2 of 10 = 5
Explain that 2/4 is the same as 1/2 using a diagram
Calculate simple unit fractions of quantities and write the result
topics.p: If {{name}} has 6 strawberries and eats half of them, can they write that as "1/2 of 6 = 3" — and explain why 2/4 and 1/2 are the same amount?

topics.ds: Compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominator
e: Order 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest
Explain that a larger denominator means smaller unit fractions
Compare 2/5 and 4/5 and explain that 4/5 is larger because it has more fifths
topics.p: If {{name}} has eaten 3/8 of a cake and a friend has eaten 5/8 of the same cake, can they tell you who has eaten more — and put those fractions in order from smallest to biggest?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving counting in tenths, fractions of quantities, equivalence, fraction addition/subtraction, and fraction comparison
e: Solve a word problem requiring finding a fraction of a quantity
Solve a problem that requires comparing or ordering fractions
Choose and apply appropriate fraction knowledge to a multi-step problem
topics.p: If a bag of 20 sweets is shared equally among 5 friends, can {{name}} work out what fraction each person gets — and how many sweets that is?

topics.ds: Recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators
e: Show that 1/2 = 2/4 using a diagram of equal parts
Use a fraction wall or bar model to find equivalent fractions
Explain why two fractions are equivalent by comparing the shaded areas
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a bar divided into 4 equal parts with 2 shaded, can they tell you that's the same as 1/2 — and draw a different bar showing the same amount another way?

topics.ds: Recognise and use fractions as numbers: place unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators on a number line
e: Place 1/2, 1/4, 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 1
Identify that 1/3 lies between 0 and 1/2 on the number line
Understand that a fraction is a single number, not just 'part of a shape'
topics.p: If you draw a number line from 0 to 1, can {{name}} mark where 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 should go — without any extra help?

topics.ds: Connect halves, quarters and eighths through repeated halving of shapes, objects and collections, and represent eighths of shapes and objects
e: Fold a paper strip in half, then half again, then half again, and label the halves, quarters and eighths
Show that 2 eighths of a pizza is the same amount as 1 quarter
Shade one-eighth of a square and one-eighth of a circle and explain how you know
topics.p: If {{name}} keeps cutting a sandwich in half, then in half again, and again, can they name the pieces as halves, quarters and then eighths?

topics.ds: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator within one whole (e.g. 5/7 + 1/7 = 6/7)
e: Calculate 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5
Calculate 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8
Explain that when denominators are the same, you add/subtract the numerators
topics.p: If a recipe calls for 2/8 of a cup of milk and then another 3/8 of a cup, can {{name}} work out the total without a calculator?

topics.ds: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares; describe shares as halves, thirds, and fourths; recognise that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape
e: Partition a circle into 3 equal parts and label each 'a third'
Partition a rectangle into 4 equal shares in more than one way
Explain that two different-looking shares can still be equal in size
topics.p: If you cut a rectangle into thirds in two different ways (three strips vs three squares), can {{name}} recognise that both give equal thirds — even though the pieces look different?

topics.ds: Count up and down in tenths; recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into 10 equal parts and from dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10
e: Count: one tenth, two tenths, three tenths … up to ten tenths (one whole)
Show that dividing a shape into 10 equal parts gives tenths
Explain that 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10
topics.p: If {{name}} splits a chocolate bar with 10 equal pieces, can they tell you each piece is one tenth — and count up from 1/10 to 10/10 in order?

topics.ds: Recognise, find, and write fractions of a discrete set of objects: unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators
e: Find 1/4 of 12 objects by dividing into 4 equal groups
Find 3/4 of 12 objects
Write the fraction of a set that is shaded or selected
topics.p: If there are 15 books on a shelf, can {{name}} work out how many two-thirds of them is — and check by grouping the books into three equal piles?

topics.ds: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator, including results greater than one whole (e.g. 5/8 + 6/8 = 11/8)
e: Calculate 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 and explain it equals 1 2/5
Subtract 2/6 from 5/6
Solve addition problems where the sum exceeds the whole: 7/8 + 3/8
topics.p: If a recipe uses 5/8 of a bag of flour and then another 6/8, can {{name}} work out the total and explain what the answer means as a mixed number?

topics.ds: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about size; record comparisons with >, =, or < symbols
e: Compare 3/8 and 3/4: same numerator, larger denominator means smaller pieces so 3/8 < 3/4
Compare 5/6 and 2/6: same denominator so 5/6 > 2/6
Justify a comparison using a visual model and explain why both fractions must refer to the same whole
topics.p: If {{name}} sees 3/5 and 3/8, can they tell you which is bigger just by thinking about the size of each piece — without needing to draw it out?

topics.n: Decimal equivalents of tenths and hundredths
topics.ds: Recognise and write decimal equivalents of any number of tenths or hundredths (e.g. 3/10 = 0.3, 27/100 = 0.27)
e: Write 7/10 as 0.7 and vice versa
Convert 45/100 to 0.45
Place 0.3 and 3/10 at the same point on a number line
topics.p: If {{name}} sees 7/10 on a price label, can they rewrite it as a decimal — and do the same thing for 43/100?

topics.ds: Read, write, and use decimal and percentage notation correctly — decimal, decimal point, tenths, hundredths, thousandths, percentage, per cent, % symbol, convert, terminating decimal — and understand the relationships between fractions, decimals, and percentages as three ways of expressing the same value
e: Read and write decimal numbers correctly, identifying the value of each digit (ones, tenths, hundredths)
Use the % symbol correctly and explain that per cent means 'out of 100'
Convert between simple fractions, decimals, and percentages (e.g. 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%) and explain why they are equal
topics.p: If {{name}} saw '0.5' and '50%' written down, could they explain that they both mean the same amount — and write them as a fraction too?

topics.ds: Round decimals with one decimal place to the nearest whole number
e: Round 3.7 to 4 and 3.2 to 3
Place 6.5 on a number line between 6 and 7 and decide it rounds to 7
Round a set of one-decimal-place numbers and explain the rounding rule
topics.p: If {{name}} measures something as 3.7 m, can they tell you whether that rounds to 3 m or 4 m — and explain why?

topics.ds: Compare numbers with the same number of decimal places up to two decimal places
e: Order 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 from smallest to largest
Compare 3.72 and 3.27 using place-value reasoning
Place three two-decimal-place numbers on a number line in order
topics.p: If {{name}} is comparing two prices — £4.75 and £4.57 — can they tell you which is more expensive without using a calculator?

topics.ds: Solve simple measure and money problems involving fractions and decimals to two decimal places
e: Calculate 1/4 of £3.20
A rope is 2.5 m long; how much is left after cutting 0.75 m?
Find 3/10 of 1 kg and express the answer in grams and as a decimal of a kg
topics.p: If a bottle holds 1.5 litres and {{name}} drinks 0.75 litres, can they work out how much is left — and write it as both a decimal and a fraction?

topics.ds: Find the effect of dividing a one- or two-digit number by 10 and 100, identifying the value of the digits as ones, tenths, and hundredths
e: Calculate 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 and identify 3 as ones and 7 as tenths
Calculate 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 and identify 4 as hundredths
Explain that dividing by 10 shifts each digit one place to the right
topics.p: If {{name}} starts with the number 48 and divides it by 10, can they tell you the answer — and explain what happened to each digit's place value?

topics.ds: Generate simple equivalent fractions and explain why they are equivalent using visual fraction models
e: Given 1/3, generate 2/6 as equivalent and show with area model
Simplify 4/8 to 1/2 and justify with a fraction strip
Complete equivalence chains: 1/4 = ?/8 = ?/12
topics.p: If {{name}} is shown a fraction bar split into 3 parts with 1 shaded (= 1/3), can they draw an equivalent bar with 6 parts that shows exactly the same amount shaded?

topics.n: Equivalent fractions on a number line
topics.ds: Understand two fractions as equivalent if they are the same size or the same point on a number line; recognise and show families of common equivalent fractions using diagrams
e: Use fraction strips to show 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6
Verify on a number line that 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point
Identify at least three fractions equivalent to 1/2 using diagrams
topics.p: If {{name}} sees that 2/4 and 1/2 land on the exact same point on a number line, can they explain in their own words why those two fractions are equal?

topics.ds: Recognise and write decimal equivalents of 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4
e: Match fractions to decimals in a sorting activity
Explain why 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25 using a hundredths grid
topics.p: If a recipe calls for 3/4 of a cup of flour, can {{name}} tell you what that is as a decimal — without looking it up?

topics.ds: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas and express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole
e: Partition a rectangle into 6 equal-area parts and label each 1/6
Show two different ways to partition a square into 4 equal parts
Given a pre-partitioned shape, write the unit fraction for one part
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to fold a square piece of paper into 8 equal parts, can they tell you what fraction of the whole square each part represents?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving increasingly harder fractions to calculate quantities, including non-unit fractions where the answer is a whole number
e: Find 3/5 of 20
Calculate 2/3 of 18 and explain the two-step process (divide then multiply)
Solve: A bag has 24 sweets, 3/8 are red — how many red sweets?
topics.p: If 3/4 of a class of 28 pupils brought their homework in, can {{name}} work out exactly how many pupils that is?

topics.ds: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a/b as a parts of size 1/b
e: Given a shape divided into 5 equal parts, identify one shaded part as 1/5
Explain that 3/4 means 3 parts each of size 1/4
Draw a model showing 2/6 as 2 pieces of a whole cut into 6
topics.p: If you cut a pizza into 6 equal slices, can {{name}} explain what 1/6 means — and then work out what 4/6 of the pizza looks like?

topics.ds: Express whole numbers as fractions (e.g. 3 = 3/1) and recognise fractions equivalent to whole numbers (e.g. 4/4 = 1, 6/1 = 6)
e: Write 5 as 5/1 and explain why
Locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point on a number line
Identify which fractions from a list equal a whole number: 6/3, 8/4, 5/2
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to write the number 3 as a fraction, can they write 3/1 — and also tell you what fraction equals exactly 1 whole, like 4/4 or 5/5?

topics.ds: Represent fractions on a number line: partition the interval 0 to 1 into b equal parts to locate 1/b, then mark off a lengths of 1/b from 0 to locate a/b
e: Partition a 0-to-1 number line into 4 equal parts and mark 1/4
Explain that each part on the line has size 1/b
Locate 1/3 and 1/6 on separate number lines
Locate 3/4 on a number line by counting three 1/4-jumps from 0
Place 5/6 on a number line and explain the process
Identify a fraction shown by a point on a pre-partitioned number line
topics.p: If {{name}} draws a number line from 0 to 1 split into 5 equal parts, can they label where 2/5 and 4/5 go — and explain how they worked it out?

topics.ds: Count up and down in hundredths; recognise that hundredths arise when dividing an object by 100 or dividing tenths by 10
e: Count from 3/100 to 12/100 in hundredths
Explain that 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100
Place several hundredths on a number line between 0 and 1/10
topics.p: If {{name}} has £1 and spends 37p, can they say that 37p is 37/100 of a pound — and count up in hundredths from 0/100 to 100/100?

topics.ds: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, including by converting to improper fractions or using properties of operations
e: Calculate 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 and express as a mixed number
Subtract 3 1/4 from 5 3/4
Solve 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 by regrouping the whole number
topics.p: If a recipe calls for 1 and 2/5 cups of oats and another batch needs 2 and 3/5 cups, can {{name}} add them together to get the total — including converting when the fifths add up past a whole?

topics.ds: Add and subtract fractions with denominators that are multiples of the same number by finding a common denominator
e: Calculate 1/3 + 1/6 by converting to sixths: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2
Calculate 3/4 − 1/8 by converting to eighths
Add 2/5 + 3/10 and simplify the answer
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to add 1/3 and 1/6, can they find a common denominator and work out the total — showing their working?

topics.ds: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with like denominators, using visual models and equations
e: A jug contains 3/4 litre of juice; 2/4 litre is poured out — how much remains?
Two pieces of ribbon are 2 3/8 and 1 5/8 inches — what is their total length?
Draw a fraction model to represent and solve a fraction word problem
topics.p: If {{name}} reads that one section of a nature trail is 3/8 km and another is 5/8 km, can they work out the total distance without a calculator?

topics.ds: Compare two decimals to hundredths (or up to three decimal places) by reasoning about size using place-value understanding; record with >, =, <
e: Compare 0.45 and 0.405 and explain which is greater
Order 3.142, 3.14, 3.2 from smallest to largest
Justify that 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700 using place-value reasoning
topics.p: If {{name}} compares 0.45 and 0.54, can they use place value to explain which is bigger — without reaching for a calculator?

topics.ds: Compare and order fractions with different numerators and denominators by creating common denominators/numerators or comparing to a benchmark such as 1/2; justify conclusions with visual models
e: Compare 3/8 and 5/12 by finding a common denominator of 24
Order 2/3, 3/5, and 7/10 from smallest to largest
Use the benchmark 1/2 to decide that 5/8 > 3/7
topics.p: If {{name}} has eaten 2/3 of their lunch and a friend has eaten 3/4 of theirs, can they work out who's eaten more — by finding a common way to compare the fractions?

topics.ds: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100 and use this to add fractions with denominators 10 and 100 (e.g. 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100)
e: Rewrite 7/10 as 70/100
Explain why 5/10 = 50/100 using a hundredths grid
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to add 3/10 and 17/100, can they rewrite 3/10 as hundredths first — and then add the two fractions together?

topics.ds: Round decimals with two decimal places to the nearest whole number and to one decimal place
e: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number (3) and to 1 d.p. (3.5)
Round 12.95 to 1 d.p. (13.0) and explain the boundary case
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole number
topics.p: If {{name}} measures a length as 4.67 m, can they round it to the nearest whole metre — and also to the nearest tenth of a metre?

topics.ds: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100; read and write decimal numbers as fractions (e.g. 0.62 = 62/100, 0.71 = 71/100)
e: Rewrite 0.62 as 62/100
Write 3/10 as 0.3 and locate on a number line
Read 0.07 and express as 7/100
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a price tag showing £0.65, can they rewrite it as a fraction — and go the other way, turning 47/100 into a decimal?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving numbers with up to three decimal places
e: Calculate the total of three measurements: 1.234 m + 0.567 m + 2.199 m
A bottle holds 1.5 litres; 0.375 l is poured out — how much remains?
Find two numbers with 3 d.p. that add to make 1
topics.p: If {{name}} is filling a tank that holds 5.000 litres and has poured in 2.375 litres, can they work out how much more is needed to fill it?

topics.ds: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to (n×a)/(n×b) using visual models; use this principle to recognise and generate equivalent fractions, including tenths and hundredths
e: Use a fraction strip to show 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9
Explain that multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number gives an equivalent fraction because the size of the whole is unchanged
Generate three fractions equivalent to 3/5 and verify with diagrams
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to make 2/3 look different without changing its value, can they multiply the top and bottom by the same number and explain why the fraction stays the same?

topics.ds: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts; decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way
e: Write two different decompositions of 5/6
Use a visual model to justify a decomposition of 2 1/8 into whole-number and fraction parts
topics.p: If {{name}} has 7/8 of a chocolate bar and gives away 3/8, can they work out what fraction is left — and then show two different ways to split 7/8 into two parts?

topics.ds: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual models and equations
e: Each person eats 3/8 of a pizza and there are 5 people — how many pizzas are needed?
A ribbon is cut into pieces of 2/3 metre; how long are 4 pieces altogether?
Between what two whole numbers does 6 × 3/4 lie?
topics.p: If each section of a garden uses 3/4 of a bag of compost and there are 4 sections, can {{name}} work out how many bags are needed in total?

topics.ds: Recognise mixed numbers and improper fractions; convert from one form to the other (e.g. 2/5 + 4/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5)
e: Convert 11/4 to 2 3/4
Convert 3 2/5 to 17/5
Write 6/5 + 4/5 = 10/5 = 2 as both improper fraction and whole number
topics.p: If {{name}} sees the fraction 9/4, can they convert it to a mixed number — and then turn 2 and 3/5 back into an improper fraction?

topics.ds: Understand a/b as a multiple of 1/b; multiply proper fractions and mixed numbers by whole numbers, supported by visual models (e.g. 3 × 2/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5)
e: Calculate 4 × 3/8 using repeated addition or the rule n × a/b = (n×a)/b
Multiply 2 1/3 × 3 and express as a mixed number
Use a visual model to show why 5 × 1/4 = 5/4
topics.p: If a recipe uses 2/3 of a cup of butter and {{name}} wants to make it three times over, can they work out how much butter they need in total?

topics.ds: Solve problems requiring knowledge of percentage and decimal equivalents of 1/2, 1/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5 and fractions with denominators that are multiples of 10 or 25
e: State that 1/5 = 20% = 0.2 and use this to find 20% of 60
Convert 3/4 to 75% and to 0.75
A shop offers 25% off a £40 item — what is the sale price?
topics.p: If {{name}} knows that 1/4 = 25% = 0.25, can they use that to work out 25% of £80 — and also find 4/5 of 60 sweets?

topics.ds: Recognise and use thousandths; relate them to tenths, hundredths, and their decimal equivalents (e.g. 1/1000 = 0.001, 35/1000 = 0.035)
e: Explain that 1 tenth = 100 thousandths
Place 0.345 on a number line between 0.34 and 0.35
topics.p: If {{name}} sees the decimal 0.003, can they write it as a fraction and tell you roughly where it sits on a number line between 0 and 0.01?

topics.ds: Understand a fraction a/b with a > 1 as a sum of fractions 1/b (e.g. 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5)
e: Express 5/8 as a sum of five copies of 1/8
Show on a number line how 4/3 is built by iterating 1/3 four times
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to show 4/5 as a sum of smaller equal fractions, can they write it out as 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5?

topics.ds: Understand the per cent symbol (%); know that per cent means ‘number of parts per hundred’; write percentages as a fraction with denominator 100 and as a decimal
e: Write 35% as 35/100 and as 0.35
Shade 40% of a 10×10 grid and write the fraction 40/100
Explain that 100% means the whole, 50% means half
topics.p: If a shop advertises 50% off, can {{name}} explain that this means half price — and write 50% as both a fraction and a decimal?

topics.ds: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator
e: Compute 2/3 + 5/4 by converting to twelfths: 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12
Subtract 1 3/5 from 3 1/4 using a common denominator
Explain the strategy of finding a common denominator and verify using a visual model
topics.p: If a recipe uses 2/3 of a cup of one ingredient and 3/4 of another, can {{name}} add those fractions together — even though the denominators are different?

topics.ds: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling with unit-fraction squares; show that the area equals the product of the side lengths
e: Tile a 2/3 × 3/4 rectangle with 1/12 squares and count to find area = 6/12 = 1/2
Explain why the number of unit-fraction tiles equals the product of the two fractions
Calculate the area of a rectangle with sides 1 1/2 and 2/3 using fraction multiplication
topics.p: If a piece of fabric is 2/3 m long and 3/4 m wide, can {{name}} work out its area — and explain how tiling it with tiny fraction-squares shows the same answer as multiplying?

topics.ds: Compare and order fractions including fractions greater than 1, by converting to common denominators or using benchmarks
e: Order 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, and 11/12 from smallest to largest
Compare 7/5 and 4/3 using common denominators
Place improper fractions and mixed numbers on a number line in correct order
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to sort 5/3, 7/4, and 2/1 in order from smallest to biggest, can they convert them to a common denominator and order them correctly?

topics.ds: Associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents for simple fractions (e.g. 3/8 = 0.375); recall and use equivalences between simple fractions, decimals, and percentages in different contexts
e: Convert 3/8 to 0.375 by dividing 3 ÷ 8
State that 1/5 = 0.2 = 20% from memory
Use fraction–decimal–percentage equivalences to compare 30%, 1/3, and 0.35 and put them in order
topics.p: If {{name}} sees 3/8 written on a worksheet, can they convert it to a decimal — and also say roughly what percentage that is?

topics.ds: Interpret and compute division of a whole number by a unit fraction (e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20); use visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division to explain why the quotient is larger than the dividend
e: Compute 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 and explain: 'How many fifths fit in 4 wholes?'
Create a story context for 6 ÷ (1/4) and solve it
Verify 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 by showing 20 × (1/5) = 4
topics.p: If you have 4 metres of ribbon and each bow needs 1/5 of a metre, can {{name}} work out how many bows you can make — and explain why the answer is bigger than 4?

topics.ds: Interpret and compute division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12); use visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division to explain the result
e: Compute (1/3) ÷ 4 = 1/12 and explain using a visual model of splitting 1/3 into 4 equal parts
Create a story context for (1/6) ÷ 3 and solve it
topics.p: If {{name}} has 1/3 of a bag of rice and splits it into 4 equal portions, can they work out what fraction of the whole bag each portion is — and explain why the answer is smaller than 1/3?

topics.n: Dividing unit fractions and whole numbers
topics.ds: Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions, using visual models and equations
e: Solve: '3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally — how much each?' (1/6 lb)
Solve: 'How many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups of raisins?' (6 servings)
Create a story context for a given unit-fraction division expression
topics.p: If {{name}} has half a pizza to share equally among 3 people, can they work out what fraction of the whole pizza each person gets — and explain the steps they took?

topics.ds: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b); solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to fractional or mixed-number answers
e: Explain that 3/4 means 3 ÷ 4 and verify by showing 3/4 × 4 = 3
Solve: '9 people share a 50-pound sack equally — how many pounds each?' and express the answer as 5 5/9
Use a visual model to show that sharing 3 wholes among 4 people gives each person 3/4
topics.p: If {{name}} shares 3 pizzas equally among 4 friends, can they work out what fraction each person gets — and explain why 3 ÷ 4 gives the same answer as 3/4?

topics.ds: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with unlike denominators, using visual models and benchmark fractions to estimate and assess reasonableness
e: Solve: 'Tara ate 2/5 of a pizza and Sam ate 1/3. How much did they eat together?'
Recognise that 2/5 + 1/2 ≠ 3/7 because 3/7 < 1/2 but the sum should exceed 1/2
Estimate a fraction sum using benchmarks (0, 1/2, 1) before computing exactly
topics.p: If {{name}} walks 1 and 1/2 miles to school and 3/4 of a mile to a friend's house, can they work out the total distance — and check whether their answer makes sense?

topics.ds: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing): compare the size of a product to a factor based on the size of the other factor without computing; explain the effect of multiplying by fractions greater than, equal to, or less than 1
e: Predict without calculating whether 3/4 × 7 is greater or less than 7
Explain why multiplying by 5/3 makes a number larger and multiplying by 2/5 makes it smaller
Relate multiplying a/b by n/n = 1 to the principle of fraction equivalence
topics.p: If {{name}} multiplies 20 by 1/4, can they predict whether the answer will be bigger or smaller than 20 — and explain why, before doing the calculation?

topics.ds: Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction, including proper fractions by proper fractions; interpret (a/b) × q as a parts of q partitioned into b equal parts; write answers in simplest form
e: Compute (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15 and show with an area model
Use a visual model to demonstrate (2/3) × 4 = 8/3 = 2 2/3
Simplify the product 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2
topics.p: If a recipe uses 2/3 of a bag of flour and {{name}} only wants to make 3/4 of the recipe, can they multiply those fractions to find out how much flour they need?

topics.ds: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, using visual fraction models or equations
e: Solve: 'A recipe needs 2 1/3 cups of flour; you want to make 1 1/2 batches. How much flour?'
Draw a fraction model to represent and solve a multiplication word problem
Check the reasonableness of a fraction product in context using estimation
topics.p: If a recipe makes 12 biscuits using 1 and 1/2 cups of sugar, and {{name}} wants to make only 2/3 of the recipe, can they work out how much sugar they need?

topics.ds: Use common factors to simplify fractions to their simplest form; use common multiples to express fractions with a common denominator
e: Simplify 18/24 to 3/4 by identifying the HCF of 18 and 24
Express 2/3 and 5/8 with a common denominator of 24
Explain why dividing numerator and denominator by a common factor produces an equivalent fraction
topics.p: If {{name}} has the fraction 12/16, can they simplify it to its lowest terms — and explain what they divided the top and bottom by?

topics.ds: Work interchangeably with terminating decimals and their corresponding fractions (such as 3.5 and 7/2 or 0.375 and 3/8); convert fluently between the two forms
e: Convert any terminating decimal to a fraction in simplest form
Convert any fraction with a denominator whose prime factors are only 2 and 5 to a terminating decimal
Explain why some fractions produce terminating decimals and others do not
topics.p: If {{name}} sees 0.375 on a calculator display, can they convert it to a fraction in its simplest form — without using the calculator?

topics.ds: Divide a fraction by a fraction using the 'keep-change-flip' method and visual models; interpret and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions
e: Divide a fraction by a fraction using the reciprocal method
Use visual fraction models to represent and explain fraction division
Create story contexts for fraction division problems and solve them
topics.p: If {{name}} has 3/4 of a litre of juice and each glass holds 3/8 of a litre, can they work out how many glasses they can fill — using fraction division?

topics.ds: Use the four operations with formal written methods applied to integers, decimals, proper and improper fractions, and mixed numbers, all both positive and negative
e: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide with positive and negative integers
Apply formal written methods to calculations with decimals of any size
Perform all four operations with proper fractions, improper fractions, and mixed numbers
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to work out −1/2 + 3/4 − 1 and 1/4 as part of a longer problem, can they do it using written methods — showing each step clearly?

topics.ds: Interpret fractions and percentages as operators — find a fraction or percentage of an amount by multiplying, understanding that 'of' means multiply (e.g., 3/4 of 200 = 3/4 × 200 = 150)
e: Calculate a fraction of a given amount by multiplying
Calculate a percentage of a given amount by converting to a decimal and multiplying
Use the operator interpretation to solve multi-step problems involving discounts, taxes, and portions
topics.p: If a £120 jacket is reduced by 35%, can {{name}} work out the sale price — by first calculating 35% of £120 and then subtracting?

topics.ds: Recognise and name common 2-D shapes (circles, triangles, rectangles including squares)
e: Name a triangle, circle, rectangle, and square when shown them
Identify a shape correctly regardless of its size or orientation
Pick out all the triangles from a mixed set of shapes
topics.p: Can {{name}} point to shapes around the house — like a clock, a window, or a pizza — and correctly name whether each is a circle, triangle, rectangle, or square?

topics.ds: Recognise and name common 3-D shapes (cubes, cuboids, pyramids, spheres, cylinders, cones)
e: Name a cube, sphere, cylinder, and cone when shown them
Identify 3-D shapes in the environment (e.g. a tin is a cylinder)
Recognise a cuboid and a pyramid among a set of solid shapes
topics.p: Can {{name}} name common 3-D shapes they find around them — like a tin of beans (cylinder), a ball (sphere), or a dice (cube)?

topics.ds: Describe the position of objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, next to
e: Describe a toy as being 'on top of' the table
Follow instructions like 'put the cube behind the box'
Use 'left' and 'right' in simple contexts
topics.p: Can {{name}} give directions to find something around the house using words like "above," "below," "beside," "in front of," or "behind"?

topics.ds: Analyse and compare 2-D and 3-D shapes using informal language to describe sides, vertices, and other attributes
e: Count the sides and corners of a shape
Compare a triangle and a rectangle by number of sides
Describe a cube as having 'square faces' and 'corners'
topics.p: Can {{name}} describe what makes two shapes different — for example, explaining that a triangle has 3 corners and 3 sides while a square has 4 of each?

topics.ds: Model shapes by building from components (e.g. sticks and clay balls) and by drawing
e: Build a triangle from three sticks and three clay balls
Draw a recognisable rectangle
Construct a cube from straws and connectors
topics.p: Can {{name}} build or draw a shape they've been shown — for example, making a cube from folded paper or copying a triangle onto dot paper?

topics.ds: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes (e.g. two triangles make a rectangle)
e: Join two triangles to make a rectangle or larger triangle
Use pattern blocks to fill a hexagon outline
Create a picture or design by combining basic shapes
topics.p: Can {{name}} fit smaller shapes together to make bigger ones — like combining two triangles to make a rectangle?

topics.ds: Distinguish two-dimensional (flat) shapes from three-dimensional (solid) shapes
e: Sort shapes into 'flat' and 'solid' groups
Explain that a circle is flat but a sphere is solid
Identify whether a given shape is 2-D or 3-D
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand the difference between a flat shape like a square and a solid shape like a cube — and can they sort everyday objects into flat or solid?

topics.ds: Order and arrange combinations of mathematical objects in patterns and sequences
e: Continue a repeating pattern of shapes or colours
Describe the rule for a given sequence of objects
Create own patterns and sequences using mathematical objects
topics.p: Can {{name}} spot a repeating pattern made of shapes or objects and continue it, or create their own repeating pattern?

topics.ds: Describe movement and direction, including whole, half, quarter, and three-quarter turns
e: Follow instructions to move forward, backward, turn left/right
Demonstrate a whole turn, half turn, and quarter turn with their body
Describe a route using directional language
topics.p: If {{name}} is playing a game where they have to turn left or right, do they understand what a quarter turn, half turn, and full turn mean?

topics.ds: Identify 2-D shapes on the surface of 3-D shapes (e.g. a circle on a cylinder, a triangle on a pyramid)
e: Point out a circular face on a cylinder or cone
Identify triangular faces on a pyramid
Recognise that the faces of 3-D shapes are 2-D shapes
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at a 3-D shape and name the 2-D shapes on its faces — for example, saying a cylinder has circles on the ends and a rectangle wrapped round the side?

topics.ds: Identify and describe properties of 2-D shapes including the number of sides and line symmetry in a vertical line
e: Count the number of sides of a given 2-D shape
Identify whether a 2-D shape has a vertical line of symmetry
Use properties (number of sides, symmetry) to describe and distinguish between shapes
topics.p: Can {{name}} count the sides of a shape and say whether it has a line of symmetry — for example, knowing that a rectangle is symmetrical but a scalene triangle is not?

topics.ds: Compose three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, right circular cylinders) and create composite shapes; build new shapes from component shapes
e: Stack cubes and prisms to build towers or structures
Combine 3-D shapes to make a new solid (e.g. cone on top of cylinder)
Describe a composite 3-D shape in terms of its component shapes
topics.p: Can {{name}} combine 3-D shapes — like stacking cubes and cylinders — to build a new composite solid?

topics.ds: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, quarter-circles) to create composite shapes, and compose new shapes from the composite shape
e: Combine two triangles to form a rectangle or larger triangle
Put together half-circles and quarter-circles to form circles or new shapes
Decompose a composite shape and describe which simpler shapes make it up
topics.p: Can {{name}} use flat shapes like triangles and rectangles to fit together and make a new larger shape — like a puzzle?

topics.ds: Distinguish defining attributes of shapes (e.g. triangles are closed and three-sided) from non-defining attributes (e.g. colour, orientation, overall size)
e: Build and draw shapes that possess defining attributes
Identify that a shape remains a triangle regardless of its size, colour, or orientation
Explain why a given shape is or is not a particular type based on its defining properties
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand that what makes a shape a triangle is having 3 sides and 3 corners — not its colour or which way it's pointing?

topics.ds: Identify and describe properties of 3-D shapes including the number of edges, vertices, and faces
e: Count the edges, vertices, and faces of common 3-D shapes
Use the terms edge, vertex (vertices), and face correctly
Describe a 3-D shape by its properties (e.g. a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices)
topics.p: Can {{name}} count the faces, edges, and vertices of a 3-D shape like a cube or triangular prism?

topics.ds: Use mathematical vocabulary to describe position, direction, and movement, including straight lines and distinguishing rotation as a turn in terms of right angles (quarter, half, three-quarter turns, clockwise and anti-clockwise)
e: Use terms such as clockwise, anti-clockwise, quarter turn, half turn, three-quarter turn
Describe a right angle as a quarter turn
Give and follow directions involving straight-line movement and turns
topics.p: Can {{name}} follow directions like "turn clockwise a quarter turn" or "move three squares to the right" on a grid or in a simple navigation game?

topics.ds: Compare and sort common 2-D and 3-D shapes and everyday objects by their properties
e: Sort a collection of 2-D shapes by number of sides
Sort 3-D shapes by number of faces or whether faces are flat/curved
Explain criteria used to sort a group of shapes
topics.p: Can {{name}} sort a collection of shapes into groups — for example, separating all the shapes with curved sides from those with only straight sides?

topics.ds: Draw 2-D shapes and make 3-D shapes using modelling materials; recognise 3-D shapes in different orientations and describe them
e: Draw a triangle, rectangle, pentagon, or hexagon accurately
Construct a cube or cuboid from modelling materials (e.g. straws and connectors)
Recognise a 3-D shape (e.g. a pyramid) when it is rotated or seen from a different angle
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a cube to look at, can they draw it on paper — and then make a cube-shaped model from modelling clay or construction materials?

topics.ds: Identify horizontal and vertical lines and pairs of perpendicular and parallel lines
e: Point out horizontal and vertical lines in shapes and real-world contexts
Identify a pair of parallel lines (lines that never meet and are always the same distance apart)
Identify perpendicular lines (lines that meet at a right angle)
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at a set of railway tracks or a window frame, can they point to which lines are parallel (never crossing) and which are perpendicular (meeting at a right angle)?

topics.n: Recognising and drawing shapes by attributes
topics.ds: Recognise and draw shapes having specified attributes (e.g. a given number of angles or equal faces); identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes
e: Draw a shape with exactly 5 sides (pentagon)
Identify all quadrilaterals in a set of mixed shapes
Name and draw a hexagon, explaining it has 6 sides and 6 angles
topics.p: If {{name}} is given instructions like "draw a shape with 5 sides" or "draw a shape with all equal angles," can they draw it correctly?

topics.ds: Identify right angles; recognise that two right angles make a half-turn, three make three-quarters, and four make a complete turn
e: Use a right-angle checker to identify right angles in shapes and the environment
Classify angles as right angles, less than a right angle, or greater than a right angle
Explain that 4 right angles make a full turn (360°)
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at the corner of a piece of paper, can they tell you that's a right angle — and that spinning all the way round takes four right angles?

topics.ds: Recognise angles as a property of shape or a description of a turn
e: Identify angles at the corners of 2-D shapes
Describe a turn (e.g. quarter turn, half turn) in terms of the angle made
Explain that an angle measures the amount of turn between two lines meeting at a point
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to point to an angle on the corner of a book or door frame, can they find it — and explain that swinging a door open is also a kind of turn (angle)?

topics.ds: Identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations; recognise line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry
e: Find all lines of symmetry in a rectangle, square, and equilateral triangle
Determine whether a given shape has a line of symmetry when rotated
Identify which shapes in a set have exactly one line of symmetry
Determine how many lines of symmetry a regular hexagon has
Draw all lines of symmetry for a given figure
Identify which figures from a set are not line-symmetric
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a picture of a butterfly or a star shape, can they draw the line (or lines) where you could fold it exactly in half so both sides match?

topics.ds: Understand that shapes in different categories may share attributes defining a larger category; classify quadrilaterals (rhombuses, rectangles, squares) and draw examples of quadrilaterals not in those subcategories
e: Explain that a square is a special rectangle and also a special rhombus
Sort shapes into a Venn diagram: quadrilaterals vs rectangles vs squares
Draw a quadrilateral that is not a rectangle, rhombus, or square
topics.p: If you show {{name}} a square, a rectangle, and a rhombus, can they explain what makes them all quadrilaterals — and what makes each one different from the others?

topics.ds: Plot specified points on a coordinate grid and draw sides to complete a given polygon
e: Plot points (1,1), (1,4), (5,4), (5,1) and join to make a rectangle
Given three vertices of a square, plot the fourth vertex
Complete a triangle by plotting the third vertex at given coordinates and drawing sides
topics.p: If {{name}} is given three coordinate pairs on a grid, can they plot each point and then connect the dots to draw the correct triangle or rectangle?

topics.ds: Describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down
e: Describe moving from (2,3) to (5,3) as 3 units to the right
Translate a shape 4 units right and 2 units up and state the new coordinates
Predict where a point will be after a given translation
topics.p: If a shape is at position (2, 3) on a grid and you tell {{name}} to move it four squares right and two squares up, can they work out its new position without drawing it first?

topics.ds: Describe positions on a 2-D grid as coordinates in the first quadrant
e: Read the coordinates of a point on a grid as (3, 5)
Explain that the first number is the horizontal distance and the second is the vertical distance
Identify the coordinates of all vertices of a shape plotted on a grid
topics.p: If {{name}} is playing a grid-based treasure map game, can they correctly say where the treasure is using two numbers — like "three across and four up" — from the corner?

topics.ds: Complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry
e: Given half a butterfly shape and a mirror line, complete the other half on a grid
Complete a symmetric pattern on squared paper with a vertical line of symmetry
Check a completed figure by folding along the mirror line
topics.p: If you show {{name}} half a shape drawn on squared paper with a mirror line marked, can they draw the missing half so the whole shape is perfectly symmetrical?

topics.ds: Identify, draw, and interpret nets of common 3-D shapes — cubes, cuboids, triangular prisms, and square-based pyramids — by predicting which 3-D shape a given flat arrangement of faces will fold into, checking whether a net will close completely, and sketching a net from a description or 3-D model; understand the relationship between the number of faces and the structure of the net
e: Draw the net of a cube, cuboid, or triangular prism and fold it mentally to identify which faces connect
Build a 3-D shape from its net and check that all faces, edges, and vertices match
Identify which of several given nets will fold into a specific 3-D shape and explain why the others won't
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a flat T-shaped piece of card with six squares, can they tell you — before folding — that it makes a cube, and point out which square will become each face?

topics.ds: Represent and carry out geometric transformations on squared paper or a coordinate grid: reflections (in horizontal, vertical, and diagonal mirror lines, including the axes), translations (described as a vector or as left/right/up/down moves), and rotations (90° or 180° about a stated centre point); describe each transformation precisely using the correct language; identify which transformation maps one shape onto its image by comparing position, orientation, and size
e: Reflect a shape in a given mirror line on a grid and label the new coordinates
Translate a shape by a given number of squares horizontally and vertically and describe the movement
Rotate a shape 90° or 180° about a given centre on a grid and check the image is congruent to the original
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a shape and its mirror image on squared paper, can they draw in the exact mirror line, and describe the reflection precisely — including where the line of reflection is — without just saying 'it flipped'?

topics.ds: Identify acute and obtuse angles; compare and order angles up to two right angles by size
e: Classify given angles as acute, right, or obtuse
Order four angles from smallest to largest by visual comparison
Identify all acute and obtuse angles in a given triangle or quadrilateral
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at the hands on a clock showing different times, can they tell you which angle between the hands is acute (sharper than a right angle) and which is obtuse (wider)?

topics.ds: Use and interpret standard geometric diagram conventions: mark right angles with a small square, equal lengths with single or double tick marks, and equal angles with arc marks; label angles in three-letter notation (∠ABC) and individual angles with a single letter or number; draw diagrams showing angles at a point, angles on a straight line, and angles inside polygons with these conventions; read diagrams with these marks to identify given information and find unknown values
e: Mark a right angle with a small square symbol in a diagram and explain what it means
Use tick marks to show equal lengths in a shape and double tick marks for a second pair of equal sides
Read and interpret angle notation (e.g. angle ABC) and identify the angle being referred to in a diagram
topics.p: If {{name}}'s maths diagram shows a small square in one corner and matching arc marks on two other angles, can they tell you what each mark means — and use them to figure out a missing angle without re-measuring?

topics.ds: Explain why the key features of 3-D objects (curved or flat faces, edges, vertices) make them suited to particular uses in everyday life
e: Explain why cans are cylinders: the curved face lets them roll and the flat ends let them stand and stack
Explain why boxes are usually rectangular prisms because flat faces and right-angled edges pack without gaps
Choose a shape for a building block that will stack safely and justify it using faces and vertices
topics.p: When {{name}} is unpacking groceries, can they explain why tins are cylinder-shaped and cereal comes in rectangular boxes?

topics.ds: Identify 3-D shapes, including cubes and other cuboids, from 2-D representations
e: Identify a cuboid from its net
Name the 3-D shape shown in an isometric drawing
Match 2-D representations to the correct 3-D shape
topics.p: If you show {{name}} a flat architect's sketch of a box or a pyramid, can they tell you the name of the 3-D shape it represents?

topics.ds: Know that angles at a point sum to 360° (one whole turn), angles on a straight line sum to 180°, and vertically opposite angles are equal; use these facts to find missing angles
e: State that two angles on a straight line add to 180°
Explain that four right angles at a point make 360°
Identify 270° as three right angles
topics.p: If three angles meet at a point and two of them are 120° and 95°, can {{name}} work out the third angle — knowing all the angles at a point add up to 360°?

topics.ds: Represent and approximate composite shapes and objects in the environment using combinations of familiar 2-D shapes and 3-D objects
e: Describe a house as a rectangular prism with a triangular prism roof
Sketch a playground slide using rectangles and triangles and label each part
Approximate the outline of a leaf or lake with a combination of familiar shapes on grid paper
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at a building, a toy or a playground, can they describe it as a combination of simpler shapes — like a box with a triangle roof?

topics.ds: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or angles of a specified size; recognise right triangles as a category
e: Sort a set of quadrilaterals into those with parallel sides and those without
Identify which triangles in a set are right triangles
Classify shapes that have both perpendicular and parallel sides
topics.p: If you show {{name}} a mixed set of triangles and quadrilaterals, can they sort them into groups — like "shapes with at least one right angle" or "shapes with parallel sides" — and explain their reasoning?

topics.ds: Know that angles are measured in degrees, where one degree is 1/360 of a full turn; understand that an angle turning through n one-degree angles has a measure of n degrees
e: Explain that a full turn is 360° and a right angle is 90°
Describe what 'one degree' means in terms of a fraction of a circle
State that an angle of 45° has turned through 45 one-degree angles
topics.p: If {{name}} knows a full circle is 360 degrees, can they tell you how many degrees a quarter turn is — and explain roughly what one single degree looks like?

topics.ds: Estimate and compare acute, obtuse, and reflex angles in degrees; classify angles by type and order them by size
e: Estimate an angle as approximately 130° and classify it as obtuse
Identify a reflex angle in a diagram and estimate it as about 270°
Order four angles from smallest to largest by estimation before measuring
topics.p: If you show {{name}} three different angles drawn on paper, can they estimate which is biggest, label each as acute, obtuse, or reflex — and then check with a protractor?

topics.ds: Draw and identify points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines; identify these in two-dimensional figures
e: Draw a pair of perpendicular lines and a pair of parallel lines
Identify all pairs of parallel sides in a trapezoid
Mark a right angle, an acute angle, and an obtuse angle in a given figure
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a piece of paper and a ruler, can they draw a line segment, mark a point, and then draw another line through that point that runs perfectly parallel to the first?

topics.ds: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor; draw given angles and sketch angles of specified measure
e: Measure an angle with a protractor and read 47°
Draw an angle of 135° using a protractor
Identify which scale on the protractor to use for an obtuse angle
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a protractor and an angle drawn on paper, can they measure it accurately and then draw a new angle of a size you specify?

topics.ds: Recognise angle measure as additive; find unknown angles by adding or subtracting on a diagram using equations with a symbol for the unknown
e: Two angles on a straight line are 65° and x°; find x = 115°
An angle is decomposed into 35° and 40°; state the whole angle is 75°
Solve: angles at a point are 120°, 90°, and x°; find x = 150°
topics.p: If two angles sit next to each other on a straight line and one is 65°, can {{name}} work out the other angle — knowing that angles on a straight line always add up to 180°?

topics.ds: Distinguish between regular and irregular polygons based on reasoning about equal sides and equal angles
e: Classify a set of polygons as regular or irregular
Explain that a regular pentagon has 5 equal sides and 5 equal angles
Identify that a rectangle is irregular (equal angles but not all equal sides) unless it is a square
topics.p: If you show {{name}} a stop sign (regular octagon) and a wonky eight-sided shape, can they explain which is regular and which is irregular — and why?

topics.ds: Recognise rotational symmetry in shapes and designs, state how many times a shape matches itself in a full turn, and create patterns with line and rotational symmetry, including by rotating a motif in dynamic geometry software
e: Turn a square tracing and show it fits onto itself 4 times in a full turn
Identify which of a pinwheel, a heart and an equilateral triangle have rotational symmetry
Use dynamic geometry software to rotate a motif by quarter turns about a point to create a design with rotational symmetry of order 4
topics.p: If {{name}} turns a pinwheel or a square tile, can they notice it looks exactly the same after part of a turn — and count how many times that happens in one full turn?

topics.ds: Name, estimate and compare straight angles, reflex angles and revolutions alongside acute, right and obtuse angles, describing each by its relationship to a right angle (without measuring in degrees)
e: Identify a straight angle as two right angles and a revolution as four right angles
Sort angles from a set of drawn shapes into acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex
Estimate whether an angle drawn between clock hands is less than or more than a straight angle
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at the hands on a clock, can they say whether the angle between them is a straight line, smaller than a right angle, or bigger than a straight line (a reflex angle)?

topics.ds: Identify, describe, and represent the position of a shape following a reflection or translation using appropriate language; know that the shape has not changed
e: Reflect a triangle in a vertical mirror line on a coordinate grid and state the new coordinates
Translate a shape 3 units right and 2 units up and describe the movement
Explain that a reflected/translated shape is congruent to the original
topics.p: If {{name}} slides or flips a shape on squared paper, can they describe exactly where it ends up and confirm the shape itself hasn't changed size or angles?

topics.ds: Use the properties of rectangles to deduce related facts and find missing lengths and angles
e: Given one side of a rectangle is 8 cm and the perimeter is 28 cm, find the other side
Explain that all angles in a rectangle are 90°
Find a missing side of a rectangle given its area and one side length
topics.p: If {{name}} knows one side of a rectangular garden is 7 m, can they tell you the length of the opposite side and all four corner angles — without measuring?

topics.ds: Understand that an angle is a geometric shape formed by two rays sharing a common endpoint (vertex); recognise angles in real-life contexts and 2-D shapes
e: Identify the vertex and arms of an angle in a diagram
Find examples of angles in the classroom (e.g. open door, clock hands)
Explain why two rays meeting at a point form an angle
topics.p: If you draw two lines starting from the same point on paper, can {{name}} tell you that the space between them is an angle — and point to the vertex where they meet?

topics.ds: Draw 2-D shapes using given dimensions and angles, using a ruler and protractor accurately
e: Draw a triangle with sides 5 cm, 7 cm and an included angle of 60°
Construct a rectangle with given length and width using a ruler and set square
Draw a regular pentagon given the side length and interior angle
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to draw a triangle with sides of 5 cm and 7 cm with a 40° angle between them, can they use a ruler and protractor to draw it accurately?

topics.ds: Recognise, describe, and build simple 3-D shapes, including making nets
e: Identify which net will fold into a given 3-D shape
Construct the net of a triangular prism and fold it to verify
Describe a 3-D shape by naming its faces, edges, and vertices
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a flat cross-shaped piece of card (a net), can they predict what 3-D shape it will make when folded up — and then fold it to check?

topics.ds: Find unknown angles in triangles, quadrilaterals, and regular polygons using angle sum properties
e: Find a missing angle in a triangle given two angles (using angle sum = 180°)
Calculate a missing angle in a quadrilateral (angle sum = 360°)
Calculate the interior angle of a regular hexagon from the angle sum formula
topics.p: If {{name}} knows that angles in a triangle always add up to 180°, and two angles in a triangle are 55° and 70°, can they work out the third angle without measuring it?

topics.ds: Compare and classify geometric shapes based on their properties and sizes; understand that attributes belonging to a category also belong to all subcategories; classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties
e: Explain why all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares
Place quadrilaterals in a hierarchy diagram showing subset relationships
Identify properties shared by all parallelograms and explain why rhombuses and rectangles are special cases
topics.p: If someone asks {{name}} "is a square also a rectangle?", can they explain why the answer is yes — because a square has all the properties of a rectangle plus equal sides?

topics.ds: Describe positions on the full coordinate grid (all four quadrants); use coordinates with negative values
e: Plot points with negative coordinates such as (−3, 4) and (2, −5) on a four-quadrant grid
Identify the quadrant in which a given point lies
Describe the position of a shape using coordinates in all four quadrants
topics.p: If {{name}} is playing a game where ships can be at negative coordinates too, can they correctly plot and read positions like (−3, 2) or (1, −4) on a grid?

topics.ds: Illustrate and name parts of circles, including radius, diameter, and circumference; know that the diameter is twice the radius
e: Label the radius, diameter, and circumference on a circle diagram
Calculate the diameter given a radius of 4.5 cm (diameter = 9 cm)
Explain the relationship between radius and diameter in their own words
topics.p: If you give {{name}} a round plate and a ruler, can they measure the diameter — and explain how the radius compares to the diameter?

topics.n: Plotting points in the first quadrant
topics.ds: Plot and read ordered pairs in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane; represent real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points and interpreting coordinate values in context
e: Plot the point (4, 7) accurately on a first-quadrant grid
Graph a set of data pairs (e.g. time vs distance) as points on the coordinate plane
Read coordinates of a plotted point and explain what they represent in a given scenario
topics.p: If you tell {{name}} a car journey passes through grid points (2, 3), (5, 7), and (8, 4) on a map, can they plot those points and describe what the journey looks like?

topics.ds: Understand a coordinate system defined by two perpendicular number lines (axes) with an origin at (0,0); know that an ordered pair (x, y) specifies a unique point where the first number gives horizontal distance and the second gives vertical distance from the origin
e: Identify the x-axis, y-axis, and origin on a coordinate grid
