Explain that (3, 5) means go 3 along the x-axis and 5 up the y-axis
Distinguish (2, 4) from (4, 2) by explaining each coordinate's meaning
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at a map with a grid and you describe a location as "3 across and 5 up from the origin", can they find the exact point — and explain what each of the two numbers tells you?

topics.ds: Describe and perform translations, reflections and rotations of shapes with dynamic geometry software where appropriate as well as by hand, recognise what changes (position, orientation) and what stays the same (side lengths, angles, shape and size), and identify symmetries in the resulting figures
e: Use dynamic geometry software to translate a triangle 3 units right and 2 units up, reflect it in a vertical line and rotate it 90 degrees about a vertex
Measure the original and each image in the software and state that side lengths and angles stay the same while position, and for reflections and rotations orientation, change
Identify the line and rotational symmetry of a design made by reflecting and rotating one shape
topics.p: If {{name}} uses a drawing app to flip, slide or turn a shape, can they explain what changed (where it is, which way it faces) and what stayed the same (its size and angles)?

topics.ds: Draw and translate simple shapes on the coordinate plane; reflect shapes in the axes
e: Translate a triangle 3 units right and 2 units down on a coordinate grid and state the new coordinates
Reflect a shape in the x-axis and list the coordinates of the reflected vertices
Explain how translation changes coordinates (add/subtract) while reflection changes the sign of one coordinate
topics.p: If {{name}} draws a triangle at coordinates (1, 2), (3, 2), and (2, 4) on a grid, can they then reflect it across the x-axis and tell you the new coordinates of each corner?

topics.ds: Recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite; find missing angles using these properties
e: Find a missing angle at a point given the other angles (total 360°)
Use the straight-line property (angles sum to 180°) to find an unknown angle
Identify vertically opposite angles and use the property that they are equal to find unknowns
topics.p: If two straight lines cross each other, can {{name}} tell you which pairs of angles are equal (vertically opposite) — and find a missing angle if you give them one of the others?

topics.ds: Use the properties of faces, surfaces, edges, and vertices of 3-D shapes (cubes, cuboids, prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres) to solve problems, including visualising cross-sections
e: Count and describe the faces, edges, and vertices of a triangular prism and a square-based pyramid
Describe the 2-D cross-section produced by slicing a cylinder horizontally or a cone vertically
Use properties of 3-D shapes to determine whether a given net will fold into a specified solid
topics.p: If {{name}} slices a cylinder straight across the middle like cutting a tin of beans in half, can they describe the shape of the cut surface? What about slicing at an angle?

topics.n: Angle sums in triangles and polygons
topics.ds: Derive and use the angle sum in a triangle (180°), use it to deduce the angle sum in any polygon ((n−2) × 180°), and calculate interior and exterior angles of regular polygons
e: Calculate a missing angle in a triangle by subtracting the known angles from 180°
Find the sum of interior angles in a hexagon by dividing it into triangles
Calculate each interior and exterior angle of a regular polygon given the number of sides
topics.p: If {{name}} knows two angles of a triangle are 50° and 70°, can they work out the third? And can they figure out the angles inside a regular pentagon?

topics.ds: Derive and apply formulae for the area of triangles, parallelograms, and trapezia, and for the volume of cuboids and other prisms (including cylinders), connecting each formula to its geometric reasoning
e: Calculate the area of a trapezium using A = ½(a + b) × h and explain why the formula works
Find the volume of a triangular prism by calculating cross-sectional area × length
Derive the formula for the volume of a cylinder as π × r² × h by reasoning from the prism formula
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to tile a triangular section of a patio with a base of 4 m and height of 3 m, can they work out the area to know how many tiles to buy?

topics.ds: Identify properties of translations, rotations, and reflections; describe and perform these transformations on given figures, and understand that the image is congruent to the original
e: Reflect a shape in a given mirror line (including diagonal lines) and state the coordinates of the image
Rotate a shape about a given centre by 90° or 180° and describe the result
Translate a shape by a given vector and verify that lengths and angles are preserved
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked to rotate a triangle 90° clockwise around a fixed point, can they work out where each corner ends up — and confirm the triangle is still the same size and shape?

topics.ds: Compare the parallel cross-sections of objects and recognise that slices of a right prism taken parallel to its end (base) faces are all congruent to those faces, while parallel slices of pyramids and cones change in size
e: Slice a play-dough triangular prism parallel to its triangular end faces and show every slice is congruent to the end face
Explain why slices of a square pyramid taken parallel to its base get smaller towards the apex
Identify which of an unsharpened hexagonal pencil, a cone and a cereal box give congruent slices when cut parallel to their end faces
topics.p: If {{name}} cuts slices off a rectangular block of cheese, parallel to its end, can they explain why every slice is the same rectangle as the end — but slices of an ice-cream cone would keep getting smaller?

topics.ds: Draw and measure line segments and angles accurately, and construct triangles from given conditions using the drawing approaches the standard calls for: ruler and protractor for two sides and the included angle (SAS) or two angles and the included side (ASA); ruler and compasses for three sides (SSS), using intersecting arcs; and dynamic geometry software; check each construction by measuring the remaining sides and angles (to within about 1 mm and 1°). Interpreting scale drawings is covered in Scale drawings and maps; deciding whether conditions give one, many or no triangles is covered in Which triangles are possible
e: Construct triangle ABC with AB = 7 cm, angle A = 40° and AC = 5 cm using a ruler and protractor, then measure BC and the other two angles
Construct a triangle with sides 6 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm using a ruler and compasses, drawing intersecting arcs from each end of the 6 cm base

Construct a triangle with angles of 50° and 60° at the ends of a 7 cm side in dynamic geometry software, measure the third angle (70°), and drag the vertices to show that the triangle can move or rotate but cannot change its shape or size while those ASA conditions hold
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to draw a triangle with sides of 7 cm and 5 cm and a 40° angle between them, could they draw it accurately with a ruler and protractor — and then measure the third side to check?

topics.ds: Use conventional geometric terms and notation to describe, sketch, and draw points, lines, parallel and perpendicular lines, right angles, regular polygons, and reflectively/rotationally symmetric polygons
e: Use correct notation for line segments (AB), angles (∠ABC), and parallel lines (AB ∥ CD)
Sketch a regular hexagon and describe its rotational and reflective symmetry
Identify and label perpendicular and parallel lines in a given figure using standard symbols
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to describe a triangle using proper geometry notation — naming its angles and sides with letters — can they do it clearly enough for someone else to draw it?

topics.ds: Derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, and circles using appropriate language, including interior angles, diagonals, symmetry, and relationships between side lengths
e: List and verify properties of a parallelogram (opposite sides parallel/equal, opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other)
Explain why a square is a special case of both a rectangle and a rhombus
Derive the relationship between the radius, diameter, and circumference of a circle
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} why the diagonals of a rectangle are always equal in length, can they explain it using the properties of the shape — rather than just measuring to check?

topics.ds: Draw polygons in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane from given vertex coordinates; find the length of a horizontal or vertical side from the coordinates of its endpoints (which share an x- or a y-coordinate) by subtracting when both endpoints lie on the same side of the axis, and by adding their distances from the axis (absolute values) when the side crosses it; and use these lengths to find perimeters, areas, missing vertices and distances in real-world and mathematical problems such as maps and plans
e: Plot (−3, 2), (4, 2), (4, −1) and (−3, −1), join them to form a rectangle, and find its side lengths (7 and 3 units), perimeter (20 units) and area (21 square units)
Explain that (−5, 6) to (−5, 1) is 6 − 1 = 5 units, while (2, −4) to (2, 3) is |−4| + |3| = 7 units because that side crosses the x-axis
Find how far the library at (−6, 3) is from the park at (2, 3) on a town map where each grid unit is 100 m (800 m)
topics.p: If {{name}} plots the corners of a vegetable patch at (−3, 2), (4, 2), (4, −1) and (−3, −1) on a grid where each square is 1 metre, could they draw it and work out how long each side is, even where the patch crosses the axes?

topics.ds: Recognise and use combinations of translations, reflections and rotations to create tessellations and other geometric patterns, using dynamic geometry software where appropriate
e: Explain why equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons tessellate but regular pentagons do not
Create a tessellation from a modified tile by translating and rotating it, describing the transformations used
Use geometry software to build a frieze pattern by repeatedly reflecting and translating a motif
topics.p: When {{name}} looks at bathroom tiles or a brick wall, can they explain why the shapes fit together with no gaps — and create their own tiling pattern by sliding, flipping or turning a shape?

topics.ds: Apply the properties of angles at a point (360°), on a straight line (180°), and vertically opposite angles to find unknown angles in multi-step problems
e: Find a missing angle using the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180°
Use vertically opposite angles are equal to set up and solve an equation for an unknown
Combine multiple angle facts in a single diagram to find several missing angles step by step
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a diagram with several angles marked at crossing lines and some unknown, can they use the rules about straight lines and crossing lines to find all the missing angles step by step?

topics.ds: Understand and use the relationship between parallel lines cut by a transversal: corresponding angles, alternate interior angles, and co-interior (same-side interior) angles; use these to find unknown angles
e: Identify alternate, corresponding, and co-interior angle pairs in a diagram with parallel lines
Explain why alternate angles are equal using the concept of translation along the transversal
Find missing angles in a parallel-line diagram using a combination of angle relationships
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a Z-shape or F-shape formed by two parallel lines and a crossing line in a diagram, can they identify the equal angles and explain why they’re equal?

topics.ds: Calculate the circumference and area of circles using the formulae C = πd (or 2πr) and A = πr², and solve problems involving perimeters and areas of composite shapes that include circular parts
e: Calculate the circumference and area of a circle given its radius or diameter
Find the perimeter or area of a composite shape made from rectangles and semicircles
Explain the relationship between π, diameter, and circumference informally
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to know how far a bicycle wheel travels in one full rotation, can they use the diameter of the wheel and π (pi) to work out the circumference?

topics.ds: Know and use the criteria for triangle congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS), use standard labelling conventions for sides and angles of triangle ABC, and determine whether two triangles are congruent
e: State which congruence criterion (SSS, SAS, ASA, or RHS) applies to a given pair of triangles
Use the notation △ABC ≅ △DEF and match corresponding sides and angles
Use two non-congruent triangles that share two sides and a non-included angle to explain why SSA is not a congruence criterion
topics.p: If {{name}} is shown two triangles where all three sides of one match all three sides of the other, can they explain why those triangles must be identical in shape and size?

topics.ds: Use ruler and compasses to perform standard constructions: perpendicular bisector of a line segment, perpendicular to a line from or at a given point, and bisecting an angle
e: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment using compasses and a straight edge
Construct an angle bisector and verify by measuring both halves
Construct a perpendicular from a point to a line using compasses only
topics.p: If {{name}} has only a ruler and a pair of compasses, can they construct a line that cuts another line segment exactly in half at a right angle — without using a protractor?

topics.ds: Understand similarity as a relationship where one shape is an enlargement of another; construct similar shapes by enlargement with a given scale factor and centre, with and without coordinate grids
e: Enlarge a shape by a given scale factor from a specified centre of enlargement
Determine the scale factor between two similar shapes by comparing corresponding sides
Explain why corresponding angles in similar shapes are equal while sides are in proportion
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to enlarge a photo so it's three times bigger, can they work out the new dimensions — and explain that the shape stays the same but all lengths increase by the same factor?

topics.n: Surface area and volume of solids
topics.ds: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the surface area and volume of right prisms (including triangular and trapezoidal prisms) and of solids composed of cubes and right prisms: find a prism's surface area as the two bases plus the rectangular side faces; find volume as base area × height, including bases that are composite polygons; for composite solids, add the volumes of the parts but find the surface area from the exposed faces only, subtracting the areas hidden where parts join; and decide whether a problem needs area, surface area or volume
e: Find the surface area of a triangular prism 10 cm long with right-triangle ends (sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm) as 2 × 6 + (3 + 4 + 5) × 10 = 132 cm²
Find the volume (40 cm³) and surface area (80 cm², not 88 cm²) of a 2 cm cube glued on top of a 4 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm block, removing the two 4 cm² faces hidden where they join
Find the soil for a planter 0.5 m deep whose L-shaped base is a 3 m × 1 m and a 2 m × 1.5 m rectangle (6 m² × 0.5 m = 3 m³), and explain why painting its outside walls needs surface area instead
topics.p: If {{name}} built a model from two boxes glued together, could they work out how much space it takes up and how much paint would cover its outside — remembering not to paint the faces that are glued together?

topics.ds: Decide whether given side and angle conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle, and explain why, predicting with a freehand sketch and testing by construction (ruler and protractor, compasses, or dynamic geometry software): three sides give exactly one triangle when each pair of sides adds to more than the third, and none otherwise — if the two shorter sides add to less than the longest, the construction arcs do not meet, and if they add to exactly the longest (e.g. 3, 4 and 7), the arcs touch only on the base line, so the sides lie flat in a straight line rather than forming a triangle; three angles must add to 180° and then fix only the shape, not the size, so many triangles fit (none if the sum is not 180°); two sides with the included angle, or two angles with the included side, give exactly one triangle; and two sides with an angle that is not between them can give two, one or no triangles
e: Show that sides of 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm make no triangle (the arcs do not meet) and that 3 cm, 4 cm and 7 cm make none either (the arcs touch on the base, giving a straight line), while 3 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm make exactly one
Explain that angles of 50°, 60° and 70° fit many triangles of different sizes, while angles of 100°, 50° and 40° fit none because they add to 190°
Sketch freehand, then construct, two different triangles with AB = 7 cm, BC = 5 cm and angle A = 40°, and explain why making the 40° angle the one between the two sides gives only one triangle
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked to make a triangle from straws 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm long, could they predict that it can't be done and explain why — and say why 'angles of 50°, 60° and 70°' could describe lots of different-sized triangles?

topics.ds: Apply Pythagoras’ Theorem (a² + b² = c²) to calculate unknown side lengths in right-angled triangles, including in real-world and coordinate-geometry contexts
e: Calculate the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle given the two shorter sides
Find a shorter side given the hypotenuse and the other short side
Use Pythagoras’ Theorem to find the distance between two points on a coordinate grid
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to check whether a shelf bracket makes a perfect right angle and the sides measure 30 cm, 40 cm, and 50 cm, can they use Pythagoras to verify?

topics.ds: Use the trigonometric ratios sin, cos, and tan in right-angled triangles to find unknown sides and angles, including setting up the correct ratio for a given problem
e: Identify which trigonometric ratio to use (SOH CAH TOA) based on the known and unknown sides
Calculate an unknown side using sin, cos, or tan and a known angle
Find an unknown angle using the inverse trigonometric function (e.g. tan⁻¹)
topics.p: If {{name}} knows a ladder is 5 metres long and leans against a wall at 70° to the ground, can they use trigonometry to work out how high up the wall it reaches?

topics.ds: Use mathematical words carefully when counting, comparing, and describing shapes and positions
e: Use 'more than', 'fewer than', and 'the same as' correctly when comparing groups
Name shapes correctly and describe their features using words like 'sides' and 'corners'
Use positional words (above, below, next to) precisely to describe where objects are
topics.p: When {{name}} talks about maths — like comparing numbers or describing shapes — do they use the right words, like "larger than", "fewer", "beside", or "corner"?

topics.ds: Notice when a calculation or pattern repeats and use this to count more efficiently or predict results
e: Notice that skip counting by 2s follows a repeating odd/even pattern
Recognise that adding 1 to any number always gives the next counting number
Use a repeated pattern (e.g. +10 on a hundred chart always moves down one row) to predict answers
topics.p: When {{name}} is counting or doing repeated additions, have they started to notice the pattern — like "5, 10, 15, 20…" — and used it to predict the next number without counting one by one?

topics.ds: Select and use familiar tools (concrete objects, fingers, ten frames) to help solve a mathematical problem
e: Choose cubes, counters, or fingers to help solve an addition or subtraction problem
Use a ten frame to organise objects for counting or comparing
Explain why a particular tool (e.g. cubes rather than fingers) was chosen for a given problem
topics.p: When {{name}} is working out a maths problem, do they reach for helpful tools — like using their fingers, counters, or a number line — to support their thinking?

topics.ds: Make sense of a problem by identifying what is being asked, choosing concrete objects or pictures to represent the situation, and explaining a pathway to the solution
e: When given a word problem within 10, explain what the problem is asking before attempting to solve
Choose objects, fingers, or drawings to represent a problem situation
After finding an answer, check it makes sense (e.g. re-count objects to verify a total)
topics.p: When {{name}} gets a maths problem they don't immediately know how to solve, do they stop and think about what the question is asking — maybe drawing a picture — before diving in?

topics.ds: Move between a real-world situation and a mathematical representation using concrete objects, drawings, diagrams, tables, number sentences, or bar models
e: Given a story about combining groups, represent it with counters or cubes and find the total
Given a set of objects, tell a simple addition or subtraction story to match
Connect a physical action (putting together, taking away) to the matching operation
topics.p: If {{name}} is working out a real-life maths problem — like sharing 8 sweets between 2 people — can they use objects or draw a picture to show what's happening before writing any numbers?

topics.ds: Show and tell how a mathematical answer was found using objects, drawings, and spoken words
e: Use objects or drawings to demonstrate how an addition or subtraction was solved
Respond to 'how do you know?' by pointing to objects or a drawing and describing what was done
Listen to a peer's explanation and say whether they agree or disagree
topics.p: After {{name}} solves a maths problem, can they explain how they got their answer — using counters, a drawing, or words — rather than just writing down the final number?

topics.ds: Notice simple patterns and structures: spot that changing order doesn't change the total, and recognise how numbers relate to each other
e: Notice that 3 + 2 gives the same answer as 2 + 3 (early commutativity)
Recognise that teen numbers are 'ten and some more' (e.g. 14 is 10 and 4)
Spot a pattern in a sequence of objects or numbers and predict what comes next
topics.p: Has {{name}} noticed that adding numbers in a different order gives the same answer — like 3 + 5 and 5 + 3 both equal 8 — and can they explain why that makes sense?

topics.n: Using objects to model real problems
topics.ds: Use objects, drawings, or simple number sentences to represent a real-world situation (early mathematical modelling)
e: Draw a picture or use objects to represent a simple real-world situation involving counting or comparing
Write or dictate a number sentence to describe a real-world situation (e.g. 'I had 5 apples and ate 2')
Use the model to answer a question about the situation
topics.p: If you describe a simple real-life situation to {{name}} — like "there are 3 birds on a fence and 2 more land" — can they write a number sentence like 3 + 2 = 5 to represent it?

topics.ds: Represent real-world problems with number sentences, bar models, or diagrams, and interpret the mathematical result back in context
e: Choose and write an appropriate number sentence for a measurement or money word problem
Draw a bar model or diagram to represent a two-step or comparison problem
Interpret the numerical answer in context (e.g. '15 cm means the ribbon is 15 centimetres long')
topics.p: When {{name}} solves a word problem by drawing a bar model or writing an equation, can they also explain what their answer means in the real-world context — like "that means each child gets 4 sweets"?

topics.ds: Move between real-world situations, drawings, and number sentences, explaining how each representation connects to the others (quantitative reasoning)
e: Write a number sentence (e.g. 14 + 5 = 19) to match a word problem and explain the connection
Draw a bar model or part-whole diagram to represent a problem, then solve using the diagram
Translate between a concrete model and a symbolic equation, describing what each number represents
topics.p: When {{name}} solves a word problem, can they draw a diagram or write a number sentence to show their thinking — and then explain how the picture and the numbers match the real situation?

topics.ds: With teacher prompting, explain and justify mathematical reasoning using drawings, number sentences, or words
e: Explain a solution strategy using a drawing or number sentence (e.g. 'I made ten first, then added the rest')
Justify why an answer is correct by showing an alternative method that gives the same result
Identify and explain an error in a worked example or a peer's solution
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} "how did you work that out?", can they show you with a drawing or explain their steps in simple words?

topics.ds: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: spot calculation patterns, describe rules for sequences, and predict results using known mathematical facts
e: Use a known doubles fact to derive a near-doubles answer (e.g. 6 + 7 = 6 + 6 + 1 = 13)
Notice that subtracting 10 from any two-digit number always reduces the tens digit by 1
Describe a rule for a pattern and use it to extend or predict (e.g. 'each time we add 5, the ones digit alternates between 0 and 5')
topics.p: When {{name}} is practising times tables or number patterns, do they spot a shortcut — like "if 6 × 7 = 42, then 6 × 8 must be 48" — and use known facts to work out ones they haven't memorised yet?

topics.ds: With teacher guidance, make sense of multi-step and more complex problems by planning a pathway to the solution, identifying relevant information, and choosing appropriate operations
e: When given a word problem within 20 or 100, identify the known information and what needs to be found
Try a strategy (drawing, number line, known fact) and switch approach if the first attempt stalls
Check the reasonableness of an answer using estimation or a different method
topics.p: If {{name}} works out that 3 children each get 12 sweets and ends up with 5, does {{name}} pause and say "that doesn't seem right" rather than just writing it down?

topics.ds: Select and use appropriate tools and representations (number lines, hundred squares, rulers, part-whole models) to support problem-solving
e: Choose a number line or hundred square to support adding or subtracting two-digit numbers
Select a ruler when a problem requires measuring length
Explain why one representation (e.g. a number line vs cubes) is more helpful for a particular problem
topics.p: When {{name}} is tackling a maths problem, do they choose a useful tool — like a number line for addition or a hundred square to count on — rather than always working in their head?

topics.ds: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct vocabulary, specify units, and use symbols accurately
e: Use the = sign correctly to mean 'is the same as' rather than 'the answer is'
Include units when giving a measurement answer (e.g. '12 cm' not just '12')
Use precise terms such as 'edge', 'vertex', 'face' when describing 3-D shapes, and 'greater than', 'less than' when comparing numbers
topics.p: When {{name}} writes or talks about a maths answer, do they include the units — like "5 centimetres" rather than just "5" — and use the right symbols like = or <?

topics.ds: Look for and use mathematical structure: apply properties of operations, place-value patterns, and relationships between shapes to solve problems efficiently
e: Use the commutative property deliberately (e.g. reorder 3 + 9 as 9 + 3 to count on from the larger number)
Use place-value structure to add or subtract tens (e.g. 47 + 10 = 57 because only the tens digit changes)
Recognise structural similarities between shapes (e.g. rectangles and squares both have 4 sides and 4 right angles)
topics.p: When {{name}} notices a pattern in their maths work — like how multiplying by 10 always adds a zero — do they use that pattern to solve similar problems more quickly?

topics.ds: Select and use appropriate tools and representations strategically, including choosing between mental methods, jottings, formal algorithms, and calculators for arithmetic with multi-digit numbers, decimals, and fractions
e: Choose a mental method for 345 + 200 but a written method for 345 + 278
Select a ruler vs a metre stick based on the object being measured
Decide when a number line is more useful than base-ten blocks for a given problem
topics.p: When {{name}} faces a maths problem, do they think about which method suits it best — like doing easy ones in their head, using a written method for bigger calculations, or sketching a diagram for geometry?

topics.ds: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: extend multiplication table patterns, derive unknown facts from known ones, and describe rules for sequences
e: Notice that all multiples of 4 are even and use this to check answers
Derive 8 × 7 from 8 × 5 + 8 × 2 by spotting the pattern
Describe a rule for a growing pattern (e.g. 'add 50 each time') and use it to predict the next terms
topics.p: When {{name}} is learning their times tables, do they use known facts to figure out ones they're not sure of — for example, using 5 × 6 = 30 to work out that 6 × 6 = 36?

topics.ds: Construct and follow multi-step mathematical arguments; identify errors in reasoning and explain why a method works or does not work
e: Explain step by step why a columnar addition method gives the correct answer
Find and explain an error in a worked example (e.g. incorrect regrouping)
Construct a simple argument for why a general statement is true (e.g. 'adding two even numbers always gives an even number')
topics.p: If {{name}} hears another child's explanation for how they solved a maths problem, can {{name}} say whether the reasoning makes sense — and if not, point out exactly where the logic goes wrong?

topics.ds: With teacher support, make sense of multi-step problems involving larger numbers or mixed operations by breaking them into parts, choosing strategies, and checking answers for reasonableness — children at this stage are developing the habit with guidance; independent strategy evaluation comes later
e: Break a two-step word problem within 1000 into sub-problems and solve each part
Estimate an answer before calculating to set a reasonableness benchmark
Check an answer using a different method or inverse operation and revise if needed
topics.p: If {{name}} gets an answer that seems way too big or too small for a maths problem, do they notice and go back to check, even without you pointing it out?

topics.ds: Look for and use mathematical structure: apply place-value patterns to three-digit operations, use multiplication/division relationships, and exploit shape properties to classify
e: Use the structure of place value to explain why adding hundreds only changes the hundreds digit
Use commutativity and the relationship between multiplication and division to derive unknown facts
Classify shapes by their structural properties (number of sides, right angles, parallel lines)
topics.p: When {{name}} is multiplying or working with larger numbers, do they use what they know about place value or number relationships to simplify the calculation — like breaking 24 × 3 into 20 × 3 + 4 × 3?

topics.ds: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, and symbolic equations involving three-digit numbers and fractions, explaining what each part represents
e: Write an equation with three-digit numbers to match a measurement or money word problem
Draw a bar model to represent a fraction problem and use it to solve
Explain how a number line diagram relates to the quantities in a word problem
topics.p: When {{name}} works through a maths problem involving fractions or three-digit numbers, can they switch between drawing a diagram, using a number line, and writing an equation — and explain what each one shows?

topics.ds: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct place-value and fraction vocabulary, specify units in measurement answers, and use notation accurately
e: Consistently specify units in measurement answers (e.g. '35 cm' not '35')
Use fraction vocabulary precisely (numerator, denominator, equivalent)
Write equations with correct notation including £/p, >, <, = and fraction symbols
topics.p: When {{name}} gives a maths answer involving measurements or fractions, do they include the correct units — like "3½ metres" or "2.5 kg" — and use the right symbols throughout?

topics.ds: Model real-world problems involving measurement, money, and time by choosing appropriate representations and interpreting results in context
e: Choose whether to use a bar model, number line, or equation for a measurement problem
Model a multi-step money problem with equations and interpret the final answer as change or total cost
Create a line plot from measurement data and use it to answer questions about the real-world situation
topics.p: When {{name}} solves a real-life maths problem — like calculating how much fabric is needed for a project — can they choose the right representation (a diagram, a table, an equation) and explain what the answer means in the real situation?

topics.ds: Use a calculator where appropriate to solve and check practical additive and multiplicative money problems in dollars and cents, reading the display as dollars and cents and checking the result with a quick estimate
e: Use a calculator to total $4.85, $12.30 and $7.95 for a shopping list and check it is about $25
Enter 10 - 6.45 to find the change from a $10 note and read the display 3.55 as $3.55
Decide that 4 x $5 is quicker mentally but 6 x $3.95 is easier on a calculator, and explain why
topics.p: When you're shopping, can {{name}} use a phone calculator to add up prices like $4.85, $12.30 and $7.95 — and tell whether the answer looks about right?

topics.ds: Select and use appropriate tools and representations strategically: choose between mental, written, and diagrammatic methods; use calculators for checking; select fraction models suited to the task
e: Decide to use mental multiplication for 25×4 but a written method for 167×3
Choose fraction strips rather than a number line to compare 3/8 and 1/4
Use a ruler and squared paper to verify area by counting squares after calculating l×w
topics.p: When {{name}} is working on maths, do they choose the right method — doing simple calculations in their head, using written working for complex ones, and sketching a diagram when a problem involves shapes or fractions?

topics.ds: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, number lines, and symbolic equations involving multiplication, fractions, and decimals, explaining what each representation shows
e: Represent a sharing problem as both a fraction diagram and a division equation
Explain how a bar model for 4 × 23 connects to the area model and the written method
Translate a decimal on a number line into a fraction and explain the equivalence
topics.p: When {{name}} works on a maths problem involving decimals or fractions, can they move between a fraction strip, a number line, and a written equation — explaining what each one is showing?

topics.ds: Construct and present multi-step mathematical arguments; critique the reasoning of others and explain clearly why a method works or fails
e: Explain why 1/3 > 1/5 using the idea that more parts means smaller pieces
Find and explain an error in a peer's column subtraction with exchanges
Present a chain of reasoning: since 6×8=48 and 6×2=12, then 6×10=60 so 6×8=60−12=48
topics.p: If a classmate claims "you can't multiply a fraction and get a bigger answer", can {{name}} think through whether that's always true — and give an example to support or challenge the claim?

topics.ds: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct fraction/decimal vocabulary, name angle types accurately, specify units in measurement and money, and use notation (=, <, >, ÷, ×) correctly
e: Distinguish between 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' and use both correctly
State an answer in the correct unit: '63 square centimetres' not just '63'
Write 15:45 in 24-hour notation and explain the distinction from 3:45 pm
topics.p: When {{name}} writes up a maths answer involving angles, fractions, or money, do they use precise vocabulary and correct notation — like writing "acute angle", "3/4", or "£2.50" rather than vague descriptions?

topics.ds: Model real-world problems involving multiplication, area, fractions, and unit conversion by choosing appropriate representations and interpreting mathematical results in context
e: Model a tiling/area problem with an array and write the corresponding multiplication
Represent a recipe-scaling problem as a fraction calculation and interpret the answer in grams
Use a bar model to set up a unit conversion problem (metres to centimetres)
topics.p: When {{name}} is solving a real-life problem — like working out the area of a room in square metres — do they choose the right maths tool for the job and interpret the final number in terms of the real situation?

topics.ds: Make sense of multi-step problems involving four operations, fractions, and area/volume by identifying sub-steps, choosing a strategy, and monitoring progress
e: Break a two-step word problem into parts and explain a plan before calculating
Choose between drawing a diagram or writing equations for a perimeter problem
Check a fraction-of-quantity answer by estimating: 3/5 of 20 must be more than half of 20
topics.p: When {{name}} tackles a complex maths problem involving area, fractions, and multiple steps, do they plan their approach — estimating roughly what the answer should be before calculating, and then checking it makes sense at the end?

topics.ds: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: extend patterns in times tables and equivalent fractions, derive unknown facts from known facts efficiently, describe general rules
e: Notice that all fractions equivalent to 1/2 have a numerator that is half the denominator
Use the pattern 3×4=12, 3×40=120, 3×400=1200 and explain the generalisation
Derive 8×7 from 8×5=40 plus 8×2=16 and describe the strategy as a general approach
topics.p: When {{name}} notices a pattern — like that multiplying by 4 is the same as doubling twice — do they use that generalisation to solve similar problems more efficiently?

topics.ds: Look for and use mathematical structure: exploit place-value patterns for ×10/×100, use the distributive property to break apart multiplications, apply fraction equivalence to compare and compute, use shape properties to classify quadrilaterals
e: Decompose 7×13 into 7×10 + 7×3 using the distributive property
Explain why multiplying by 10 shifts digits one place left using place-value structure
Use the fact that a square is a special rectangle to reason about quadrilateral properties
topics.p: When {{name}} is comparing fractions or working out a percentage, do they look for underlying patterns — like spotting that 50% is always half, or that equivalent fractions all sit at the same point on a number line?

topics.ds: Select and use tools and representations strategically: choose between mental methods, formal written methods, protractors, fraction strips, and diagrams based on the demands of the problem
e: Choose mental multiplication for 25 × 40 but long multiplication for 347 × 26
Select a protractor to verify an estimated angle rather than relying on visual inspection alone
Choose a common-denominator approach vs. benchmark comparison for ordering fractions, and explain why
topics.p: When {{name}} faces a geometry or proportion problem, do they choose the right tool — like a protractor for angles or a fraction strip for comparing fractions — rather than always defaulting to one method?

topics.ds: Make sense of complex multi-step problems involving large numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages by analysing what is known and unknown, planning multi-step strategies, and evaluating reasonableness through estimation and inverse operations
e: Break a three-step problem involving unit conversion and multiplication into sub-problems and solve systematically
Estimate 4,832 × 7 as roughly 5,000 × 7 = 35,000 to check a calculated answer of 33,824
Identify that a percentage answer over 100% doesn't make sense in context
topics.p: When {{name}} faces a complex multi-step maths problem involving percentages, large numbers, or fractions, do they pause to identify what's known, estimate an answer, and then check their final result makes sense?

topics.ds: Look for and use mathematical structure: exploit the relationship between fractions, decimals, and percentages; use factor pairs to simplify multiplication; apply angle facts to find unknowns; use properties of regular polygons systematically
e: Use the structure 25 × 16 = 25 × 4 × 4 = 100 × 4 = 400 by exploiting factor pairs
Recognise that 0.75 = 3/4 = 75% and use whichever form is most efficient for the problem
Use the fact that angles on a straight line sum to 180° as a structural tool to find missing angles
topics.p: When {{name}} notices that fractions, decimals, and percentages are just different ways of writing the same thing, do they use that understanding to switch between them fluidly when it makes a calculation easier?

topics.ds: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, number lines, bar models, and symbolic equations involving multi-digit multiplication, fractions, decimals, and percentages, explaining connections between representations
e: Represent a scaling problem as both a bar model and a multiplication equation
Show how 0.35, 35/100, and 35% all represent the same quantity on a hundredths grid
Translate a line-graph reading into a subtraction equation to find the difference
topics.p: When {{name}} solves a problem involving percentages or multi-digit multiplication, can they show the same situation using a bar model, a number line, and an equation — and explain what each one represents?

topics.ds: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct vocabulary for primes, factors, multiples, angle types, and polygon regularity; specify units including cm², m³, °; use notation for squares/cubes and percentages accurately
e: Distinguish 'factor' from 'multiple' in a written explanation
Write an area answer as 48 cm² (not just 48) and a volume estimate as approximately 60 cm³
Use 5² notation correctly and read it as 'five squared'
topics.p: When {{name}} talks or writes about maths involving primes, percentages, or polygons, do they use the precise technical words — like "prime factor", "obtuse angle", or "regular hexagon" — correctly and confidently?

topics.ds: Model real-world problems involving scaling, unit conversion, area/perimeter, and percentage by selecting appropriate mathematical representations and interpreting results in context
e: Model a recipe-scaling problem with multiplication and fractions, then interpret the answer in grams
Represent a room-carpet problem by drawing a scale diagram and applying the area formula
Use a percentage bar model to find a sale price and explain the answer in £
topics.p: When {{name}} is solving a real-world maths problem — like scaling a recipe or converting units — do they choose a sensible representation, carry out the maths, and then explain what the result means in the real situation?

topics.ds: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: extend patterns in equivalent fractions and percentage conversions, derive unknown facts from known facts, describe general rules for sequences and predict terms
e: Notice that multiplying any number by 25 can be done by multiplying by 100 then dividing by 4, and explain why
Describe the general rule for a sequence and predict the 20th term
Generalise: to find 10% divide by 10, to find 5% halve 10%, and use this to find 35% of any number
topics.p: When {{name}} sees a sequence of equivalent fractions — like 1/2, 2/4, 3/6… — can they describe the rule and use it to find the next few terms, or to quickly convert between fractions and percentages?

topics.ds: Construct and present logical mathematical arguments involving multiple steps; critique others' reasoning about fractions, angles, or calculations and clearly explain errors or alternative methods
e: Prove that 3/4 > 2/3 using a common denominator argument and a visual model
Find and explain an error in a long multiplication where a partial product was misaligned
Present a chain of reasoning to show that angles in a triangle sum to 180° by tearing and arranging
topics.p: If {{name}} and a classmate solve the same maths problem differently, can {{name}} compare the two approaches, explain which method is more efficient, and identify any errors in either working?

topics.ds: Use a calculator efficiently and appropriately to solve multi-step addition, subtraction, multiplication and division problems, deciding when a calculator is the best tool and checking the result with an estimate
e: Use a calculator to find the total of 1468 + 2975 + 813 and check it against an estimate of about 5300
Decide whether to use mental strategies or a calculator for 400 x 3 and for 387 x 46, and explain the choice
Spot that a calculator answer of 4 150 for 83 x 5 must be a keying error because 80 x 5 = 400
topics.p: When {{name}} uses a calculator for homework, do they check the answer looks about right with a quick estimate — and know when it's faster to do it in their head?

topics.ds: Communicate with mathematical precision: use correct vocabulary for ratio, proportion, algebra, volume, coordinate geometry, and circle parts; specify units including cm³, m³, and miles/km; use notation for algebraic expressions and order of operations accurately
e: Use 'radius', 'diameter', and 'circumference' correctly when describing a circle
Distinguish between an expression, an equation, and a formula in mathematical writing
Specify units correctly when presenting volume calculations (e.g. 60 cm³ not just 60)
topics.p: When {{name}} writes up maths involving algebra or 3-D shapes, do they use precise language — like "algebraic expression", "cubic centimetres", or "coordinates" — and apply the correct notation throughout?

topics.ds: Make sense of complex multi-step problems involving ratio, proportion, algebra, negative numbers, and all four operations with fractions and decimals by analysing given and unknown quantities, planning solution strategies, and evaluating reasonableness using estimation and inverse operations
e: Break down a three-step ratio problem into sub-problems and plan a solution pathway
Identify which quantities are known/unknown in an algebraic word problem and set up equations
Use estimation to check whether a decimal division answer is reasonable before finalising
topics.p: When {{name}} faces a complex maths problem involving algebra, ratio, or fractions with multiple steps, do they break it into manageable parts, estimate what's reasonable, and verify their answer using a different approach?

topics.ds: Select and use tools and representations strategically: choose between mental methods, formal written methods, algebraic approaches, coordinate grids, and technology based on the demands of the problem
e: Explain why long division is more appropriate than mental methods for 4,752 ÷ 13
Choose a coordinate grid approach to verify a translation rather than computing from a description alone
Select a formula-based approach rather than counting cubes to find volume efficiently
topics.p: When {{name}} chooses how to tackle a maths problem, do they pick the most efficient approach — using algebra for a complex generalisation, a coordinate grid for a geometry problem, or mental arithmetic for a simple calculation?

topics.ds: Construct and present logical mathematical arguments involving multiple steps and formal reasoning; critique others' reasoning about fractions, algebra, ratio, or geometry and clearly explain errors or alternative approaches
e: Prove that a given angle must be 60° by chaining angle facts in a logical sequence
Find and explain the error in a peer's fraction division calculation
Construct a counter-example to disprove a false conjecture (e.g. 'multiplying always makes bigger')
topics.p: When {{name}} presents a multi-step maths solution, do they lay out their reasoning clearly enough that someone else could follow every step — and can they spot the flaw if a worked solution contains a logical error?

topics.ds: Recognise and use repeated reasoning to generalise: describe algebraic rules for nth terms, use properties of operations to simplify, and verify generalisations with specific cases
e: Explain that the interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2) × 180° based on the pattern for triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons
Predict the 20th term of a linear sequence by identifying and applying the general rule
Generalise that dividing by n always gives a denominator of n in the fraction, for any whole numbers
topics.p: When {{name}} finds the rule for a number sequence — like "add 7 each time" or "multiply the position number by 3" — can they use that rule to find any term without having to list all the ones before it?

topics.ds: Look for and use mathematical structure: exploit the hierarchy of 2-D shapes to deduce properties; use order of operations and algebraic structure to simplify expressions; connect fraction–decimal–percentage equivalences; use ratio structure to solve proportion problems efficiently
e: Use the property that all rectangles are parallelograms to deduce missing angle facts
Recognise that 3 × (n + 5) = 3n + 15 by applying distributive structure
Use the equivalence 1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5% flexibly to solve a comparison problem
topics.p: When {{name}} is simplifying an algebraic expression or comparing ratios, do they look for the underlying structure — like using the order of operations or spotting that two ratios are equivalent — to make the calculation more efficient?

topics.ds: Model real-world problems involving ratio, scale, volume, unit conversion, and proportional reasoning with appropriate tools, diagrams, or equations
e: Choose a bar model or double number line to represent a ratio problem and solve it
Model a volume problem with a labelled diagram, apply the formula, and interpret the result in context
Determine whether a measurement answer should be rounded and to what degree of accuracy
topics.p: When {{name}} uses maths to solve a real problem — like calculating the volume of a container or working out a percentage discount — do they decide how precise their answer needs to be and explain what it means in context?

topics.ds: Move fluently between real-world situations, diagrams, coordinate grids, algebraic expressions, tables, and symbolic equations involving fractions, ratio, and algebra, explaining connections between representations
e: Translate a word problem into an algebraic equation and also represent it on a bar model
Plot data from a table onto a coordinate grid and interpret the relationship
Explain how a pie chart, a fraction, and a percentage all represent the same proportion
topics.p: When {{name}} is working on an algebra or ratio problem, can they move fluidly between a graph, a table of values, a written equation, and a real-world story — explaining how each representation shows the same relationship?

topics.ds: Compare and describe capacity and volume using language such as full, empty, more than, less than, half full
e: Compare two containers and say which holds more/less
Use 'half full' and 'quarter full' to describe a container
Solve practical problems like 'Which cup has more water?'
topics.p: If {{name}} has two cups of different sizes, can they tell you which holds more water — and describe one as "more full" or "less full" than the other?

topics.ds: Use comparative language for time: quicker, slower, earlier, later
e: Compare two events and say which was quicker/slower
Use 'earlier' and 'later' correctly to describe daily events
Solve practical problems like 'Who finished first?'
topics.p: If {{name}} finishes their dinner before a sibling, can they tell you who finished earlier — and which one was quicker?

topics.ds: Compare two objects directly by length or height and describe the difference using language such as long, short, tall, longer, shorter, taller, double, half
e: Stand two children back-to-back and say who is taller/shorter
Directly compare the heights of two towers and describe one as taller
Use 'longer' and 'shorter' to compare two ribbons placed side by side
topics.p: If {{name}} stands next to the kitchen table and the front door, can they tell you which is taller — and whether they themselves are shorter or taller than each one?

topics.ds: Describe and identify measurable attributes of objects such as length, height, weight, and capacity; use comparative language (longer, shorter, heavier, lighter, more, less)
e: Identify that a pencil has length and can be measured
Describe multiple attributes of one object (e.g. a bottle has height, weight, and capacity)
Use words like 'long', 'heavy', 'full' to describe objects
topics.p: If {{name}} picks up a water bottle and a book, can they tell you which is heavier and which is taller — without any measuring tools?

topics.ds: Compare two objects directly by mass or weight and describe the difference using language such as heavy, light, heavier than, lighter than
e: Heft two objects and say which is heavier/lighter
Use a simple balance to compare the weight of two objects
Describe one object as 'heavier than' another
topics.p: If {{name}} holds a bag of apples in one hand and a feather in the other, can they tell you which is heavier and use words like "much heavier than" to describe the difference?

topics.ds: Sequence events in chronological order using language such as before, after, next, first, today, yesterday, tomorrow, morning, afternoon, evening
e: Order three daily events using 'first', 'next', 'last'
Use 'yesterday', 'today', 'tomorrow' correctly
Describe an event as happening in the 'morning' or 'afternoon'
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} to describe what happened this morning in order, can they use words like "first", "then", "after that" — putting breakfast before leaving for school?

topics.ds: Measure and begin to record capacity and volume using non-standard and standard units
e: Measure capacity by counting how many cups fill a container
Begin to use litres as a unit of capacity
Record capacity measurements with a number and unit
topics.p: If {{name}} fills a jug using a small cup, can they count how many cups it takes — and understand that this tells you how much the jug holds?

topics.ds: Recognise and know the value of different coins and notes
e: Identify 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2 coins
Know that a £2 coin is worth more than a 50p coin
Recognise £5 and £10 notes
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a handful of coins, can they name each one — like 2p, 5p, 20p — and sort them from least to most valuable?

topics.ds: Recognise and use language relating to dates, including days of the week, weeks, months, and years
e: Name the seven days of the week in order
Name the twelve months of the year in order
Understand that a year is made up of months and weeks
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} what day it is today, what day yesterday was, and what month we're in, can they answer all three — and tell you how many months are in a year?

topics.ds: Measure and begin to record time in hours, minutes, and seconds
e: Use a sand timer or stopwatch to time an activity
Begin to understand that 1 minute = 60 seconds
Record a duration in simple terms (e.g. 'it took about 2 minutes')
topics.p: If {{name}} watches the second hand go all the way round a clock, can they count that as one minute — and estimate roughly how many minutes their favourite TV show lasts?

topics.ds: Measure and begin to record lengths and heights using non-standard and standard units
e: Measure the length of a table using cubes and record the result
Begin to use a ruler to measure in centimetres
Record a measurement as a number with a unit
topics.p: If {{name}} measures the length of a book using small cubes laid end to end, can they count how many cubes it takes — and then try measuring the same book with a ruler?

topics.ds: Measure and begin to record mass/weight using non-standard and standard units
e: Use a balance to compare masses of two objects
Measure mass using non-standard units (e.g. 'this book weighs 5 cubes')
Begin to read a simple scale for mass
topics.p: If {{name}} uses balance scales to compare two objects, can they tell you which is heavier — and if given weights like 100g, can they balance an object on the scale?

topics.n: Telling Time: Hours and Half Hours
topics.ds: Tell and write the time to the hour and half past the hour on analogue clocks and digital displays (e.g. 3 o'clock = 3:00, half past 7 = 7:30), and draw clock hands to show these times, placing the hour hand halfway between two numbers for half past
e: Read an analogue clock showing 3 o'clock and one showing half past 7
Write half past 7 as 7:30 and match the digital times 3:00 and 7:30 to the right analogue clocks
Draw the hands on a blank clock face for half past 2, with the minute hand on 6 and the hour hand halfway between 2 and 3
topics.p: If you point to a clock showing 3 o'clock or half past two, can {{name}} tell you the time, say which digital time (3:00 or 2:30) matches it — and draw hands on a blank clock face to show a time you call out?

topics.ds: Find different combinations of coins that equal the same amount of money
e: Show that 50p can be made with 2×20p + 1×10p, or 5×10p, or 1×50p
Systematically find multiple coin combinations for a given total
Explain why different coin sets give the same total
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to make exactly 30p, can they find two or three different ways to do it using different combinations of coins?

topics.ds: Recognise Australian coins (5c, 10c, 20c, 50c, $1, $2) and notes ($5, $10, $20, $50, $100), know that a coin's size does not show its value, and solve simple purchase problems within $20 or 20 cents using real coins and virtual money (on-screen coins and notes)
e: Sort a mixed handful of real Australian coins into cents coins and dollar coins and explain why the small $2 coin is worth more than the larger 50c coin
Pay exactly for a $7 toy in a money app by dragging a virtual $5 note and a virtual $2 coin
Find the total cost of a $5 book and a $3 pen and say whether a $10 note is enough
topics.p: When {{name}} plays shop, can they name the Australian coins and notes — like the $1, $2 and 50c coins and the $5 note — and work out if they have enough to buy two things?

topics.ds: Choose and use appropriate standard units to measure length (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C), and capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit
e: Measure the length of a table in centimetres using a ruler
Weigh an object in grams using a scale
Measure the capacity of a container in millilitres using a measuring jug
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} whether to measure a swimming pool or a piece of paper in cm or m, can they pick the sensible unit for each — and explain why?

topics.ds: Compare and order lengths, mass, and capacity and record results using >, <, and =
e: Measure two objects and write 45cm > 32cm
Order three containers by capacity after measuring each
Use = when two measurements are the same
topics.p: If {{name}} measures three pieces of string as 15 cm, 9 cm, and 22 cm, can they put them in order from shortest to longest — and write that using a < symbol?

topics.ds: Compare and order the mass and capacity of objects indirectly, using a balance or a third object or container as a go-between, and explain the reasoning
e: Use a balance to show the apple is heavier than a block and the block is heavier than the egg, so the apple is heavier than the egg
Pour water from two bottles into the same jug to find which bottle holds more
Order three containers by capacity using cups of rice and explain the order
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to know which of two bottles holds more water, can they work it out by pouring each into the same jug and comparing?

topics.ds: Order three objects by length and compare the lengths of two objects indirectly using a third object
e: Put three ribbons in order from shortest to longest
Use a piece of string to compare the heights of two objects that cannot be placed side by side
Explain that if A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C
topics.p: If {{name}} has three pencils of different lengths but can only compare two at a time, can they figure out which is longest — by using a third pencil as a go-between?

topics.ds: Measure the length of an object using same-size length units laid end to end with no gaps or overlaps
e: Measure a book by laying paper clips end to end and counting them
Understand that the length measurement is the number of units that span the object
Avoid gaps and overlaps when placing units
topics.p: If {{name}} is measuring the length of a table using identical toy bricks, can they lay them end to end with no gaps — and tell you how many bricks long the table is?

topics.ds: Solve simple money problems involving addition and subtraction, including giving change
e: Calculate the total cost of two items priced in pence
Work out change from 50p after buying an item costing 35p
Solve 'How much more money do I need?' problems
topics.p: If {{name}} buys a snack for 45p and pays with a £1 coin, can they work out how much change they should get — and count it back?

topics.n: Number of minutes in an hour
topics.ds: Know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day
e: State that there are 60 minutes in an hour
State that there are 24 hours in a day
Use these facts to solve simple time problems
topics.p: If {{name}} knows there are 60 minutes in an hour, can they tell you how many minutes are in 2 hours — and how many hours make a whole day?

topics.ds: Recognise and use symbols for pounds (£) and pence (p) and combine amounts to make a particular value
e: Write £1.50 or 150p correctly
Combine coins to make a given total, e.g. 50p + 20p + 5p = 75p
Read prices written with £ and p symbols
topics.p: If {{name}} picks up coins worth 50p, 20p, and 10p, can they write the total using the p symbol — and tell you if that's enough to buy something costing 75p?

topics.ds: Compare and sequence intervals of time
e: Order three events by how long they took
Compare the duration of two activities (e.g. 'the race took longer than the walk')
Sequence intervals on a timeline
topics.p: If {{name}} knows a film takes 2 hours and a car journey takes 45 minutes, can they tell you which takes longer — and put a few daily activities in order of how long they take?

topics.ds: Tell and write the time to five minutes on analogue clocks, including quarter past and quarter to the hour, write these times in digital form, and draw clock hands to show them
e: Read an analogue clock showing 3:25 and write the time in digital form as 3:25
Write 'quarter past 9' as 9:15 and 'twenty to four' as 3:40
Draw clock hands to show twenty to four, with the minute hand on 8 and the hour hand just before 4
topics.p: If the clock shows quarter to four, can {{name}} tell you the time — and draw hands on a blank clock face to show twenty past three?

topics.ds: Solve word problems involving lengths within 100, using addition and subtraction with drawings and equations
e: Solve 'The rope is 45 cm long. I cut off 18 cm. How long is it now?'
Draw a diagram (e.g. a ruler drawing) to represent a length word problem
Write an equation with a symbol for the unknown to represent the problem
topics.p: If {{name}} has a piece of rope 75 cm long and cuts off 28 cm, can they work out how much rope is left — and draw a number-line diagram to show it?

topics.ds: Tell and write times to five minutes on analogue and digital clocks with a.m. or p.m. (before or after midday), relating times to daily events and using the words morning, afternoon, evening, noon and midnight. Roman-numeral clock faces and the 24-hour clock are covered in Roman numeral and 24-hour clocks
e: Say whether school starts at 8:45 a.m. or 8:45 p.m., and whether bedtime is 7:30 a.m. or 7:30 p.m.
Write 'twenty-five past four in the afternoon' as 4:25 p.m.
Explain that 12 noon is midday, so times just after it are p.m., while times just after midnight are a.m.
topics.p: If a clock shows 7:45, can {{name}} tell you the time in words — and say whether breakfast would be at 7:45 a.m. or 7:45 p.m.?

topics.ds: Measure, compare, add, and subtract lengths (m/cm/mm), mass (kg/g), and volume/capacity (l/ml) using standard units
e: Measure a length in centimetres and millimetres
Weigh an object using grams and kilograms
Add two measurements in the same unit (e.g. 250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml)
topics.p: If {{name}} pours 350 ml into a jug and then adds another 275 ml, can they work out the total — and tell you how much more is needed to reach 1 litre?

topics.ds: Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressing the length difference in terms of a standard length unit
e: Measure two objects and calculate the difference in length
Express the difference using the correct unit (e.g. '7 cm longer')
Solve a comparison problem: 'How much taller is the bookshelf than the desk?'
topics.p: If a pencil is 16 cm and a crayon is 9 cm, can {{name}} work out how much longer the pencil is — without measuring them side by side?

topics.ds: Compare durations of events and calculate the time taken by particular events or tasks
e: Work out that a TV show from 5:17 p.m. to 5:43 p.m. lasted 26 minutes
Compare a 35-minute bus journey with a 40-minute walk and say which takes longer and by how much
Solve 'The lesson starts at 10:15 and ends at 11:00. How long is it?' (45 minutes)
topics.p: If {{name}} starts cooking at 4:15 p.m. and finishes at 5:00 p.m., can they work out how long the cooking took?

topics.ds: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimetres, and metres
e: Estimate the length of a classroom object before measuring it
Use a known reference (e.g. width of a finger ≈ 1 cm) to make reasonable estimates
Check estimates by measuring and evaluate how close they were
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at a car parked outside, can they estimate roughly how many metres long it is — and then check whether their guess was reasonable?

topics.ds: Identify common uses of halves, quarters and eighths in relation to events and time, such as half-time in a game, half an hour, a quarter of an hour, and an activity split into eight equal time parts
e: Describe half-time in a football game as the point when half the playing time is over, and explain that half an hour is 30 minutes because an hour is split into 2 equal parts
Show a quarter of an hour on a clock face as a quarter of the way round
Represent a 16-minute class activity as a strip of eight equal 2-minute parts, colour one part and say it is one eighth of the activity (2 minutes)
topics.p: If a 16-minute game is split into 8 equal turns, can {{name}} work out that each turn is one eighth of the game — 2 minutes — and do they know that half an hour is 30 minutes?

topics.ds: Add and subtract amounts of money to give change, using both £ and p in practical contexts
e: Calculate the total cost of two or three items priced in pounds and pence
Work out the change from £5 or £10
Record money calculations using £ and p notation correctly (e.g. £3.47)
topics.p: If {{name}} buys a book for £3.50 and a pencil for £1.25 with a £5 note, can they work out exactly how much change they should receive?

topics.ds: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, metre sticks, and measuring tapes
e: Choose the most appropriate tool for measuring a given object
Align the zero mark of a ruler with the end of the object and read the measurement
Measure lengths in inches, feet, centimetres, and metres using the correct tool
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to measure a piece of fabric about 80 cm long, can they pick the right tool — a short ruler or a tape measure — and use it accurately?

topics.ds: Measure the perimeter of simple 2-D shapes
e: Measure each side of a rectangle and add the lengths to find the perimeter
Calculate the perimeter of a regular shape given the side length
Explain that perimeter is the total distance around a shape
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to put a decorative border around a rectangular picture frame 20 cm wide and 30 cm tall, can they work out the total length of border needed?

topics.ds: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths to the nearest whole unit and display the data on a line plot
e: Measure the lengths of several objects and record the data
Create a line plot with a horizontal scale marked in whole-number units
Interpret a line plot to answer questions about the data
topics.p: If {{name}} measures the length of ten leaves to the nearest cm and records the results, can they display the data on a simple number-line plot — grouping leaves of the same length?

topics.ds: Measure the length of an object using two different length units and describe how the measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen
e: Measure a desk in both centimetres and inches and compare the two numbers
Explain that measuring with a smaller unit gives a larger number
Predict whether a measurement in centimetres will be greater or less than in inches
topics.p: If {{name}} measures the same book in centimetres and then in inches, can they explain why the numbers are different even though the book hasn't changed size?

topics.ds: Solve practical money transactions with Australian money involving addition, subtraction and equal groups — totals, change and costs of several identical items — and explain the answer in terms of the purchase
e: Work out the total cost of a $4 drink and a $7 sandwich and the change from a $20 note
Find the cost of 3 apples at 50c each by repeated addition
Make 85c using the fewest Australian coins and explain the choice
topics.p: At the canteen, if {{name}} buys a $4 drink and a $7 sandwich with a $20 note, can they work out how much change they should get?

topics.ds: Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately
e: Determine the total value of a collection of coins
Solve a word problem about making change with US currency
Use $ and ¢ symbols correctly in answers
topics.p: If {{name}} has 2 quarters, 1 dime, and 3 pennies, can they work out the total — and tell you whether that's enough to buy something costing 65 cents?

topics.ds: Recognise, read and show quarter past and quarter to the hour on an analog clock, linking each to a quarter turn of the minute hand
e: Read a clock showing 3:15 as 'quarter past three'
Set the hands of a clock to quarter to seven
Explain that the minute hand has turned a quarter of the way round at quarter past
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at an analog clock and the big hand points to the 3, can they say it's 'quarter past'? And can they recognise 'quarter to' when it points to the 9?

topics.ds: Tell and write the time from analogue clocks with Roman-numeral faces (I to XII, including IV, which some clocks show as IIII, and IX), knowing that the minute positions are the same as on a clock with ordinary numbers; and read and write times on 12-hour and 24-hour clocks, knowing that the 24-hour clock runs from 00:00 at midnight to 23:59. Times from 1:00 a.m. to 11:59 a.m. keep the same hour (7:05 a.m. = 07:05); times from 1:00 p.m. to 11:59 p.m. are 12 hours more (3:20 p.m. = 15:20). The 12 o'clock hour is the exception to both: 12:20 p.m., just after noon, stays 12:20, and 12:20 a.m., just after midnight, becomes 00:20. Fluent conversion between 12- and 24-hour times is developed in Year 4
e: Read a Roman-numeral clock with the minute hand on IX and the hour hand between IV and V as quarter to five (4:45)
Match the Roman numerals I to XII to the hour positions on a blank clock face, including IV (or IIII), IX and XII
Write 3:20 p.m. as 15:20 and 7:05 a.m. as 07:05, then write 12:20 p.m. as 12:20 and 12:20 a.m. as 00:20, explaining why adding 12 works only for p.m. times from 1 p.m. onwards
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a clock with Roman numerals where the minute hand points to IX and the hour hand is between IV and V, can they read it as quarter to five — and say what time 15:20 on a 24-hour clock means?

topics.ds: Choose a smaller uniform informal unit when a measurement needs to be more accurate, recognising that a smaller unit gives a larger count, for length, mass and capacity
e: Measure a book with pencils (about 2) and then with paperclips (about 9) and explain why the paperclip count is bigger
Choose teaspoons instead of cups to measure how much a small glass holds and explain why
Explain why '3 and a bit hand spans' is less accurate than measuring the same table in counting cubes
topics.p: If {{name}} measures a book with pencils and gets 'about 2', can they see that using smaller paperclips would give a more exact measurement — and a bigger number?

topics.ds: Tell, write and estimate the time to the nearest minute on analogue and digital clocks, using vocabulary such as o'clock, a.m./p.m., morning, afternoon, noon and midnight; record and compare times and durations in seconds, minutes and hours
e: Read 7:43 from an analogue clock face and write it on a digital display
Estimate whether brushing teeth takes about 2 seconds, 2 minutes or 2 hours, then time it to check
Compare 1 minute 20 seconds with 75 seconds and say which is longer
topics.p: If the kitchen clock shows 7:43, can {{name}} read the exact time and write it as it would look on a digital clock — and say which is longer, 1 minute 20 seconds or 75 seconds?

topics.ds: Know the number of seconds in a minute and the number of days in each month, year, and leap year
e: State that there are 60 seconds in a minute
Name the months and state the number of days in each
Explain that a leap year has 366 days and occurs every 4 years
topics.p: If you ask {{name}} how many days are in September and whether this year is a leap year, can they answer both — and tell you how many seconds are in a minute?

topics.ds: Read a calendar to identify today's date and the day of the week for a given date, and determine the number of days between two events
e: Find 15 March on a calendar page and say which day of the week it is
Write today's date from the classroom calendar in day-month form
Count how many days from 3 June to a birthday on 17 June
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at the family calendar, can they find today's date and count how many days are left until their birthday or the school holidays?

topics.ds: Read, write, and convert time between analogue and digital 12-hour and 24-hour clocks
e: Convert 3:45 pm to 15:45 in 24-hour time
Read 19:30 and state the 12-hour equivalent as 7:30 pm
Match a set of 12-hour and 24-hour times
topics.p: If a train timetable shows a departure at 14:35, can {{name}} convert that to 12-hour clock time — and tell you whether that's morning or afternoon?

topics.ds: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in, square ft)
e: Count unit squares to find the area of an L-shaped figure
Measure the area of a book cover using square-centimetre tiles
Compare areas of two shapes by counting their unit squares
topics.p: If {{name}} draws a shape on squared centimetre paper, can they find its area by counting the squares — including making a sensible estimate for any partial squares?

topics.ds: Use tiling to demonstrate the distributive property: the area of a rectangle with sides a and (b+c) equals a×b + a×c; use area models to represent the distributive property
e: Tile a 3×(4+2) rectangle and show it decomposes into 3×4 and 3×2
Use an area model to compute 6×13 as 6×10 + 6×3
Draw an area model showing 5×(7+3) = 5×7 + 5×3
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to work out 6 × 13 by splitting it into 6 × 10 and 6 × 3, can they draw a rectangle divided into two parts to show why that method works?

topics.ds: Find the area of a rectangle by tiling it with unit squares and show that the result equals the product of the side lengths
e: Tile a 4×6 rectangle and count 24 squares, then verify 4×6=24
Explain why the number of rows times the number in each row gives the area
Draw a rectangle on squared paper, tile it, and write the multiplication
topics.p: If a rectangular room is 4 m long and 3 m wide, can {{name}} work out its area by tiling it with 1-metre squares in their head — and explain why that equals 4 × 3?

topics.ds: Recognise area as additive; find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing into non-overlapping rectangles and summing their areas
e: Decompose an L-shape into two rectangles, find each area, and add them
Find the area of a floor plan shaped like a T by splitting into rectangles
Solve: A room is L-shaped (3m×5m plus 2m×4m) — what is the total area?
topics.p: If {{name}} is given an L-shaped room on squared paper, can they split it into two rectangles, find the area of each part, and add them to get the total area?

topics.ds: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas
e: Calculate the area of a 7 cm × 9 cm rectangle as 63 cm²
Draw a rectangle with area 36 square units and label its side lengths
Solve: A garden is 8 m by 5 m — what is its area?
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to carpet a room that is 5 m by 4 m, can they work out how much carpet to buy — using multiplication rather than counting squares?

topics.ds: Convert between different units of measure (e.g. kilometre to metre, hour to minute, minute to second, year to month, week to day)
e: Convert 3 km to 3000 m
State 2 hours = 120 minutes
Convert 5 weeks to 35 days
topics.p: If {{name}} is told a journey is 3.5 km, can they convert that to metres — and also turn 2 hours 15 minutes into just minutes?

topics.ds: Recognise the relationship between dollars and cents (100 cents = 1 dollar), read and write amounts in $ and c notation (e.g. $3.45 and 345c), represent the same amount with different combinations of Australian coins and notes, and calculate change in dollars and cents
e: Write $2.70 as 270c and 450c as $4.50
Show $3.60 in two different ways using Australian coins and notes
Work out the change from a $10 note for a purchase costing $6.40
topics.p: At the shops, can {{name}} read a price like $3.45, explain that it means 3 dollars and 45 cents, and work out the change from a $10 note?

topics.ds: Solve word problems involving elapsed time by adding and subtracting time intervals in minutes, including using a number line
e: A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end?
Calculate how many minutes between 9:20 and 10:05
Use a number line to show the elapsed time between two events
topics.p: If {{name}} starts football practice at 3:20 p.m. and it lasts 75 minutes, can they work out what time it finishes — using a number line to help?

topics.ds: Estimate, compare, and calculate different measures including money in pounds and pence
e: Estimate the length of the classroom in metres
Compare 1.5 kg and 1200 g and identify which is heavier
Calculate the total cost of 3 items at £2.45, £1.30, and £0.75
