topics.p: If {{name}} is comparing three items costing £2.85, £3.10, and £2.50, can they put them in order from cheapest to most expensive — and work out the total cost?

topics.ds: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths to the nearest half and quarter inch; display the data on a line plot with a scale marked in whole numbers, halves, and quarters
e: Measure five objects to the nearest 1/4 inch
Create a line plot showing the lengths of classmates' pencils in half-inches
Read a line plot and answer questions about the data
topics.p: If {{name}} measures ten pencil lengths to the nearest quarter inch, can they record the data and plot it on a number line split into quarters — then spot which length appears most?

topics.ds: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using grams, kilograms, and litres; solve one-step word problems involving mass or volume
e: Estimate the mass of a textbook in grams or kilograms
Read a scale to measure liquid volume in litres
Solve: 3 bags weigh 250 g each — what is the total mass?
topics.p: If {{name}} is filling bottles that each hold 250 ml from a 2-litre container of juice, can they work out how many bottles they can fill?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving perimeters of polygons: find perimeter from side lengths, find an unknown side length, and explore rectangles with same perimeter but different areas (or vice versa)
e: Calculate the perimeter of a rectangle with sides 8 cm and 5 cm
Find the missing side of a pentagon with perimeter 30 cm and four known sides
Draw two rectangles both with perimeter 24 cm but different areas
topics.p: If a rectangle has a perimeter of 24 cm and one side is 8 cm, can {{name}} work out the length of the other side — without drawing it?

topics.ds: Understand that a unit square has one square unit of area and that the area of a plane figure is the number of unit squares that cover it without gaps or overlaps
e: Identify a unit square and state its area is 1 square unit
Explain why a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units
Distinguish between area and perimeter as different measurements
topics.p: If {{name}} counts the small squares inside a rectangle drawn on squared paper, can they tell you the area — and explain what "one square unit" means?

topics.ds: Apply the area formula (l × w) and perimeter formula (2l + 2w) for rectangles including squares in real-world and mathematical problems; calculate and compare areas using standard units (cm², m²) and estimate areas of irregular shapes
e: Find the width of a room given area = 48 m² and length = 8 m
Calculate the area of a square with side 7.5 cm
Estimate the area of an irregular pond drawn on a cm² grid
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to carpet a room 6.5 m × 4 m, can they calculate the area — and also work out how many metres of skirting board are needed around the edge?

topics.ds: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system (km/m/cm/mm, kg/g, l/ml, hr/min/sec); convert between different metric units and express measurements in terms of a smaller unit; record equivalents in conversion tables
e: Convert 3.5 km to 3,500 m
Complete a conversion table for cm and mm: (1,10), (2,20), (3,30)...
Express 2 kg 350 g as 2,350 g
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to convert 3.5 kg to grams, can they do it confidently — and also fill in a simple two-column table showing the same measurements in kg and g?

topics.ds: Measure and estimate the volume of solids by counting unit cubes: build cuboids from 1 cm³ cubes and count them, count the cubes in models and drawings (including hidden cubes), estimate how many cubes will fill a box and check by filling it, and record volumes in cubic units (cm³, in³, ft³ or improvised units)
e: Build a 3 × 2 × 2 cuboid from 1 cm³ cubes and state its volume as 12 cm³
Count the cubes in a drawing of a solid built from cubes, including the hidden ones at the back, and give the volume in cubic units
Estimate how many centimetre cubes will fill a small box, then fill it to check
topics.p: If {{name}} has a small cardboard box, can they estimate how many sugar cubes would fit inside and then fill it to check — and count the cubes in a picture of a cube model, including the hidden ones at the back?

topics.ds: Estimate the capacity of containers in litres and millilitres by comparing them with known measures (e.g. a 1-litre bottle) and check by filling with water; distinguish a container's capacity (how much it can hold) from the volume of liquid in it. Estimating the volume of solids with 1 cm³ cubes is covered in Counting Unit Cubes
e: Estimate whether a mug holds about 30 ml, 300 ml or 3 litres, then check with a measuring jug
Estimate the capacity of a jug by comparing it with a 1-litre bottle, then fill it with water to check
Explain that a 1-litre jug half full of water has a capacity of 1 litre but holds 500 ml of water
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at a saucepan, can they estimate whether it holds about half a litre, 2 litres or 10 litres — and check by filling it with water from a 1-litre jug?

topics.ds: Use estimation and rounding to check and explain the reasonableness of money calculations in dollars and cents, including rounding cash totals to the nearest 5 cents as Australian shops do, and solve practical financial problems
e: Estimate the total of $4.95, $2.10 and $7.85 as about $15 before calculating the exact total
Round a cash total of $12.37 to $12.35 and $8.48 to $8.50 and explain the 5-cent rule
Decide whether $36 change from $50 is reasonable after buying items costing $6.90 and $8.15
topics.p: At the supermarket, can {{name}} round the prices in the trolley to estimate the total before you pay — and tell whether the change you get back looks about right?

topics.ds: Solve word problems involving distances, time intervals, liquid volumes, masses, and money using the four operations with fractions or decimals; represent with diagrams including number lines
e: A 2.5 kg bag of flour is split equally into 4 portions — what does each weigh?
A journey takes 1 hr 45 min; what time do you arrive if you leave at 09:20?
Three ribbons of 0.75 m, 1.2 m, and 0.95 m — what is the total length?
topics.p: If {{name}} is planning a 4.5 km walk and has already walked 1.75 km, can they work out how far is left — and estimate how long the remaining walk might take?

topics.ds: Make a line plot to display measurement data in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions using line plot data
e: Create a line plot of seed growth measurements in 1/8-inch increments
Use a line plot to find the difference between the longest and shortest specimens
Calculate the total length of all items in a line plot by adding the fractional measurements
topics.p: If {{name}} records caterpillar lengths as fractions of an inch and plots them on a number line, can they work out the total length of three caterpillars by adding the fractions from the plot?

topics.ds: Understand and use approximate equivalences between metric units and common imperial units (inches, pounds, pints)
e: State that 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm and use this to estimate length in inches
Know that 1 kg ≈ 2.2 pounds and estimate a person's weight in pounds
Convert approximately between litres and pints (1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints)
topics.p: If {{name}} hears that a baby weighs 7 pounds, can they give a rough idea of that in kilograms — using the approximate conversion they know?

topics.ds: Measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres
e: Find the perimeter of an L-shaped figure by identifying all side lengths
Calculate the perimeter of a composite shape where some sides must be deduced
Draw a composite rectilinear shape with a perimeter of 40 cm
topics.p: If {{name}} is given an L-shaped garden plan with all the side measurements labelled, can they add all the sides together to find the total perimeter?

topics.ds: Interpret unmarked and partial units on scaled instruments and read digital instruments when measuring length, mass, capacity, duration and temperature, using appropriate units
e: Read 500 g on kitchen scales numbered every 200 g where the pointer sits halfway between 400 g and 600 g
Read 175 ml on a jug marked every 50 ml and 23 degrees on a thermometer marked every 2 degrees
Read and record a time of 1 minute 26.4 seconds from a digital stopwatch and a length of 12.7 cm on a ruler
topics.p: When {{name}} helps with baking, can they read the scales when the pointer is between two numbers — like halfway between 400 g and 600 g?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving converting between units of time (hours↔minutes, minutes↔seconds, years↔months, weeks↔days)
e: Convert 3 hours 25 minutes to 205 minutes
A programme lasts 150 seconds — express in minutes and seconds
How many days are in 8 weeks and 3 days?
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to convert 2 hours 35 minutes into just minutes, can they do it — and then convert 180 seconds into minutes and seconds?

topics.ds: Recognise volume as an attribute of solid figures; understand that a unit cube (side length 1 unit) has 'one cubic unit' of volume and can be used to measure volume; a solid packed with n unit cubes has volume n cubic units
e: Explain what 'volume' means for a 3D shape and how it differs from area
Identify a unit cube and explain that it represents one cubic unit of volume
Determine the volume of a small solid by counting the unit cubes that fill it
topics.p: If {{name}} builds a solid shape using small cubes, can they count the cubes to find the volume — and explain what "one cubic centimetre" means in everyday terms?

topics.ds: Find the area of parallelograms and triangles by relating them to rectangles: rearrange a parallelogram (cut off a triangle and move it) into a rectangle with the same base and perpendicular height; see a right triangle as half of a rectangle and any triangle as half of a parallelogram (or as two right triangles); use the resulting formulae A = b × h for parallelograms and A = ½ × b × h for triangles, always using the perpendicular height rather than a slanted side, including when the height falls outside an obtuse triangle; and recognise when an area formula can be used (rectangles, parallelograms, triangles) and when another method is needed, such as counting or estimating squares for an irregular shape
e: Cut a right-angled triangle off one end of a parallelogram with base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm, move it to the other end to make an 8 cm × 5 cm rectangle, and state the area as 40 cm²

Show that a right triangle with legs 6 cm and 4 cm is half of a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle (12 cm²), and that an obtuse triangle with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm, drawn outside the triangle, is half of a parallelogram (42 cm²)

Decide that a formula gives the area of a parallelogram with base 10 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm (50 cm², not the 60 cm² from its slanted 6 cm side) but not of an irregular leaf shape, whose area must be estimated by counting squares
topics.p: If {{name}} is cutting triangular pieces of cloth where the base is 8 cm and the height is 5 cm, can they use a formula to work out the area of each piece?

topics.ds: Solve practical financial problems in Australian dollars and cents — planning a budget, comparing best buys by unit price, and checking reasonableness by estimation — using a calculator or spreadsheet where appropriate
e: Plan a class party for $60 by choosing items and totalling their costs in a spreadsheet or on a calculator
Decide whether a 2 kg bag of rice for $5.80 or a 500 g bag for $1.60 is better value and explain why
Estimate whether a list of 5 items fits a $25 budget before calculating the exact total
topics.p: If {{name}} has $25 to spend on supplies for a school camp, can they plan what to buy, keep a running total, and work out which pack size is better value?

topics.ds: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given system (e.g. 5 cm to 0.05 m) using decimal notation to up to three decimal places; convert between smaller and larger units of length, mass, volume, and time
e: Convert 3,250 g to 3.25 kg using decimal notation
Convert 0.45 km to 450 m
Explain the relationship between mm, cm, m, and km using powers of 10
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to convert 5 cm to metres and write the answer as a decimal, can they do it — and also convert 2.45 kg into grams?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving the calculation and conversion of units of measure, using decimal notation and multi-step reasoning in real-world contexts
e: Solve: 'A recipe uses 0.75 kg of flour. How many grams are needed for 3 batches?'
Compare 2.5 litres and 2,450 ml by converting to the same unit
Solve a multi-step problem involving time, distance, and unit conversion
topics.p: If {{name}} is filling a fish tank that holds 60 litres and the tap fills it at 3.5 litres per minute, can they work out how long it will take to fill the tank?

topics.ds: Convert between miles and kilometres using the approximate relationship (5 miles ≈ 8 km)
e: Convert 40 miles to approximately 64 km
Explain why the conversion factor between miles and km is approximately 1.6
Use the miles↔km relationship to compare a 10 km race with a 6-mile run
topics.p: If {{name}} is driving 40 miles to a theme park, can they use the rule that 5 miles ≈ 8 km to estimate roughly how many kilometres that is?

topics.ds: Recognise that shapes with the same area can have different perimeters and vice versa; explore this relationship systematically
e: Draw two rectangles with area 24 cm² but different perimeters
Find two shapes with perimeter 20 cm but different areas
Explain why a long thin rectangle and a square can have the same area but different perimeters
topics.p: If {{name}} has 12 square tiles to arrange, can they make different-shaped rectangles and notice that the area stays the same (12 tiles) but the perimeters are all different?

topics.ds: Recognise volume as additive; find volumes of composite solid figures made of two or more non-overlapping right rectangular prisms
e: Decompose an L-shaped solid into two cuboids and calculate total volume
Solve a real-world problem requiring the volume of a composite figure (e.g. a step-shaped structure)
Explain why splitting a composite solid into rectangular prisms allows calculation of total volume
topics.p: If an L-shaped swimming pool is made of two rectangular sections, can {{name}} find the volume of each section separately and add them to get the total volume of the pool?

topics.ds: Find the volume of right rectangular prisms by packing with unit cubes and show it equals l × w × h (or base area × height); apply V = l × w × h and V = B × h to solve real-world problems; calculate, estimate, and compare volumes of cubes and cuboids in standard units (cm³, m³); and recognise that the formula applies to cuboids, while an irregular solid built from cubes must be counted or split into cuboids
e: Use V = l × w × h to find the volume of a cuboid 4 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm = 60 cm³
Explain why packing a prism with unit cubes gives the same result as multiplying edge lengths
Compare the 60 cm³ cuboid with an irregular model built from 58 centimetre cubes, explaining that the formula works for the cuboid but the model's cubes must be counted
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to work out how much soil fits in a plant box that is 40 cm long, 20 cm wide, and 15 cm deep, can they use a formula to calculate the volume?

topics.ds: Find the area of polygons such as trapezoids, kites, rhombuses, irregular quadrilaterals and other rectilinear or non-rectilinear polygons by decomposition or composition: decompose the shape into rectangles and triangles and add the parts, or compose it into an enclosing rectangle and subtract the pieces outside; record the dimensions used for each piece, check that the pieces neither overlap nor leave gaps, and apply this to real-world problems such as floor plans, gardens and signs, giving answers in square units. The focus is the decomposition and composition strategy, which works for any polygon whether or not a dedicated formula is known
e: Find the area of a trapezoid with parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm and height 4 cm by splitting it into a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle and two triangles with a combined base of 4 cm (24 + 8 = 32 cm²)
Find the area of a kite with diagonals 8 cm and 6 cm by enclosing it in an 8 cm × 6 cm rectangle and subtracting the four corner triangles (48 − 24 = 24 cm²)
Work out the turf needed for a garden shaped like a 12 m × 8 m rectangle with a right triangle (legs 8 m and 3 m) attached to one end (96 + 12 = 108 m²)
topics.p: If {{name}} has a plan of a garden shaped like a rectangle with a triangle on one end, could they split it into the rectangle and the triangle, work out each area and add them to find how much turf to buy?

topics.ds: Solve and estimate financial problems in Australian dollars involving percentage discounts, adding the 10% GST to prices given before GST (recognising that GST-inclusive prices already contain it), and account balances that go below zero
e: Work out the sale price of an $80 jacket with a 25% discount and estimate it first as about $60
For a $45 price given before GST, find the 10% GST of $4.50 and the GST-inclusive price of $49.50, and explain why a price already marked 'GST inclusive' does not get another 10% added
Show a bank balance of $20 that drops by $35 as -$15 on a number line and explain what it means
topics.p: If {{name}} sees an $80 jacket marked 25% off, can they work out the sale price — and for a $45 price shown before GST, work out what you'd pay once the 10% GST is added?

topics.ds: Use a spreadsheet or calculator where appropriate to solve financial problems with decimals and percentages — totalling decimal amounts, applying percentage discounts, and adding 10% GST to prices given before GST — checking results by estimation and justifying the choice of tool
e: Build a spreadsheet budget that adds and subtracts amounts such as $12.85, $7.60 and $3.95 and check the running total by rounding
Use a spreadsheet formula to apply a 15% discount to a list of prices and check one result by estimating 15% of $64.90 as about $10
Use a formula to add 10% GST to prices given before GST, and explain why 10% is not added again to a price already marked 'GST inclusive'
topics.p: Could {{name}} set up a simple spreadsheet for a class fundraiser that totals the costs, takes 15% off sale items, and checks the totals with a quick estimate?

topics.ds: Represent right rectangular prisms, triangular prisms and pyramids with rectangular or triangular bases using nets made of rectangles and triangles; use the solid's dimensions to label every face on the net; find the surface area as the sum of the face areas, in square units; distinguish surface area (the area covering the outside) from volume (the space inside); and apply this to real-world problems such as wrapping, painting or making boxes, including deciding which faces to include (e.g. an open-topped box)
e: Draw the net of a 5 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm cuboid, label each rectangle's dimensions, and find the surface area as 2 × (20 + 15 + 12) = 94 cm²
Use the net of a square-based pyramid with 6 cm base edges and triangular faces of height 5 cm to find its surface area (36 + 4 × 15 = 96 cm²)
Find the card needed for an open-topped box 30 cm × 20 cm × 10 cm, leaving out the top (600 + 2 × 300 + 2 × 200 = 1,600 cm²), and explain why the answer is in cm² rather than cm³
topics.p: If {{name}} wants to wrap a shoebox 30 cm long, 20 cm wide and 10 cm tall, could they sketch the box unfolded flat, work out the area of each rectangle and add them up to find how much paper is needed?

topics.ds: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths by packing it with cubes whose edge is a suitable unit fraction of a unit (e.g. 1/2 or 1/4), working out the volume of one such cube (a cube with 1/2-unit edges has volume 1/8 cubic unit), counting the cubes and multiplying; show that this gives the same result as multiplying the edge lengths; and apply V = l × w × h and V = B × h with fractional or mixed-number edge lengths in real-world and mathematical problems
e: Show that 8 cubes with 1/2 cm edges fit exactly into a 1 cm cube, so each has a volume of 1/8 cm³
Pack a 1½ cm × 1 cm × 2½ cm prism with 1/2 cm cubes (3 × 2 × 5 = 30 cubes), find its volume as 30 × 1/8 = 3¾ cm³, and check that 1½ × 1 × 2½ gives the same answer
Find how much sand fills a box 2¼ ft long, 1½ ft wide and 2/3 ft deep using V = l × w × h (2¼ ft³)
topics.p: If {{name}} has a gift box 2½ inches long, 1½ inches wide and 2 inches tall, could they work out its volume — and show why filling it with little half-inch cubes gives the same answer?

topics.ds: Understand division as sharing equally into groups or as grouping (how many groups of a given size can be made)
e: Share 10 counters equally between 2 plates
Group 12 objects into sets of 3 and count 4 groups
Use concrete objects to solve 'How many groups of 2 in 8?'
topics.p: If {{name}} has 12 grapes to share equally between 3 friends, can they work out that each friend gets 4 — and explain what they did?

topics.ds: Use arrays to represent multiplication and division situations
e: Build an array of 3 rows of 4 objects to show 3 × 4
Read an array and state the total
Use an array to solve a simple division problem (e.g. 12 objects in rows of 4 → 3 rows)
topics.p: If {{name}} sees eggs arranged in 3 rows of 4 in a box, can they use that grid layout to work out both '3 × 4 = 12' and '12 ÷ 3 = 4'?

topics.ds: Understand multiplication as repeated addition and grouping equal sets
e: Explain that 3 groups of 2 is the same as 2 + 2 + 2
Use objects to make equal groups and count the total
Recognise an array as showing equal rows
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to count 4 bags with 3 apples in each, can they see that instead of counting all 12 one by one, they could add 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 — or say '4 groups of 3'?

topics.ds: Represent practical equal-sharing and grouping situations with virtual materials (dragging on-screen objects onto plates or into groups) as well as physical objects, using counting or subitising to check each share
e: Share 10 on-screen strawberries equally onto 2 plates by dragging them and say each plate has 5
Drag 12 virtual blocks into groups of 3 and count the groups
Share 6 real crackers between 3 teddies, then repeat the share on screen and check it matches
topics.p: If {{name}} uses a tablet game to share 10 strawberries between 2 plates, can they make the shares equal — and share real crackers between teddies the same way?

topics.ds: Understand and apply the commutative property of multiplication and recognise that division is not commutative
e: Explain that 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 and show this with an array rotated
Use commutativity to choose the easier calculation
Demonstrate that 12 ÷ 3 ≠ 3 ÷ 12
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that 4 × 7 gives the same answer as 7 × 4 — so they can choose whichever order is easier to remember from their times tables?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving multiplication and division using arrays, repeated addition, mental methods, and known facts
e: Solve 'There are 5 bags with 2 apples in each. How many apples?' using repeated addition or known fact
Solve 'Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children' using grouping
Draw an array to solve a multiplication problem in context
topics.p: If you tell {{name}} 'you have 5 bags with 4 marbles in each — how many altogether?', can they figure it out using objects, a drawing, or mental adding?

topics.ds: Recognise odd and even numbers
e: Identify whether a given number is odd or even
Explain that even numbers can be divided into 2 equal groups
Spot the pattern: even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8
topics.p: If you give {{name}} a number like 37 or 84, can they quickly tell you whether it's odd or even — and explain how they know?

topics.ds: Read, write, and interpret the symbols ×, ÷, and = in multiplication and division number sentences
e: Read 3 × 4 = 12 aloud as 'three times four equals twelve'
Write a multiplication sentence to match an array
Read 12 ÷ 3 = 4 aloud correctly
topics.p: If you write '6 × 4 = 24' or '15 ÷ 3 = 5' on paper, can {{name}} tell you what the times sign, division sign, and equals sign each mean?

topics.ds: Model practical equal-sharing and grouping problems up to about 30 with diagrams, physical objects and virtual materials (dragging on-screen objects into equal groups or arrays), and solve them using skip counting or repeated addition
e: Solve 'share 18 stickers equally among 3 friends' by dragging on-screen stickers into 3 groups and say each friend gets 6
Solve 'how many bags of 5 apples can we make from 20?' with real apples or counters and skip count the bags
Draw a diagram of 4 tables with 4 chairs each and check the total of 16 with an on-screen array
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to share 18 stickers equally among 3 friends, can they work it out by sorting them into groups — either with the real stickers or on a tablet?

topics.ds: Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5, and 10 multiplication tables
e: Quickly answer 5 × 3 = 15 from memory
Quickly answer 20 ÷ 5 = 4 from memory
Recite the 2, 5, and 10 times tables fluently
topics.p: Can {{name}} quickly recall times table facts from the 2s, 5s, and 10s — like '5 × 6 = 30' or '20 ÷ 2 = 10' — forwards and backwards?

topics.ds: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends
e: Count objects in a 3×4 array and write 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
Explain that each row has the same number of objects so the total can be found by repeated addition
Draw a rectangular array to model a given repeated-addition equation
topics.p: If {{name}} sees 4 rows of 5 stickers on a sheet, can they use repeated addition — '5 + 5 + 5 + 5' — to find the total, and write it as an equation?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving multiplication and division, including scaling problems and correspondence problems where n objects are connected to m objects
e: Solve a scaling problem (e.g. 'the ribbon is 3 times as long')
Solve a correspondence problem (e.g. '4 shirts and 3 trousers — how many outfits?')
Solve a missing-number multiplication or division problem
topics.p: If a recipe for 4 people needs 3 eggs, can {{name}} work out how many eggs are needed for 8 people — recognising it as a doubling or scaling problem?

topics.ds: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them
e: Divide a rectangle into equal rows and columns of unit squares
Count the total number of squares using repeated addition or skip counting
Relate the rows-and-columns structure to a rectangular array
topics.p: Can {{name}} draw lines to divide a rectangle into a neat grid of equal squares, then count all the squares to find the total?

topics.ds: Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4, and 8 multiplication tables
e: Recall 3 × 1 through 3 × 12 and corresponding division facts
Recall 4 × 1 through 4 × 12 and corresponding division facts
Recall 8 × 1 through 8 × 12 and corresponding division facts
topics.p: Can {{name}} quickly recall facts from the 3, 4, and 8 times tables — like '8 × 7 = 56' or '36 ÷ 4 = 9' — without having to work them out each time?

topics.ds: Write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using known tables, including two-digit × one-digit, using mental and progressing to formal written methods
e: Calculate 23 × 4 using partitioning (20 × 4 + 3 × 4)
Calculate 96 ÷ 8 using known table facts
Begin to use a formal written layout for short multiplication
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out sums like '23 × 4' or '68 ÷ 4' — either in their head using times table knowledge, or by writing it out step by step?

topics.ds: Recall multiplication and division facts for multiplication tables up to 12 × 12
e: Recall any fact from the 1–12 times tables rapidly
Recall the corresponding division fact for any multiplication fact
Use known facts to check or derive answers in calculations
topics.p: Can {{name}} recall any multiplication or division fact from all the times tables up to 12 — like '9 × 8 = 72' or '132 ÷ 12 = 11' — quickly and accurately?

topics.ds: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem (e.g. find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8)
e: Explain that 32 ÷ 8 = ? is the same as 8 × ? = 32
Use a known multiplication fact to find a division answer
Describe the relationship between multiplication and division as inverse operations
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out '32 ÷ 8' by asking 'what do I multiply 8 by to get 32?' — using times table knowledge rather than a separate division method?

topics.ds: Recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations
e: List all factor pairs of a given number (e.g. 24: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6)
Use commutativity to reorder a multiplication for easier mental calculation
Explain what a factor pair is and how commutativity helps
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to multiply '4 × 15', can they spot that splitting it into '4 × 5 × 3 = 20 × 3 = 60' is a clever shortcut — using factor pairs to make it easier?

topics.ds: Fluently multiply and divide within 100 using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division
e: Answer any single-digit multiplication fact within 3 seconds
Answer any related division fact within 3 seconds
Use known facts to derive unknown facts (e.g. 9 × 7 from 10 × 7 − 7)
topics.p: Can {{name}} answer any times table fact up to 10 × 10 quickly — and also give the related division facts, like '63 ÷ 9 = 7' from knowing '9 × 7 = 63'?

topics.ds: Use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally, including multiplying by 0 and 1, dividing by 1, and multiplying together three numbers
e: Calculate 40 × 6 = 240 mentally using place value
Explain why any number × 0 = 0 and any number × 1 = the number itself
Multiply three numbers mentally by choosing a useful pair first (e.g. 2 × 7 × 5 = 2 × 5 × 7 = 70)
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out things like '6 × 0', '1 × 35', or '100 ÷ 100' instantly in their head — using what they know rather than working everything out from scratch?

topics.ds: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities
e: Solve an equal-groups word problem using multiplication
Solve a measurement division problem (e.g. 'How many 4-cm pieces from a 28-cm ribbon?')
Solve an array/area word problem using multiplication
topics.p: If you tell {{name}} 'there are 7 boxes with 9 pencils in each — how many pencils?', can they recognise it as a multiplication problem and solve it correctly?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving multiplying and adding, including using the distributive law, integer scaling problems, and harder correspondence problems
e: Use the distributive law to solve 14 × 6 as 10 × 6 + 4 × 6
Solve a scaling problem (e.g. 'A tower is 3 times as tall as a 15 m building')
Solve a correspondence problem (e.g. '3 types of bread, 4 types of filling — how many different sandwiches?')
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to work out '5 × 23', can they split it into '5 × 20 + 5 × 3 = 100 + 15 = 115' — rather than just jumping straight to a written method?

topics.ds: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 using strategies based on place value and properties of operations
e: Calculate 7 × 30 = 210 by reasoning 7 × 3 tens = 21 tens = 210
Explain why multiplying by a multiple of 10 adds a zero to the product
Use this skill to estimate products of larger numbers
topics.p: Can {{name}} quickly work out '7 × 40' or '6 × 80' by first doing the single-digit multiplication and then placing the zero — getting 280 and 480?

topics.ds: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table) and explain them using properties of operations
e: Notice that all products of 5 end in 0 or 5 and explain why
Observe that the sum of two even numbers is always even
Identify a pattern in the multiplication table and explain it using commutativity or the distributive property
topics.p: Can {{name}} spot patterns in times tables — like all multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5 — and explain why that pattern happens?

topics.ds: Apply properties of operations (commutative, associative, distributive) as strategies to multiply and divide
e: Use commutativity: if 6 × 4 = 24 then 4 × 6 = 24
Use the distributive property: 8 × 7 = 8 × 5 + 8 × 2 = 40 + 16 = 56
Use associativity to multiply three numbers: 2 × 3 × 5 = 6 × 5 = 30
topics.p: Can {{name}} use tricks like breaking up a number — working out '6 × 14' as '6 × 10 + 6 × 4 = 60 + 24 = 84' — to make multiplication easier?

topics.ds: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers (e.g. 8 × ? = 48, ? × 6 = 42)
e: Find the missing factor in 7 × ? = 63
Find the missing dividend in ? ÷ 5 = 9
Explain the strategy used (e.g. using the related multiplication fact)
topics.p: If {{name}} sees '8 × ? = 48' or '? ÷ 6 = 7' written on paper, can they figure out what number goes in the blank?

topics.ds: Interpret whole-number quotients (e.g. 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share or the number of equal groups)
e: Explain that 56 ÷ 8 can mean sharing 56 into 8 equal groups or making groups of 8
Draw a picture to represent a division expression
Match a division expression to a word problem involving equal sharing or grouping
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that '56 ÷ 8' could mean 'if 56 things are shared between 8 people, how many does each person get?' — not just recite the answer '7'?

topics.ds: Interpret products of whole numbers (e.g. 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7)
e: Explain that 4 × 6 means 4 groups of 6 objects
Draw a picture or array to represent a multiplication expression
Match a multiplication expression to a word problem involving equal groups
topics.p: If {{name}} sees '5 × 7' written down, can they explain it means 5 groups with 7 in each group — not just recite the answer '35'?

topics.ds: Multiply two-digit and three-digit numbers by a one-digit number using formal written layout
e: Set out and solve 47 × 6 using short multiplication
Set out and solve 234 × 5 using short multiplication with carrying
Check the answer using estimation (e.g. 234 × 5 ≈ 200 × 5 = 1000)
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out '347 × 6' by setting it out formally in a column — multiplying each digit separately and carrying where needed?

topics.ds: Solve multi-step word problems using the four operations with whole numbers, including interpreting remainders in context; represent with equations using a letter for the unknown; check with estimation
e: 52 children go on a trip in minibuses holding 9 each — how many minibuses are needed? (interpret remainder)
A shop sells packs of 6 pencils for £1.50 each — how much do 5 packs cost?
Represent a two-step problem with an equation using n for the unknown
topics.p: If {{name}} reads 'a school buys 7 boxes of 24 pens and shares them equally between 8 classes', can they work through all the steps and decide sensibly what to do with any remainder?

topics.ds: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1–100; identify common factors and common multiples of two numbers; use these concepts to solve problems
e: State the first five multiples of 7
Find the common factors of 24 and 36
Find all common factors of 36 and 48
Identify the first three common multiples of 6 and 8
Determine whether a given number (e.g. 97) is prime and justify the reasoning
topics.p: Can {{name}} list all the factor pairs for a number like 36 — (1, 36), (2, 18), (3, 12), (4, 9), (6, 6) — and find factors that two numbers share?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving multiplication and division using knowledge of factors, multiples, squares, and cubes
e: Is 156 a multiple of 6? Explain how you know
Find two square numbers that add to make 100
Use factor pairs to simplify 24 × 25 as 6 × (4 × 25) = 6 × 100 = 600
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked to find all the square numbers less than 100, can they work through it systematically and give you the correct list: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81?

topics.ds: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using formal written methods including long multiplication; illustrate with area models
e: Calculate 2,347 × 6 using formal written layout
Calculate 34 × 27 using long multiplication
Draw an area model for 45 × 23 and connect to the written method
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out something like '2,346 × 7' or '43 × 28' using the formal column method — setting it out carefully and working through all the steps?

topics.ds: Multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts, including related facts and place-value adjustments
e: Calculate 40 × 60 mentally by using 4 × 6 = 24 then appending zeros
Derive 7 × 15 by calculating 7 × 10 + 7 × 5
Calculate 360 ÷ 9 mentally using 36 ÷ 9 = 4
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out things like '24 × 5' or '360 ÷ 8' in their head — using clever connections to known facts rather than needing to write anything down?

topics.ds: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison (e.g. 35 = 5 × 7 means 35 is 5 times as many as 7); represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as equations
e: Explain that '4 times as many' means multiply by 4
Write an equation for: Sarah has 3 times as many stickers as Tom, who has 8 stickers
Distinguish multiplicative comparison from additive comparison in word problems
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at '35 = 5 × 7' and explain it as '35 is five times as many as 7' — understanding it as a comparison, not just a multiplication fact?

topics.ds: Solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number
e: A blue ribbon is 3 times as long as a red ribbon of 7 cm — how long is the blue ribbon?
36 is 4 times a number — what is the number?
Explain why 'Sam has 5 more' is additive but 'Sam has 5 times as many' is multiplicative
topics.p: If you say 'Maya has 4 times as many stickers as Tom, and Tom has 6 — how many does Maya have?', can {{name}} recognise this as a multiplication problem and solve it?

topics.ds: Multiply and divide whole numbers and those involving decimals by 10, 100, and 1000
e: Calculate 3.45 × 100 = 345
Calculate 72 ÷ 1000 = 0.072
Explain that multiplying by 10 shifts each digit one place to the left
topics.p: Can {{name}} quickly work out '4.7 × 100' or '3,600 ÷ 1,000' — knowing that digits shift left or right in the place-value chart depending on whether they're multiplying or dividing?

topics.ds: Explain and use the properties of odd and even numbers when adding, subtracting and multiplying, e.g. odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd, and any whole number multiplied by an even number is even
e: Explain with paired counters why the sum of two odd numbers is always even
Predict without calculating whether 347 + 129 is odd or even and justify it
Explain why 6 x 37 must be even
topics.p: Without adding them up, can {{name}} tell you whether 347 + 129 will be odd or even — and explain why?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of prime numbers, prime factors, and composite numbers; establish whether a number up to 100 is prime; recall prime numbers up to 19
e: Explain that a prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself
Determine whether 51 is prime or composite and justify the answer
List all prime numbers up to 19 from memory
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you what makes a number 'prime' — that it only divides exactly by 1 and itself — and give some examples like 7, 11, and 13?

topics.ds: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule; identify apparent features of the pattern not explicit in the rule and explain informally why they occur
e: Given 'start at 1, add 3', generate terms and notice they alternate odd/even
Given a shape pattern, predict the next three terms and describe the rule
Explain why starting at 2 and adding 4 always gives even numbers
topics.p: If {{name}} is told 'start at 3 and multiply by 2 each time', can they write out the pattern — 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 — and spot any interesting features in how it grows?

topics.ds: Divide numbers up to four digits by a one-digit number using short division (and place-value/array strategies); interpret remainders appropriately for the context
e: Calculate 4,932 ÷ 6 using short division
Solve 125 ÷ 8 and interpret: 15 remainder 5 means 15 full bags with 5 left over
Use the multiplication–division relationship to check a division answer
topics.p: Can {{name}} use the short division ('bus stop') method to work out something like '2,457 ÷ 6', and decide what to do with any remainder left over?

topics.ds: Recognise and use square numbers and cube numbers, and the notation for squared (²) and cubed (³)
e: Identify 49 as 7² and explain that 7 × 7 = 49
Calculate 4³ = 64 and explain it means 4 × 4 × 4
List the first ten square numbers
topics.p: Does {{name}} know that '5²' means 5 × 5 = 25 and '3³' means 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 — and can they work out other squared and cubed numbers?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and problems involving simple rates
e: A recipe for 4 people needs 200 g of flour — how much for 6 people?
If 3 kg costs £12, how much does 5 kg cost?
Scale a shape by a factor of 1/2 and find the new dimensions
topics.p: If a recipe serves 4 and {{name}} wants to make it for 6, can they scale up each ingredient — for example, changing '2 cups of flour' to '3 cups'?

topics.ds: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions and evaluate expressions containing these grouping symbols
e: Evaluate 3 × (4 + 5) by computing inside the parentheses first
Evaluate {2 × [3 + (7 − 1)]} with nested grouping symbols
Insert parentheses into an expression to make it equal a target value
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at '3 × (4 + 5)' and work out the brackets first — getting '3 × 9 = 27' — rather than just multiplying left to right?

topics.ds: Use a calculator or spreadsheet where appropriate to multiply larger numbers and to divide, check results by estimation, and interpret a decimal calculator answer to a division in context as a whole number, a remainder, a fraction or a decimal
e: Use a calculator for 2365 x 48 and check the answer against an estimate of 2000 x 50 = 100 000
Divide 250 by 8 on a calculator, read 31.25, and interpret it as 32 buses needed, 31 full boxes with 2 left over, or 31.25 cm of ribbon each, depending on the problem
Choose a mental strategy for 47 x 10 and a calculator for 3847 x 26, and justify each choice
topics.p: If {{name}} divides 250 by 8 on a calculator and sees 31.25, can they work out what that means for the problem — like needing 32 buses, not 31.25?

topics.ds: Multiply one-digit numbers with up to two decimal places by whole numbers (e.g. 3.47 × 6)
e: Correctly compute 4.56 × 7 using a written method
Use place-value reasoning to explain why 3.2 × 5 = 16.0
Model a decimal multiplication using an area diagram or expanded form
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out '3.47 × 6' — keeping the decimal point in the right place and carrying correctly through each column?

topics.ds: Divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal written short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to context
e: Use short division to compute 3,648 ÷ 16 efficiently
Explain when short division is more appropriate than long division
Interpret a remainder as a decimal or fraction in a measurement context
topics.p: Can {{name}} use short division to work out something like '2,184 ÷ 12' — keeping track of each digit and carrying any remainders into the next column?

topics.ds: Use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places; divide decimals to hundredths by whole numbers
e: Compute 14.76 ÷ 4 using a written method to get 3.69
Explain how to continue long division past the decimal point to obtain a decimal quotient
Solve a context problem that requires dividing a decimal amount equally (e.g. sharing £18.60 among 5 people)
topics.p: Can {{name}} use a written method to calculate something like '17 ÷ 4 = 4.25' — carrying the division past the decimal point to get a decimal answer rather than a remainder?

topics.ds: Divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit divisor using formal written long division, interpreting remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate
e: Compute 4,752 ÷ 13 using long division and express the remainder as a fraction
Decide whether to round up or down a division remainder in a real-life context (e.g. buses needed)
Explain each step of the long division algorithm for a 4-digit ÷ 2-digit calculation
topics.p: Can {{name}} use long division to work out something like '1,848 ÷ 24' — going through the steps of divide, multiply, subtract, and bring down until they reach the answer?

topics.n: Estimation to check answers to calculations
topics.ds: Use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy
e: Estimate 487 × 23 by rounding to 500 × 20 and use this to check a calculated answer
Determine whether an exact answer or an estimate is more appropriate in a given context
Spot an unreasonable answer by comparing with a quick mental estimate
topics.p: Before {{name}} works out a large multiplication or division, can they estimate what the answer should be roughly — and then check whether their final answer is in the right ballpark?

topics.ds: Create and use algorithms with steps and decisions, and digital tools such as spreadsheets, to experiment with factors, multiples and divisibility, and describe the patterns that emerge
e: Write an algorithm that tests every number from 1 to 24 and records it if 24 divided by it leaves no remainder
Use a spreadsheet column of multiples of 6 and highlight those that are also multiples of 4
Describe the pattern found when listing numbers between 1 and 50 that have exactly two factors
topics.p: Can {{name}} set up a list or spreadsheet to find all the numbers that divide into 24 — and spot patterns, like which numbers have only two factors?

topics.ds: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers (up to 4 digits by 2 digits) using the formal written method of long multiplication
e: Correctly compute 2,463 × 37 using long multiplication
Explain each partial product in a long multiplication and why they are added
Multiply a four-digit number by a two-digit number without procedural errors
topics.p: Can {{name}} use long multiplication to work out something like '2,347 × 24' — setting it out in two rows, one for the units and one for the tens, then adding the results?

topics.ds: Perform mental calculations including with mixed operations and large numbers, using strategies such as partitioning, compensation, and derived facts
e: Mentally compute 45 × 8 by partitioning into 40 × 8 + 5 × 8
Use known facts to derive 6.5 × 4 mentally
Solve a multi-operation mental calculation such as 250 × 3 + 500 and explain the strategy used
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out a mixed calculation like '(200 × 6) + 350 − 75' entirely in their head — keeping track of each step without writing anything down?

topics.ds: Multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100, and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places, understanding that digits shift position in the place-value chart
e: Compute 3.456 × 100 = 345.6 correctly
Compute 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 correctly
Explain why multiplying by 10 shifts each digit one place to the left
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out '4.6 ÷ 1,000 = 0.0046' — knowing that each division by 10 shifts digits one place to the right, even past the decimal point?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, deciding which operations and methods to use and why; solve multi-step problems in contexts
e: Solve a three-step word problem involving a mix of all four operations
Explain why particular operations were chosen for each step of a multi-step problem
Identify and correct an error in a multi-step solution that used the wrong operation
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a multi-step problem mixing different operations — like working out the total cost of several items at different prices — can they plan and carry out each step correctly?

topics.ds: Understand and apply the conventional order of operations (PEMDAS/BODMAS) to carry out calculations involving the four operations
e: Explain why 8 + 2 × 5 = 18 (not 50) by referencing multiplication before addition
Evaluate a multi-step expression like 12 ÷ 3 + 4 × 2 correctly as 12
State the correct order: brackets, then orders/exponents, then multiplication/division (L→R), then addition/subtraction (L→R)
topics.p: If {{name}} sees '8 + 4 × 3', do they get 20 — not 36 — because they know to do the multiplication before the addition?

topics.ds: Solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy
e: Compute a division and round the result to one decimal place as specified
Determine the appropriate degree of accuracy for a measurement context (e.g. round to nearest penny)
Solve a problem where an unrounded decimal answer must be interpreted in context (e.g. whole containers needed)
topics.p: If {{name}} calculates an answer of 8.63 but the question asks for it to the nearest whole number, can they round it correctly to 9 — and explain why that level of precision matters in context?

topics.ds: Write simple numerical expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them (e.g. recognise that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921)
e: Write an expression for 'add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2' using parentheses
Explain what 4 × (365 − 12) represents without computing it
Compare two expressions and determine which is larger without evaluating
topics.p: Can {{name}} look at '4 × (5 + 3)' and say 'that's 4 times the result of adding 5 and 3' — reading the expression as a description of a calculation, without having to work it out first?

topics.ds: Use estimation and rounding to check the reasonableness of answers when multiplying and dividing decimals (including by multiples of powers of 10), identifying misplaced decimal points
e: Estimate 4.87 x 30 as about 5 x 30 = 150 before calculating 146.1
Decide whether 63.6 / 20 = 31.8 is reasonable by rounding to 60 / 20 = 3 and find the error
Round 2.46 x 400 to 2.5 x 400 = 1000 to check a calculated answer of 984
topics.p: If {{name}} works out 4.87 x 30 and gets 1461, do they notice it can't be right because 5 x 30 is only about 150?

topics.ds: Use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors, multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor (HCF), lowest common multiple (LCM), and prime factorisation including product notation and the unique factorisation property
e: Express any integer as a product of its prime factors using index notation
Find the HCF and LCM of two numbers using prime factorisation
Apply the unique factorisation theorem to explain why every number has exactly one set of prime factors
topics.p: Can {{name}} find the highest common factor of two numbers like 24 and 36 — working out the biggest number that divides exactly into both — and explain how they found it?

topics.ds: Use conventional notation for the priority of operations including brackets, powers, roots, and reciprocals; apply BIDMAS/BODMAS consistently to evaluate complex numerical expressions
e: Evaluate expressions involving brackets, indices, and all four operations in the correct order
Explain why the order of operations is necessary to avoid ambiguity
Use the reciprocal of a number and understand that a number multiplied by its reciprocal gives 1
topics.p: Can {{name}} evaluate a complex expression like '5 + 2³ ÷ 4' correctly — applying the right order of operations, handling the power before the division and division before the addition?

topics.ds: Multiply and divide with positive and negative integers and rational numbers, understanding the rules for the sign of the product or quotient
e: Apply the sign rules when multiplying two integers (positive × negative, negative × negative)
Apply the sign rules when dividing two integers
Solve multi-step real-world problems involving all four operations with positive and negative rational numbers
topics.p: If {{name}} knows that a negative times a negative makes a positive, can they use that rule to work out calculations like '−3 × −4 = 12' — and explain why it makes sense?

topics.ds: Recognise and use relationships between operations including inverse operations; use these relationships to check answers and simplify calculations
e: Use addition and subtraction as inverse operations to check and solve problems
Use multiplication and division as inverse operations to check and solve problems
Recognise that squaring and square-rooting are inverse operations
topics.p: If {{name}} works out '252 ÷ 7 = 36', can they immediately use the inverse to check — '36 × 7 = 252' — without having to redo the division?

topics.ds: Read and write number words from one to twenty
e: Read the word 'twelve' and identify it as 12
Write the word form of a given number 1–20
Match numeral cards to number word cards
topics.p: Can {{name}} write number words like 'fourteen' or 'twenty' — and read them on a birthday card or in a story book without needing help?

topics.ds: Name, represent and order numbers from 0 to at least 20 using physical and virtual materials (number cards, on-screen ten frames and number tracks) and numerals
e: Put the cards 14, 3, 19, 0 and 8 in order from smallest to largest
Show 13 on an on-screen twenty frame by dragging counters, then drag the numeral 13 to its place on a virtual number track
Say the number that comes just before 13 and just after 13
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a handful of number cards between 0 and 20 — like 14, 3, 19 and 8 — can they lay them out in order from smallest to biggest?

topics.ds: Read and write numerals from 0 to 100
e: Read two-digit numerals up to 100 correctly
Write any number 0–100 as a numeral from dictation
topics.p: Can {{name}} read and write any number up to 100 — both as a numeral and by saying what it means?

topics.ds: Read and write numerals from 0 to 20
e: Read any numeral 0–20 when shown it
Write numerals 0–20 legibly from dictation
Represent a number of objects with the correct written numeral
topics.p: Can {{name}} read a number like '17' written on paper and write it themselves — and do they know what each digit means?

topics.ds: Understand that the teen numbers (11–19) are composed of ten ones and some further ones (early place value)
e: Compose 14 as a group of ten and four ones using objects
Decompose 17 into 10 + 7 and record as an equation
Explain that 13 is 'one ten and three ones'
topics.p: If {{name}} has 14 building blocks, can they see it as one full tower of 10 and 4 left over — understanding 'teen' numbers as ten-and-some-more?

topics.ds: Mentally find 10 more or 10 less than a given two-digit number without counting
e: Given 56, quickly say 66 is 10 more and 46 is 10 less
Explain that adding 10 increases the tens digit by 1
Answer '10 more than 73' without using fingers or counting on
topics.p: Can {{name}} quickly tell you what is 10 more than 43 or 10 less than 71 — without counting up or down one at a time?

topics.ds: Understand that 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a 'ten'
e: Group 10 single cubes into one rod of 10 and explains why
Explain that 10 ones is the same as 1 ten
Exchange 10 ones for a single tens block
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that ten single objects bundled together make 'one ten' — and that this is why we write 10 with a 1 in the tens place and a 0 in the ones place?

topics.ds: Compare and order two-digit numbers using the symbols >, =, and <, based on place value understanding
e: Correctly place > or < between 34 and 43
Order a set of two-digit numbers from smallest to largest
Explain a comparison by referring to the tens digit first, then ones
topics.p: If you show {{name}} the numbers 34, 67, and 21, can they put them in order from smallest to largest — and use the symbols > or < correctly?

topics.ds: Recognise, represent and order numbers to at least 120, including 101 to 120, using physical materials (bundled straws, base-ten blocks), virtual materials (on-screen base-ten blocks, digital number charts), numerals, number lines and charts
e: Continue a number chart past 100 to 120 and point to 107 and 116
Show 112 with bundles of ten straws and loose straws, then build it again with on-screen base-ten blocks
Drag 98, 120, 104 and 111 onto an on-screen number line in order from smallest to largest
topics.p: If {{name}} is counting a big jar of buttons past 100, can they keep going to 120, show a number like 112 with bundles of ten, and put 104, 98 and 111 in order?

topics.ds: Read and write numbers to at least 100 in words
e: Read 'fifty-seven' and write the numeral 57
Write 'eighty-three' when shown the numeral 83
Read and write all decade words (twenty, thirty … ninety) correctly
topics.p: Can {{name}} write 'seventy-four' or 'one hundred and three' as number words — and read them correctly when they appear in a book or on a sign?

topics.n: Place value understanding and number facts
topics.ds: Use place value understanding and number facts to solve problems
e: Use knowledge that 34 = 30 + 4 to help add 34 + 20 = 54
Solve 'I think of a number, add 10, and get 45. What was my number?'
Apply partitioning to solve a problem in an unfamiliar context
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked 'which number is closest to 50 — 47 or 54?', can they use their number knowledge to answer quickly and explain why?

topics.ds: Count to 120 starting at any number less than 120; read and write numerals to 120
e: Count from 47 to 120 without errors
Read the numeral 108 correctly
Write the numeral for one hundred and fifteen
topics.p: Can {{name}} start counting from any number up to 120 — for example, starting at 87 and counting up to 120 without losing track?

topics.ds: Partition and rename two-digit numbers in standard and non-standard ways (e.g. 34 = 3 tens 4 ones = 2 tens 14 ones) using physical and virtual base-ten materials, recognising that the total stays the same
e: Show 34 with real base-ten blocks as 3 tens and 4 ones, then trade a ten to show 2 tens and 14 ones
Partition 52 in three different ways with an on-screen base-ten app (e.g. 5 tens 2 ones, 4 tens 12 ones, 3 tens 22 ones) and record each
Explain why 4 tens and 6 ones and 3 tens and 16 ones are the same number
topics.p: If {{name}} has 34 counters made up of 3 bags of ten and 4 loose ones, can they show the same number another way — like 2 bags of ten and 14 loose ones?

topics.ds: Identify, represent and estimate numbers to 100 using different representations: place a two-digit number on a 0–100 number line marked in tens, represent it with base-ten blocks (tens and ones), drawings, bead strings or hundred squares, and estimate 'about how many' objects in a set before counting to check
e: Mark 47 in about the right place on a 0–100 number line marked in tens (between 40 and 50, nearer 50)
Show 63 as 6 tens and 3 ones with base-ten blocks, as a drawing of sticks and dots, and on a hundred square
Estimate 'about how many' objects are in a set of 30–50 without counting, then count to check
topics.p: If {{name}} has a number line from 0 to 100 marked in tens, can they point to roughly where 47 goes — and show 47 another way, such as 4 tens and 7 ones with blocks or a drawing?

topics.ds: Understand that the multiples of 10 (10, 20, 30 … 90) represent one to nine tens and 0 ones
e: Explain that 30 means 3 tens and 0 ones
Represent 50 using 5 tens rods and no unit cubes
Match decade numbers to their tens representation
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that 60 means 6 tens and no ones — and that this is why the ones column has a zero as a placeholder?

topics.n: The two digits of a two-digit number
topics.ds: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones
e: Explain that in 47, the 4 represents 4 tens (40) and the 7 represents 7 ones
Use base-ten blocks to show a two-digit number as tens and ones
Identify the tens digit and ones digit in any two-digit number
topics.p: If {{name}} sees the number 47, can they tell you there are 4 tens (forty) and 7 ones — rather than just reading the digits as 'four seven'?

topics.ds: Find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number up to 1000
e: Given a three-digit number, state what is 10 more and 10 less
Given a three-digit number, state what is 100 more and 100 less
Explain the strategy using place-value understanding (e.g. only the tens/hundreds digit changes)
topics.p: Can {{name}} quickly work out '10 more than 342' or '100 less than 875' in their head — knowing which digit changes and which stays the same?

topics.ds: Understand that 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred'
e: Explain that 10 groups of 10 ones make 100
Bundle ten tens sticks into one hundred and describe what happened
Represent 100 using base-ten blocks showing 10 tens
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that ten full tens stacked together make one hundred — and that this is why 100 has a 1 in the hundreds place and zeros in the rest?

topics.ds: Represent and order numbers to at least 1000 using physical base-ten blocks and virtual materials (on-screen base-ten blocks and interactive number lines), connecting each representation to the numeral
e: Build 347 with real base-ten blocks and again with on-screen base-ten blocks and say how many hundreds, tens and ones
Drag 608, 680, 86 and 860 onto an on-screen 0-1000 number line in order
Show on screen that 10 hundreds blocks make 1000 and write the numeral
topics.p: If {{name}} uses a maths app with hundreds, tens and ones blocks, can they build 347 on screen and with real blocks — and put 608, 680 and 860 in order on a number line?

topics.ds: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members
e: Pair objects and determine whether there is one left over (odd) or not (even)
Count a group by 2s to determine if the total is even
Write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends (e.g. 8 = 4 + 4)
topics.p: If {{name}} has a group of 14 objects, can they tell you whether that number is odd or even — for example by pairing them up to see if any are left over?

topics.ds: Compare and order numbers up to 1000 using >, =, and < symbols, based on place-value understanding
e: Compare two three-digit numbers by examining hundreds first, then tens, then ones
Use >, =, and < correctly to record comparisons of three-digit numbers
Order a set of numbers up to 1000 from smallest to largest
topics.p: If you give {{name}} a set of three-digit numbers like 456, 231, and 789, can they put them in order and use > and < correctly?

topics.ds: Solve number problems and practical problems involving place value of numbers up to 1000
e: Solve a problem that requires identifying how many hundreds, tens, or ones are in a number
Apply place-value knowledge to a practical context (e.g. counting money in pounds)
Explain the strategy used to solve a place-value problem
topics.p: If {{name}} is told 'I have 4 hundreds, 3 tens, and 7 ones — what number is that?', can they put it together and tell you 437?

topics.ds: Read and write numbers to 1000 in numerals, number names, and expanded form
e: Read a three-digit numeral aloud correctly
Write a three-digit number in words (e.g. 'three hundred and forty-two')
Write a number in expanded form (e.g. 600 + 30 + 7)
topics.p: Can {{name}} read and write numbers up to 1,000 — both as numerals and in words — like reading '642' as 'six hundred and forty-two'?

topics.ds: Identify, represent and estimate three-digit numbers using different representations: place a number on a 0–1000 number line marked only in hundreds or unmarked, estimate the value of a marked point, and represent a number with base-ten blocks (hundreds, tens and ones), a place-value chart and a drawing, including numbers with a zero digit and non-standard partitions
e: Mark 346 in about the right place on a 0–1000 number line marked in hundreds (between 300 and 400, a little before halfway), and estimate that an unlabelled point three-quarters of the way along is about 750
Represent 507 with base-ten blocks and on a place-value chart, showing the empty tens column as 0
Match a drawing of 3 hundreds, 14 tens and 2 ones to the numeral 442
topics.p: If {{name}} sees a number line from 0 to 1000 marked only in hundreds, can they point to roughly where 346 goes — and show 346 another way, such as hundreds, tens and ones blocks or a place-value chart?

topics.ds: Understand that the multiples of 100 (100–900) each represent a number of hundreds with 0 tens and 0 ones
e: Identify that 300 means 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones
Place multiples of 100 on a number line to 1000
Read and write multiples of 100 and explain their place-value structure
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that 700 means 7 hundreds with no tens and no ones — and show what that looks like using base-ten blocks or a drawing?

topics.n: The three digits of a three-digit number
topics.ds: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones
e: State the value of each digit in a three-digit number (e.g. in 362, the 3 represents 3 hundreds)
Partition a three-digit number into hundreds, tens, and ones (e.g. 485 = 400 + 80 + 5)
Explain why 706 has 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones
topics.p: If {{name}} sees the number 348, can they tell you there are 3 hundreds, 4 tens, and 8 ones — rather than just reading the digits as 'three four eight'?

topics.ds: Find 1000 more or less than a given number
e: Given 4,562, state that 1000 more is 5,562 and 1000 less is 3,562
Explain using place value that only the thousands digit changes
Apply this skill to numbers beyond 10,000
topics.p: Can {{name}} quickly work out '1,000 more than 3,456' or '1,000 less than 7,200' in their head — knowing only the thousands digit changes?

topics.ds: Order and compare numbers beyond 1000
e: Compare two four-digit numbers using >, <, and = by examining digits from the highest place value
Order a set of numbers up to 10,000 from smallest to largest
Justify the ordering using place-value reasoning
topics.p: Can {{name}} put a set of four-digit numbers like 4,321, 1,876, and 9,045 in order from smallest to largest — comparing them digit by digit?

topics.ds: Count backwards through zero to include negative numbers
e: Count backwards from 5 through zero: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2 …
Place negative numbers on a number line
Understand that negative numbers are less than zero and use them in context (e.g. temperature)
topics.p: Can {{name}} count backwards past zero into negative numbers — like 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2, −3 — without hesitating at zero?

topics.ds: Identify, represent, and estimate numbers up to 10,000 using different representations
e: Represent a four-digit number on a place-value chart or with base-ten materials
Estimate where a number falls on a 0–10,000 number line
Match different representations of the same number (e.g. expanded form, place-value counters, numeral)
topics.p: Can {{name}} mark a number like 6,400 roughly in the right place on a number line that goes from 0 to 10,000 — and explain how they decided where to put it?

topics.ds: Recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)
e: State the value of each digit in a four-digit number (e.g. in 7,345 the 7 represents 7 thousands)
Partition a four-digit number into thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones
Compose a four-digit number from given place-value parts (e.g. 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 = 3,452)
topics.p: If {{name}} sees the number 5,347, can they tell you the value of each digit — that the 5 means 5,000, the 3 means 300, the 4 means 40, and the 7 means 7?

topics.ds: Solve number and practical problems involving place value with increasingly large positive numbers
e: Solve a problem requiring rounding, comparing, or ordering numbers beyond 1000
Apply place-value knowledge in a practical context (e.g. population figures, distances)
Explain the strategy used, referencing place-value understanding
topics.p: If {{name}} is asked 'what is the largest 4-digit even number you can make from the digits 3, 7, 1, and 8?', can they work through it systematically and give you an answer?

topics.ds: Read, write, order, and compare whole numbers up to at least 1,000,000 using base-ten numerals, number names, expanded form, and place-value understanding
e: Write 403,072 in words and in expanded form
Compare 548,301 and 543,801 using < and explain the reasoning
Order four six-digit numbers from smallest to largest
topics.p: Can {{name}} read and write numbers into the millions — like 1,340,000 — and put a set of large numbers in order correctly?

topics.ds: Read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and understand that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value
e: Read and write Roman numerals I, V, X, L, C and combinations up to 100
Convert between Roman numerals and Hindu-Arabic numerals (e.g. XLIV = 44)
Explain that Roman numerals have no zero and no place-value system
topics.p: Can {{name}} read Roman numerals like XIV (14) or XLII (42) — and do they know why we stopped using Roman numerals for most things once zero and place value were invented?

topics.ds: Round any number to the nearest 10, 100, or 1000
e: Explain the rounding rule using a number line (which multiple is closer)
Apply rounding to estimate calculations
topics.p: Can {{name}} round a number like 4,738 to the nearest 10 (4,740), 100 (4,700), or 1,000 (5,000) — and explain which digit they look at to decide?

topics.ds: Count forwards and backwards in steps of powers of 10 (10, 100, 1000, 10,000, 100,000) for any given number up to 1,000,000
e: Count on in 10,000s from 462,000
Count back in 100,000s from 800,000
Identify the next three terms: 375,000; 475,000; 575,000; ...
topics.p: Can {{name}} count forwards and backwards in steps of 1,000 or 10,000 from any starting number — like 34,500, 44,500, 54,500 — without losing track?

topics.ds: Interpret negative numbers in context (temperature, sea level, bank balance); count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero
e: Place –3, –1, 0, 2, 5 on a number line
The temperature is –4°C and rises by 7 degrees — what is the new temperature?
Count backwards from 3 in ones: 3, 2, 1, 0, –1, –2
topics.p: If the temperature drops to −5°C overnight and rises to 3°C by day, can {{name}} place both on a number line and say how many degrees warmer the daytime temperature is?

topics.ds: Recognise that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (e.g. 700 ÷ 70 = 10)
e: Explain that the 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300
Complete: 700 ÷ 70 = __ and explain using place-value reasoning
State how many times greater the value of the 5 in 50,000 is than the 5 in 5,000
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that in 700, the 7 is worth 10 times more than in 70 — because moving one place to the left multiplies the value by 10?

topics.ds: Read Roman numerals to 1000 (M) and recognise years written in Roman numerals
e: Read MCMXCIX as 1999
Write 2024 in Roman numerals (MMXXIV)
Explain the subtractive principle: IV = 4 not IIII
topics.p: Can {{name}} read Roman numerals like MMXIX (2019) or CDXLIV (444) — and recognise the year a film or building was made when it's shown in Roman numerals?

topics.ds: Round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, or 100,000 using place-value understanding
e: Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000 (460,000)
Round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000 and explain the boundary case
Use rounding to estimate the sum of 387,412 + 214,560
topics.p: Can {{name}} round a large number like 346,712 to the nearest 1,000 (347,000) or 10,000 (350,000) — identifying which digit to look at for each rounding?

topics.ds: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, and rounding whole numbers up to 1,000,000
e: What is the largest six-digit number with digits summing to 15?
A stadium holds 67,450 people. Round to the nearest thousand for a news report
Order the populations of five cities and find the difference between the largest and smallest
topics.p: If {{name}} is told the population of a city is 2,347,819, can they read that number aloud correctly and say roughly how many millions it is?

topics.ds: Round decimals to any place using place-value understanding; round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy
e: Round 3.4567 to 2 decimal places (3.46)
Use rounding to estimate 4.83 × 2.17 ≈ 5 × 2 = 10
topics.p: Can {{name}} round a decimal like 3.748 to one decimal place (3.7) or two decimal places (3.75) — and explain which digit they look at to decide?

topics.ds: Use negative numbers in context (temperature, finance, sea level); calculate intervals across zero
e: The temperature falls from 3°C to −5°C — what is the drop? (8 degrees)
Calculate the difference between a bank balance of −£120 and £350
Order −7, −3, 0, 2, 5 on a number line and find the interval from −7 to 5
topics.p: If a bank account goes from −£45 to +£120, can {{name}} work out the total change — counting through zero to get £165?

topics.ds: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding, and negative numbers up to 10,000,000
e: A country's population is 8,274,500 — round to the nearest million for a headline
Order the depths of three ocean trenches given in metres including negative values
Estimate the total attendance at three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000
topics.p: If {{name}} reads that the distance to the Moon is about 384,400 km, can they round it to the nearest 10,000 km and say whether it's closer to 380,000 or 390,000?

topics.ds: Explain patterns in zeros when multiplying by powers of 10 and in decimal-point placement when multiplying/dividing by a power of 10; use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10 (e.g. 10³ = 1000)
e: Write 10⁴ = 10,000 and explain the exponent means four factors of 10
Explain why 3.4 × 10² = 340 by describing the decimal shift
Predict 2.56 × 10³ without calculating and explain the pattern
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why 10² = 100 and 10³ = 1,000, and why multiplying by 10 just adds a zero — connecting the pattern of zeros to place value?

topics.ds: Recognise that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left
e: Explain that the 4 in 0.04 is 1/10 of the 4 in 0.4
State that a digit moving one place left is ×10 and one place right is ÷10
Compare the value of the 6 in 6,000 and in 0.006
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that in 4.56, the digit 5 is worth 5 tenths — ten times less than the 5 in 54, and ten times more than the 5 in 0.056?

topics.ds: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form; compare using >, =, < based on place-value meaning
e: Compare 0.372 and 0.38 using place-value reasoning
Write 'five and sixty-two thousandths' as 5.062
topics.p: Can {{name}} read and write decimals like 3.047 or 0.625, say what each digit means (3 ones, 0 tenths, 4 hundredths, 7 thousandths), and put a set of decimals in order?

topics.ds: Read, write, order, and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit
e: Write 4,302,561 in words
Order four seven-digit numbers from smallest to largest
State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200 as seven million
topics.p: Can {{name}} read and write numbers up to 10 million — like 4,302,617 — and say the value of any digit in the number?

topics.ds: Identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (e.g. in 4.378, the 7 represents 7 hundredths)
e: State the value of each digit in 2.635 (2 ones, 6 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths)
Explain the relationship between adjacent decimal places (each place is ten times smaller)
Write a number given digit values (e.g. 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths = 4.073)
topics.p: In the number 4.378, can {{name}} tell you that the 7 represents 7 hundredths — not 7 tenths or 7 thousandths?

topics.ds: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from zero on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude in real-world contexts; distinguish absolute value comparisons from ordering statements
e: Define absolute value as distance from zero on a number line
Calculate the absolute value of positive and negative rational numbers
Distinguish between comparing absolute values and comparing signed numbers in real-world contexts
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell you that the absolute value of −7 is 7 — because it's 7 steps from zero on a number line regardless of direction — and use this idea to compare distances?

topics.ds: Round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy including to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures
e: Round numbers to a given number of decimal places
Round numbers to a given number of significant figures
Choose an appropriate degree of accuracy for a given context
topics.p: Can {{name}} round a measurement like 12.3746 km to 2 decimal places (12.37 km) or 3 significant figures (12.4 km) — and explain when each level of precision is appropriate?

topics.ds: Understand and use place value for decimals, measures, and integers of any size; extend the number system to include all positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a single number line
e: Identify the value of any digit in numbers of any size including decimals
Place positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a number line
Use place value to compare and order numbers across the full number system
topics.p: Can {{name}} place a mix of numbers — like 3, −2, 0.5, −1.75, and ¼ — all on the same number line, in the right order?

topics.ds: Order positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a number line; use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values including negative numbers and mixed representations
e: Order a mixed set of positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions
Use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ correctly in mathematical statements
Compare numbers presented in different forms such as 0.75 and 3/4
topics.p: If {{name}} is given a mixed list like 2.5, −3, ¾, 0, and −0.5, can they put them in order from least to greatest using a number line if needed?

topics.ds: Use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube, and higher); recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, and 5; distinguish between exact representations of roots and their decimal approximations
e: Calculate squares, cubes, and higher integer powers of whole numbers
Find square roots and cube roots of perfect squares and perfect cubes
