Recognise key powers (powers of 2 up to 2¹⁰, powers of 3 up to 3⁵, etc.) and distinguish exact roots from approximations
topics.p: Can {{name}} work out that √25 = 5 and ∛27 = 3 — knowing these are the inverse of squaring and cubing — and say whether √50 is closer to 7 or 8?

topics.ds: Use approximation through rounding to estimate answers and calculate possible resulting errors expressed using inequality notation a < x ≤ b; understand upper and lower bounds of rounded values
e: Estimate the answer to a calculation by rounding all values appropriately
Calculate upper and lower bounds of a rounded measurement
Express error intervals using inequality notation
topics.p: If a length is measured as 7 cm to the nearest cm, can {{name}} say the actual length could be anywhere from 6.5 cm to 7.5 cm — understanding that rounding creates a range of possible values?

topics.ds: Interpret and compare numbers in standard form A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer; convert between ordinary numbers and standard form
e: Convert large and small numbers into standard form A × 10ⁿ
Convert numbers from standard form back to ordinary notation
Compare and order numbers given in standard form
topics.p: Can {{name}} write 3,400,000 as 3.4 × 10⁶ and convert back — understanding that standard form is a shorthand for very large or very small numbers?

topics.ds: Appreciate the infinite nature of the sets of integers, real numbers, and rational numbers; position integers on a number line and distinguish between rational and irrational numbers
e: Explain that rational numbers can be written as a fraction of two integers and have terminating or repeating decimals
Give examples of irrational numbers and explain why their decimal expansions neither terminate nor repeat
Appreciate that between any two numbers there are infinitely many other numbers
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that numbers like √2 and π can't be written as exact fractions — and that their decimal expansions go on forever without repeating?

topics.ds: Use probability language to describe and compare the likelihood of everyday events using words such as certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible
e: Place five everyday events (e.g. 'the sun will rise tomorrow', 'it will snow in July', 'I'll flip heads') on a scale from impossible to certain
Use 'likely', 'unlikely', 'certain', 'impossible', and 'even chance' correctly to describe different events
Explain why pulling a red ball from a bag of mostly red balls is 'likely' but not 'certain'
topics.p: Does {{name}} use words like "certain," "likely," "unlikely," and "impossible" correctly — for example, knowing that rolling a 7 on a normal die is impossible but rolling an even number is likely?

topics.ds: Conduct simple probability experiments — flipping a coin, rolling a die, pulling coloured counters from a bag — record results, and compare experimental outcomes with expected theoretical outcomes
e: Flip a coin 20 times, record heads and tails in a tally chart, and describe what they notice about the results
Roll a die 30 times and compare how often each number came up with what they expected
Pull counters from a bag, record results, and explain whether the outcomes matched their prediction
topics.p: Has {{name}} ever done an experiment like flipping a coin or rolling a die lots of times, recorded the results in a tally chart, and noticed any patterns in what came up?

topics.ds: Understand that 'equally likely' means every outcome has exactly the same chance of occurring; identify whether a given situation has equally likely outcomes (a fair coin, a fair die, a spinner with equal sections) or unequally likely outcomes (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with unequal sections)
e: Explain that a fair coin has equally likely outcomes because heads and tails each have the same chance
Identify whether a spinner with unequal sections has equally likely outcomes or not, and explain why
Give an example of a situation with equally likely outcomes and one without, explaining the difference
topics.p: Can {{name}} tell the difference between a fair situation — like rolling a normal die where every number has the same chance — and an unfair one, like a bag with many more of one colour than another?

topics.ds: Run repeated probability experiments and compare experimental (relative frequency) results with theoretical predictions; understand and demonstrate that as the number of trials increases, the experimental probability tends towards the theoretical probability — and that short runs can give very different results
e: Roll a die 60 times and compare experimental frequencies with the expected 10 per number
Explain why experimental results don't exactly match theoretical predictions but get closer with more trials
Predict what would happen if the experiment were repeated 600 times instead of 60
topics.p: If {{name}} flips a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads, do they understand why this doesn't mean heads is "more likely" — and that the more times you flip, the closer the results get to 50:50?

topics.ds: Identify whether events in chance experiments and everyday situations are independent (one does not affect the other) or dependent (the first outcome changes the chances of the next)
e: Explain that getting heads on one coin flip does not change the chance of heads on the next flip
Explain why taking a red marble out of a bag and not putting it back changes the chance of drawing red next
Sort five described pairs of events into independent and dependent
topics.p: If {{name}} flips a coin and gets heads three times in a row, do they understand the next flip is still 50-50 — but that taking a lolly from a bag without putting it back does change what's left?

topics.ds: Compare the likelihood of different events and order them from least to most likely — including situations with unequal outcomes such as a bag with more of one colour than another, or a spinner with sections of different sizes — and explain reasoning using informal language
e: Order four or more events from least likely to most likely and justify each placement
Compare likelihoods when outcomes are not equally likely — e.g. 'Drawing red from a bag with 7 red and 3 blue is more likely than drawing blue'
Explain why some events are closer to 'even chance' and others are closer to 'certain' or 'impossible'
topics.p: If a bag has 8 red counters and 2 blue ones, does {{name}} understand that picking red is much more likely than picking blue — and can they put different events in order from least to most likely?

topics.ds: Describe the probability of simple equally-likely outcomes using unit fractions: the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6, flipping heads is 1/2, picking one specific colour from three equally represented colours is 1/3; place these fractional probabilities on a 0-to-1 probability scale
e: State that the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6 and explain why
Express the probability of picking a red card from a standard deck as 26/52 or 1/2
Write the probability of a simple event as a fraction: favourable outcomes over total outcomes
topics.p: If {{name}} flips a fair coin, do they know the probability of getting heads is 1/2 — and can they express similar simple probabilities as fractions and place them on a 0-to-1 scale?

topics.ds: Calculate the probability of a simple event with equally likely outcomes using the formula: probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes; express the result as a fraction in its simplest form; apply to rolling dice, drawing from bags, and other simple chance situations
e: Calculate the probability of drawing a blue marble from a bag of 3 blue and 7 red as 3/10
Use the formula P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes to solve at least three different problems
Explain why increasing the number of favourable outcomes increases the probability
topics.p: If there are 3 red and 7 blue balls in a bag, can {{name}} work out the probability of picking a red one and express it as a fraction in its simplest form?

topics.ds: Understand that when all possible outcomes of a trial are listed, their probabilities must add up to 1; use this to find the probability of an event NOT happening: P(not A) = 1 − P(A); apply this shortcut to avoid counting all unfavourable outcomes directly
e: List all outcomes of spinning a 4-colour spinner and verify their probabilities add up to 1
Calculate P(not rolling a 3) as 1 − 1/6 = 5/6 using the complement rule
Spot an error in a probability table where the values don't sum to 1 and explain what's wrong
topics.p: If the probability of it raining tomorrow is 0.3, can {{name}} work out the probability of it NOT raining — and explain why all probabilities in a situation must add up to 1?

topics.ds: Understand probability as a measure expressed as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain); place events on the probability scale; express probabilities as fractions, decimals, and percentages
e: Place events on a number line from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), expressing positions as fractions or decimals
Explain that a probability of 0.5 means 'even chance' and connect this to the informal word 'likely'
Convert between informal language ('very unlikely') and a numerical position on the 0-to-1 scale
topics.p: Can {{name}} write the same probability as a fraction, a decimal, and a percentage — for example, knowing that an even chance is ½, 0.5, and 50%?

topics.ds: Understand and apply the rule that probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes sum to one; use this to find the probability of a complementary event (P(not A) = 1 − P(A))
e: Verify that probabilities of all outcomes listed for a spinner sum to 1
Calculate the probability of NOT rolling a 6 as 1 − 1/6 = 5/6
Identify an error in a probability distribution where the values do not sum to 1
topics.p: If a spinner has three sections and one has a probability of 0.4 and another has 0.35, can {{name}} work out the probability of landing on the third section without being told?

topics.ds: Record, describe, and analyse the frequency of outcomes from probability experiments to develop an understanding of relative frequency as an estimate of probability
e: Conduct a coin-toss experiment, record results in a frequency table, and calculate relative frequencies
Compare experimental results with theoretical probability and explain discrepancies
Predict that relative frequency approaches theoretical probability as the number of trials increases
topics.p: If {{name}} rolls a die 60 times and records the results, can they compare how often each number came up with what they'd expect in theory — and explain why they might not match perfectly?

topics.ds: Run chance simulations with an increasing number of trials using digital tools (spreadsheet random functions or online simulators), repeating each run size several times, and explain that relative frequencies tend to stabilise near the expected proportion as the number of trials grows, even though any single longer run need not be closer than a shorter one
e: Simulate runs of 10, 100 and 1000 dice rolls with a spreadsheet random-number function, repeating each run size 5 times, and record the proportion of 6s in every run
Plot the proportions for each run size and show that the 10-roll results spread widely while the 1000-roll results cluster near 1/6
Explain that results tend to settle near the expected 1/6 as trials increase, but a particular 1000-roll run can still be further from 1/6 than a lucky 10-roll run
topics.p: If {{name}} uses a computer to 'roll a dice' 10 times, then 1000 times, and repeats each a few times, can they notice that the 1000-roll results bunch more closely around one-sixth sixes — while knowing any single run can still be a bit off?

topics.ds: Understand probability as a measure on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain); use the language of probability including likely, unlikely, certain, and impossible
e: Place everyday events on a 0-to-1 probability scale with justification
Explain why a fair six-sided die gives each number a probability of 1/6
Distinguish between equally likely outcomes (fair coin) and unequally likely outcomes (biased spinner)
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain that probability goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), place events on that scale as numbers, and tell you whether a game is fair or not?

topics.ds: Develop a probability model (a list of all the outcomes of a chance process with a probability for each, adding to 1) and use it to find probabilities of events: a uniform model gives every outcome the same probability (e.g. selecting a student at random from a class); a non-uniform model uses probabilities estimated from the observed frequencies of a chance process (e.g. how a tossed paper cup lands); compare a model's probabilities with observed frequencies and, when they disagree, explain whether the difference is plausibly chance variation or a sign that the model does not fit (e.g. a biased die or unequal spinner sections)
e: Use a uniform model to find that a randomly chosen student from a class of 25 with 12 girls is Jane with probability 1/25 and is a girl with probability 12/25
Toss a paper cup 50 times (e.g. 31 on its side, 13 open end up, 6 open end down), write a model with probabilities 0.62, 0.26 and 0.12, and explain why the three outcomes are not equally likely
Compare 600 rolls of a die that showed 160 sixes with the 100 sixes a fair-die model predicts, and argue that a difference this large suggests the die is biased rather than just chance
topics.p: If {{name}} flips a paper cup 50 times and records whether it lands on its side, open end up or open end down, could they turn the results into a probability for each way of landing — and say whether the three are equally likely?

topics.ds: Enumerate sets and their unions and intersections systematically using tables, grids, and Venn diagrams to organise and count outcomes
e: List the elements in the union and intersection of two sets using a Venn diagram
Use a two-way table to enumerate all possible outcomes of two combined events
Shade regions of a Venn diagram to represent A ∪ B, A ∩ B, and A′ (complement)
topics.p: Can {{name}} use a table or Venn diagram to systematically list all the possible outcomes of two events — like rolling two dice — and use it to count favourable outcomes?

topics.ds: Design and use a simulation to estimate the probability of a compound event: choose a random device (coins, dice, spinners, counters drawn with replacement, random-digit tables, or calculator or software random numbers) and a mapping whose probabilities match the situation; define one complete trial (what is generated and when the trial stops) and the event being counted; run many trials; and estimate the probability as the event's relative frequency. Explain why the model fits (each simulated outcome has the same probability as the real one, and successive outcomes are independent when the real ones are), and why different runs give different estimates that become more consistent as the number of trials grows; where a theoretical value can be found (e.g. with a tree diagram), compare it with the estimate
e: Map random digits 0–3 to 'type A' and 4–9 to 'not type A' to model donors who are type A with probability 40%, and explain why the mapping fits (4 of the 10 equally likely digits)

Define one trial as reading digits until the first 0–3 appears, count it as a success if at least four digits were needed, run 50 trials and report the relative frequency as the estimated probability that at least four donors are needed
Explain why two groups who each ran 50 trials estimated 0.18 and 0.26, and why pooling their trials (or running 500) gives a more reliable estimate
topics.p: If 40% of blood donors are type A, could {{name}} use random numbers or a spinner to act out lots of donor queues, estimate how often at least four donors are needed before the first type A — and explain why doing it again gives a slightly different answer?

topics.ds: Generate theoretical sample spaces for single and combined events using listing, tables, and tree diagrams, and calculate theoretical probabilities as the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes
e: List all 36 outcomes when rolling two dice and find P(total = 7)
Draw a tree diagram for two successive events and multiply along branches for combined probabilities
Calculate the probability of a combined event using a sample space diagram and simplify the fraction
topics.p: Can {{name}} draw a tree diagram to map out all possible outcomes of a two-step probability situation — like flipping a coin and then rolling a die — and calculate the probability of any particular combination?

topics.ds: Construct and interpret Venn diagrams with two or three sets to organise and count outcomes; use systematic listing and the product rule for counting to enumerate all possible outcomes of combined events
e: Draw a two-circle Venn diagram to sort 30 students by whether they like football, like cricket, or like both
Shade the intersection A ∩ B and the union A ∪ B on a Venn diagram and explain what each region represents
Use a completed Venn diagram to calculate P(A), P(B), P(A ∩ B), and P(A ∪ B)
topics.p: If {{name}} surveys a class about which sports they play and draws a Venn diagram to show the results, can they use it to find out how many students play both sports — and calculate the probability of picking one of those students at random?

topics.ds: Represent ratio and proportion problems using bar models (rectangular strips divided into equal parts labelled with quantities) and tape diagrams (segmented strips showing part-to-part and part-to-whole relationships); use these visual models to set up and solve unequal sharing, scaling, and percentage problems — drawing the diagram first, then reading off the answer
e: Draw a bar model to represent a ratio problem — e.g. sharing £20 in the ratio 3:2 by drawing 5 equal blocks
Use a bar model to solve a proportion problem and explain each step
Compare bar models with other representations (tables, double number lines) and explain when each is most useful
topics.p: If {{name}} needs to share 30 stickers between two friends in a 2:3 ratio, can they draw a bar model — splitting a strip into 5 equal boxes — and use it to work out each share without just guessing?

topics.ds: Know and use the vocabulary of ratio and proportion — ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, unequal, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole, and out of — and understand the difference between ratio (comparing parts to parts) and proportion (comparing a part to the whole)
e: Explain the difference between a 'ratio' and a 'proportion' using a concrete example like mixing paint
Use 'per cent' correctly and convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages in context
Define 'scale factor' and use it to describe how a shape has been enlarged or reduced
topics.p: If {{name}} is sharing something 3 ways and 2 ways, can they explain the difference between a ratio (like 3:2) and a proportion (like 3 out of 5) — showing they know what each word means?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving the calculation of percentages of amounts (e.g. 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison
e: Calculate 15% of 360 by finding 10% and 5% and combining
Compare two discounts given as percentages of different original prices
Explain a strategy for finding any percentage of an amount using known percentage facts
topics.p: If a jumper originally costs £40 and is 15% off, can {{name}} work out how much the discount is and what the sale price would be?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving the relative sizes of two quantities where missing values can be found by using integer multiplication and division facts
e: If the ratio of red to blue beads is 3:5 and there are 15 blue beads, find the number of red beads
Use multiplication facts to find the missing value: 'For every 2 apples there are 5 oranges; if there are 20 oranges, how many apples?'
Explain the multiplicative relationship between two quantities in a ratio context
topics.p: If a recipe uses 3 eggs for every 200g of flour, can {{name}} work out how many eggs would be needed for 600g of flour?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known or can be found
e: Find the missing side of a similar rectangle given a scale factor of 3
Determine the scale factor between two similar triangles from given side lengths
Use a scale factor to enlarge or reduce a shape and verify that all sides are in the same ratio
topics.p: If {{name}} has a scale drawing where 1 cm represents 5 m, and a room measures 3.5 cm on the plan, can they work out the real length of the room?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving unequal sharing and grouping using knowledge of fractions and multiples
e: Share 40 sweets between two children in the ratio 3:5
Solve: 'Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam gets three times as many as Jo. If there are 30 altogether, how many does each get?'
Use fraction knowledge to explain why sharing in ratio 2:3 means one person gets 2/5 of the total
topics.p: If three friends share a bag of 24 sweets so that one person gets twice as many as each of the others, can {{name}} work out how many each person receives?

topics.ds: Use compound units such as speed (distance ÷ time), unit pricing (cost ÷ quantity), and density (mass ÷ volume); solve problems involving compound units
e: Calculate average speed given distance and time, converting between km/h and m/s if needed
Compare unit prices of two products sold in different quantities to find the better deal
Use the density formula to find mass, volume, or density given the other two values
topics.p: If a car travels 150 miles in 2.5 hours, can {{name}} work out its average speed — and use the same idea to solve problems about price per kilogram or density of a material?

topics.ds: Divide a given quantity into two parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express the division as a fraction of the whole
e: Share £60 between two people in the ratio 2:3 by finding the value of one part
Express the result of sharing 24 sweets as 10 and 14 in ratio form as 5:7
Solve problems involving three-part ratios (e.g. divide 180 in the ratio 1:2:3)
topics.p: If £60 is shared between two people in the ratio 2:3, can {{name}} work out how much each person gets?

topics.ds: Express one quantity as a fraction of another where the result may be less than 1 or greater than 1, and interpret the meaning in context
e: Express 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours (= 3/8)
Express a larger quantity as a fraction of a smaller one and explain why the result exceeds 1
Simplify the resulting fraction and interpret its meaning in the original context
topics.p: If there are 15 boys and 20 girls in a class, can {{name}} express the number of boys as a fraction of the whole class and say whether that fraction is less than or greater than a half?

topics.ds: Define percentage as 'number of parts per hundred'; interpret percentages and percentage changes as a fraction or a decimal; express one quantity as a percentage of another; compare quantities using percentages; work with percentages greater than 100%
e: Convert fluently between percentages, fractions, and decimals
Express one quantity as a percentage of another
Calculate percentage increases and decreases and interpret percentages greater than 100%
topics.p: If a shop says a TV is 130% of its original price, does {{name}} understand what that means — and can they work out the new price from the original?

topics.ds: Know and use advanced vocabulary of multiplicative reasoning — direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor — accurately in problem-solving contexts
e: Distinguish between 'direct proportion' and 'inverse proportion' with real-world examples
Use 'rate', 'speed', and 'density' correctly and explain what units they are measured in
Calculate using compound measures — e.g. work out the speed of a car that travels 120 miles in 2 hours
topics.p: If {{name}} is solving a problem about speed or density, can they explain what 'compound unit' means and tell the difference between direct proportion (more of one means more of the other) and inverse proportion (more of one means less of the other)?

topics.ds: Represent proportional relationships using double number lines (two parallel number lines aligned at 0) and ratio tables; recognise that equivalent ratios generate straight lines through the origin when graphed
e: Plot pairs of proportional values on a coordinate grid and draw the straight line through the origin
Explain why a directly proportional relationship always passes through (0,0)
Read a proportion graph to find an unknown value — e.g. 'If 3 kg costs £6, how much does 5 kg cost?'
topics.p: If {{name}} is comparing the cost of buying different numbers of cinema tickets, can they sketch a proportion graph — a straight line through zero — and use it to read off the cost of any number of tickets without recalculating each time?

topics.ds: Use ratio notation to describe the relationship between two or more quantities, simplify ratios to their simplest form, and convert between ratio and fraction representations
e: Write a ratio from a word problem and simplify it (e.g. 12:8 = 3:2)
Convert a ratio to equivalent fractions of a whole (e.g. 3:2 means 3/5 and 2/5)
Simplify ratios involving decimals or fractions by finding a common multiplier
topics.p: If a smoothie recipe uses orange juice and mango juice in the ratio 3:2, can {{name}} simplify that ratio, express it as a fraction, and work out how much of each is needed for a given total amount?

topics.ds: Use a scale, given as a ratio (e.g. 1:50), as a statement such as '1 cm represents 2 m', or as a scale factor, to work out actual lengths from a scale drawing or map and drawing lengths from actual lengths; reproduce a scale drawing at a different scale by finding each new drawing length, either through the actual length or from the ratio of the two scales; and solve map, room-plan and design problems with consistent units, converting between mm, cm, m and km before or after scaling. Areas from scale drawings and the area factor are developed in the follow-on topic Area from scale drawings
e: On a 1:50 room plan, find that a 9 cm wall is 450 cm = 4.5 m long, and that a 1.2 m doorway should be drawn 2.4 cm wide
Redraw a 1:50 plan at 1:100 by halving every drawing length (the 9 cm wall becomes 4.5 cm), and check one length by converting it back to the actual 4.5 m
Find the real distance between two towns 6.5 cm apart on a 1:25,000 map and give it in kilometres (162,500 cm = 1.625 km)
topics.p: If {{name}} looks at a house plan where 1 cm stands for 50 cm, could they work out how long a 9 cm wall really is — and redraw the plan half the size to fit a smaller sheet of paper?

topics.ds: Convert freely between related standard units of measurement (time, length, area, volume/capacity, mass) using decimal notation to up to three decimal places where appropriate
e: Convert between area units such as cm² and m² using the square of the linear scale factor
Perform multi-step conversions (e.g. convert 2.5 hours to seconds via minutes)
Convert volume units such as cm³ to litres and explain the relationship
topics.p: Can {{name}} convert between units confidently — for example, changing kilometres to metres, kilograms to grams, or hours and minutes to just minutes — including multi-step problems?

topics.ds: Find actual areas from a scale drawing or map, either by converting each drawing length to an actual length before multiplying or by using the area factor; explain why, when every length is multiplied by a scale factor k, areas are multiplied by k² (both dimensions are scaled), and avoid the mistake of applying the length factor to an area; convert between square units consistently (e.g. 1 m² = 10,000 cm²); and apply this to map, room-plan and design problems such as flooring, turf, paint or land area
e: Find the actual floor area of a room drawn 6 cm × 4 cm on a 1:50 plan by converting to 3 m × 2 m (6 m²), and check it with the area factor 50² = 2,500 (24 cm² × 2,500 = 60,000 cm² = 6 m²)
Show by drawing that enlarging a 2 cm × 1 cm rectangle by scale factor 3 gives a 6 cm × 3 cm rectangle containing 9 copies of the original, so the area factor is 3² = 9, not 3
Find the real area of a park shown as 8 cm² on a 1:10,000 map (8 × 10,000² cm² = 80,000 m²), giving the answer in square metres
topics.p: If a room is drawn 6 cm by 4 cm on a plan where 1 cm stands for 50 cm, could {{name}} work out how much carpet the real room needs — and explain why a room twice as long and twice as wide would need four times as much carpet, not twice as much?

topics.ds: Solve problems involving percentage increase, percentage decrease, finding the original value after a percentage change, and calculating simple interest
e: Calculate a 15% increase on £240 using a decimal multiplier (× 1.15)
Find the original price before a 20% discount resulted in a sale price of £64
Calculate simple interest on £500 at 3% per annum for 4 years
topics.p: If a bike originally costs £250 and its price goes up by 8%, can {{name}} work out the new price — and if a savings account earns 3% simple interest per year, how much interest would £500 earn in 4 years?

topics.ds: Recognise and solve problems involving direct proportion (as one quantity increases, the other increases at a constant rate) and inverse proportion (as one increases, the other decreases), including graphical and algebraic representations
e: Identify whether a real-world relationship is direct or inverse proportion and justify the choice
Set up and solve a direct-proportion equation (e.g. if 4 pens cost £6, find the cost of 10)
Sketch graphs showing direct proportion (straight line through origin) and inverse proportion (curve)
topics.p: Does {{name}} understand the difference between quantities that grow together at the same rate (direct proportion) and ones where one goes up as the other goes down — like more workers meaning fewer days to finish a job (inverse proportion)?

topics.ds: Understand that a multiplicative relationship between two quantities can be expressed as a ratio; use ratio notation; simplify ratios
e: Explain why 'for every 2 red beads there are 5 blue beads' can be written as 2:5 or as 2/5 of the blue count
Identify the multiplicative relationship in a table of values (e.g. y is always 3 times x)
Connect the ratio a:b to the fraction a/b and to the linear function y = (a/b)x
topics.p: Can {{name}} explain why a ratio like 3:4 is really the same as the fraction ¾ — and show how that relationship connects to a straight-line graph through the origin?

edges: Understanding a/b as a parts of size 1/b is prerequisite to understanding a/b as sum of 1/b
Odd/even is about whether a number can be divided into 2 equal groups
Even numbers connect to counting in 2s
Factor/multiple knowledge is prerequisite to solving problems with them
Square/cube number knowledge is prerequisite to solving problems with them
Reading a clock requires recognising numerals 1–12
Understanding 'half past' benefits from the concept of halves
GB route: Year 1 experience of hours, minutes and seconds as units of time supports reading o'clock and half-past times; soft because this node is GB-only
Counting a collection in equal groups uses skip counting
Seeing equal groups as repeated addition supports quantifying collections
Bundling into tens draws on knowing a ten is ten ones
Recognising small groups instantly speeds up counting collections in groups
Finding common denominators requires simplification/common multiples skills
Mixed number operations benefit from mixed/improper conversion
Unlike-denominator add/sub extends Y5 add/sub with related denominators
Congruence criteria are exactly the sets of conditions that determine a unique triangle, and explaining why SSA fails uses the two-triangle case
Determining congruence requires constructing triangles from given conditions
Triangle congruence criteria require standard labelling conventions
Formal short multiplication extends Y3 written multiplication
Written multiplication requires fluent table facts
Number line representation skills support placing numbers as lengths
Number line representations support addition/subtraction within 100
GB route: Year 6 similar-shape and scale-factor problems are the groundwork for scale drawings; soft because this node is GB-only
Scale diagrams and maps require 'scale factor' as a precisely defined term
Scale diagrams use proportional relationships that can be represented on double number lines
Redrawing a plan at a new scale needs line segments measured and drawn accurately
Map and plan problems require converting between mm, cm, m and km to keep units consistent (e.g. 162,500 cm = 1.625 km)
US route: interpreting multiplication as scaling (enlarging or reducing) underpins applying a scale factor; soft because this node is US-only
Scales such as 1:50 and 1:25,000 are ratios, and moving between drawing and actual lengths (or between two scales) uses ratio notation and simplification
Sharing on screen builds on equal sharing with real objects
Seeing equal groups as repeated addition supports grouping tasks
Counting through zero is prerequisite to interpreting negative numbers in context
Understanding fraction as division supports reasoning about quotients
Whole ÷ unit-fraction uses inverse relationship with fraction multiplication
Understanding unit-fraction ÷ whole helps contrast with whole ÷ unit-fraction
Rearranging a² + b² = c² to find a shorter side uses formula rearrangement
Pythagoras requires understanding triangle angle sums and properties
Cross-subject: interpreting categorical data by asking/answering questions relies on the English skill of asking relevant questions to seek information
Interpreting data requires having data organised and represented first
Enumerating sets for probability requires understanding that all outcomes sum to 1
Counting objects requires choosing appropriate tools (cubes, ten frames)
Unknown angle problems exercise constructing chains of reasoning
Age 8-9 constructing arguments is prerequisite to age 9-10 level
Comparing fractions with different denominators requires constructing logical arguments
Critiquing others' mathematical reasoning and explaining errors applies the universal error-analysis habit to peer arguments
Age 7-8 repeated reasoning builds on age 6-7
Skip counting patterns exercise generalising from repetition
Multiplication table patterns exercise repeated reasoning
Scale factor problems often involve computing scaled lengths/perimeters/areas
Scale factor problems for similar shapes can be represented as ratio bar models
Similar shapes and scale requires 'scale', 'equivalent', and 'proportion' as defined terms
Scale factor problems are a specific application of ratio/proportion
Similarity requires understanding shape properties — equal angles, proportional sides
Y6 unit conversion with decimals extends Y5 metric conversion
Modelling shapes by building/drawing requires knowing their attributes (sides, vertices)
Knowing 60 min = 1 hour and 24 hours = 1 day extends from measuring time in hours/minutes/seconds
Y4 unit conversion feeds into time-specific conversions
Elapsed time problems are prerequisite to time conversion problems
Fluent recall of facts to 20 builds from strategic calculation within 20
Deriving facts to 100 benefits from place value understanding
The complement rule P(not A) = 1 − P(A) requires understanding probability as a number that lies between 0 and 1
Using the complement rule is easier once students can calculate basic probabilities and see that favourable + unfavourable outcomes cover all possibilities
Solving missing-number problems benefits from knowing the inverse relationship
Finding unknowns in equations requires understanding what = means
Checking requires multiplying and dividing by multiples of powers of 10
Checking decimal products requires multiplying decimals
Rearranging formulae uses the same inverse-operation techniques as solving equations
Rearranging formulae requires fluent substitution to verify results
Rearranging formulae to change the subject is an application of inverse operations to algebraic expressions
Cross-subject: communicating with mathematical precision at ages 10-11 benefits from understanding formal vs informal vocabulary register
Y6 precision extends Y5 mathematical vocabulary
Circle vocabulary (radius, diameter, circumference) is key Y6 precision content
Angle definition builds on understanding right angles
Angle definition builds on classifying acute/obtuse angles
Miles↔km conversion extends Y5 imperial/metric approximation
Money word problems require fluent addition/subtraction within 100
Rearranging to y = mx + c form uses formula rearrangement skills
Plotting linear graphs requires understanding what y = mx + c represents
Area models connect multiplication to visual representations
Age 7-8 quantitative reasoning is prerequisite to age 8-9 level
Decimal equivalents exercise fluency between fraction and decimal representations
Fraction addition supports solving fraction problems
Finding fractions of discrete sets is prerequisite to harder fraction-of-quantity problems
Line plots with half/quarter inch are prerequisite to 1/8-inch line plots
Fraction addition/subtraction supports solving problems from line plot data
Knowing that a triangle's angles add to 180° explains why three angles must sum to 180°; soft because this GB topic is not in the US route, where the angle sum is used informally until 8.G.5
Testing whether conditions give one, many or no triangles is done by attempting the SSS, SAS and ASA constructions with ruler, protractor, compasses or software
Conditions are stated with triangle notation (AB, angle A), and explaining 'included' versus 'non-included' angles relies on it
Knowing time unit relationships supports duration calculations
Calculating event durations requires reading time to the minute
Calculating decimal equivalents requires understanding fraction as division
Extends Y5 percentage/decimal equivalents to broader range of fractions
Recalling equivalences between fractions, decimals, and percentages requires all three sets of vocabulary
Builds on Y5 understanding of percentages
Understanding fraction as division builds on fraction × whole number (inverse reasoning)
Division leading to fractions connects to long division skills
Measuring capacity with units requires first being able to compare capacities
Extends telling time to include a.m./p.m. and 24-hour notation
Measuring and drawing angles with a protractor requires knowing how to mark and label angles using standard notation
Naming straight and reflex angles supports measuring them in degrees
Using a protractor requires understanding degree measurement
Decimal equivalents of 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 support percentage equivalence problems
Must understand % concept before solving % problems
Writing/interpreting expressions requires understanding grouping symbols
Distinguishing a sample from its population requires first identifying the population and attribute a statistical question is about
Random selection is defined as giving every member an equal chance of being chosen, which requires understanding equally likely outcomes
Estimating money totals requires reading and calculating in dollars and cents
Checking money calculations uses estimation by rounding
Y4 estimate/compare/calculate measures is prerequisite to word problems with fractions/decimals
Decimal notation supports measurement problems with decimals
Unit conversion supports measurement word problems
Writing 3:20 p.m. as 15:20 and 07:05 as 7:05 a.m. relies on knowing which times are before and after midday
Reading a Roman-numeral face uses the same five-minute positions and hand-reading skills as an ordinary clock face
Direct and inverse proportion require 'direct proportion' and 'inverse proportion' as precisely understood contrasting terms
Direct and inverse proportion with graphical representations requires reading and plotting proportion graphs (y = kx through origin)
Proportion problems require dividing quantities in given ratios
